  • v0.28 (14 November 2026)

Changelog == v0.29 (22 November 2026) ————————

Upgrading from 0.28. No name is removed in this release (0.28 deprecated none). The names deprecated in this release (see Deprecated) still work, with a FutureWarning or DeprecationWarning naming the replacement, and are removed in v0.30.

Added.

  • Accelerated life tests: what user tests found missing. A parametric regression’s mean_cb(Z) bounds the mean life (an accelerated life model’s MTTF at a stress) by the delta method on its log, or by the parametric bootstrap; method="lr" refuses, naming quantile_cb. An accelerated life model has activation_energy() (Arrhenius, Eyring and their inverses: E_a in eV with its interval, beside E_a / k_B in kelvin), which its printout now reports; common_shape_test(), the likelihood-ratio test of one shape at every stress level against a shape for each (levels with fewer than two failures left out, with a warning); and plot_life_stress(p=...), a life (median, a B-life or the mean) against stress with its bounds and the test levels and data marked.

  • Copulas of more than two lifetimes: Gaussian and Student-t. Gaussian.fit and StudentT.fit take data with any number of axes D of two or more (they refused three). With more than two the copula has a correlation matrix: structure="unstructured" (the default; a correlation per pair of series, rho_i_j) or "exchangeable" (one rho), searched in coordinates that keep the matrix positive definite, with the Student-t’s nu. The model is a CopulaModel whose points are (x_1, ..., x_D) rows: sf, cdf, pdf, random, correlation, conditional_cdf(x, of, given) (one series given others), matrices of kendall_tau, spearman_rho and tail_dependence, covariance, standard_errors, param_cb, cb on the joint survival and CDF, aic/bic and to_dict. from_params takes the pairs’ correlations or a correlation matrix. Each series of a row keeps its own right, left or interval censoring: the likelihood of a row with one or two censored series is in closed form and with three a deterministic integral accurate to about 1e-9. Refused, saying what to do: rows with four or more censored series, and truncation, for more than two series. With two series nothing changes. See “More than two lifetimes” in Multivariate Modelling with SurPyval.

  • Vine copulas: a bivariate family per pair of series. surpyval.multivariate.Vine builds the copula of two or more series from the bivariate copulas, a pair-copula per pair arranged in trees: Vine.fit(x, margins=..., structure="d" | "c", families=, order=, truncate=, candidates=). By default the order is the path (or the roots) of strongest absolute Kendall’s tau and each pair-copula’s family is chosen by AIC among the built-in families and rotations, tree by tree; those estimates start a maximum likelihood fit of every parameter (how="IFM" or "MLE"). The model has pdf, random (the inverse Rosenblatt transform), edges (each pair-copula’s family, parameters and Kendall’s tau), aic, standard errors, param_cb, to_dict and fit_from_df; Vine.from_params builds one. With two series it is the bivariate copula. Refused, saying what to use: censored and truncated rows (the Gaussian and Student-t copulas take censored rows), the joint sf, cdf and cb (estimate them from draws), kendall_tau_cb and spearman_rho_cb (a vine’s measures are a matrix, one per pair: bound a pair’s parameter with param_cb), and conditional distributions other than the last series given the others. See “Vines” in Multivariate Modelling with SurPyval.

  • A hazard ratio, ``hr``, on every parametric model. Weibull.from_params([1000, 2], hr=1.5) has 1.5 times the hazard of the Weibull at every age: its survival is the model’s raised to hr. It applies over the offset, limited failure population and zero inflation (a mass f0 at 0 becomes 1 - (1 - f0) ** hr), so the models at hr = 1 - b and hr = b together make the model. Every function follows from the cumulative hazard, precise in both tails; qf and draws go through isf. A Weibull’s and an exponential’s moments, entropy, mean residual life and restricted mean stay in closed form (the Weibull at scale alpha * hr ** (-1 / beta), the exponential at rate hr * lambda); other distributions integrate. hr is known, not a parameter: it is in extras and with_params(..., hr=), kept by rescale_time, printed, pickled, and saved as "hr" under schema 5, which SurPyval 0.28 refuses. With hr = 1 every value and seeded draw is unchanged. Probability models (Bernoulli, Binomial, FixedEventProbability, ExactEventTime) refuse it. fit(..., hr=) fits data with a known hazard ratio (maximum likelihood; never estimated); its Wald and bootstrap bounds and param_cb hold hr fixed, and the likelihood-ratio bounds on a function and the bounds on the mean, mean residual life and restricted mean refuse, saying to use the bootstrap refits. See Hazard Ratio.

  • Joint models: any number of path parameters varying between items, by Laplace’s approximation (``integration=”laplace”``). A grid of 7 values of each varying parameter stops at five (16,807 nodes an item); a sixth was refused. The fits now take integration="laplace": each item’s integral from the integrand’s height at the item’s most likely parameters and its curvature there, q^2 + q + 1 evaluations for q varying parameters (21 for four, 43 for six) and no grid. It is the default beyond five, where "grid" and "pruned" are refused saying so, and an option below; up to five the default is still the full grid, and those fits are unchanged. The fit maximises the approximated likelihood exactly (its gradient follows each item’s most likely parameters as they move, and the standard errors come from differences of that gradient), and the model says integration == "laplace", prints it, saves and restores it. With no marker effect it reproduces the closed form to 1e-8 an item, in six dimensions too. On the recovery study’s pumps (two varying parameters, read monthly) its estimates were within 0.02 standard errors of the full grid’s, and on a fleet with four varying parameters within 0.001, in 9 seconds where the full grid took 555; a recovery study of 200 such fleets covered the truth 89% to 98% of the time on the 139 whose fits had standard errors (the other 61 put the six correlations at the edge of a valid correlation matrix). It is weaker where items have few, noisy readings (0.10 to 0.18 standard errors off with at most five readings a pump, 0.23 to 0.41 with at most three): the fit warns, with the count, when more than 15% of the items have three readings or fewer (the share from a study whose rule was fixed before it ran), saying to use a grid or fewer varying names. It refuses truncated items, saying to use a grid. A Laplace fit predicts on the full grid up to five varying parameters and by Laplace’s approximation beyond. Beyond five the fit also starts from the marker’s own mixed model, settled first, since each item’s own fitted path is too wild to start from; with up to five that start is tried only where the usual one could not be used (“The joint fit could not start”), so no fit that ran before changes. See “Laplace’s approximation” in Joint Models.

  • Joint models: competing failure modes. JointPH fits (WeibullJointPH) take the mode of each failure (a record’s event_type, e with arrays, e_col with a DataFrame). With two or more modes each has a Weibull baseline, hazard coefficients and marker effects of its own ("bearing: alpha", "bearing: beta", "bearing: marker_effect", …), so a reading can warn of one way of failing and not of another, and an item that fails by one mode is no longer at risk of the others. shared=["marker_effect"] (or "beta", or a hazard covariate) gives the modes that parameter in common, and model.likelihood_ratio_test(shared_model) tests the two fits against each other. The model keeps causes, shared and n_events_by_cause, its summary() has a part for each mode, and its sf, cb and predict are of failing by any mode. A failure found at an inspection (left or interval censored) is fitted with its mode. Refused, saying what to do: a failure with no mode, a mode on an item still running, a mode with fewer failures than parameters of its own, JointAFT and how="two-stage". One mode, or no event types, gives the same model as before, bit for bit. A model with modes saves as schema 5. See “More than one way to fail” in Joint Models.

  • Copulas with non-parametric margins have standard errors and bounds. A copula fitted with both margins KaplanMeier on complete data with no tied values (the maximum pseudo-likelihood estimate from the ranks) has covariance(), standard_errors() and param_cb(): the rank-based covariance of Genest, Ghoudi and Rivest (1995), which adds to the copula’s score the change in it from each margin’s ranks being estimated. They raised a ValueError before. Every fitted copula model also has the case bootstrap, method="bootstrap" (with n_boot, 200, and random_state) on covariance, standard_errors, param_cb and cb: the units are resampled, the margins and the copula fitted again, and the bounds are the refits’ percentile intervals. Where the rank-based covariance does not apply (censored, truncated or tied data, a margin that is not KaplanMeier, or one parametric margin with one non-parametric) the default call refuses, says which of these it is and names method="bootstrap"; cb on the joint sf or ff with a non-parametric margin has the bootstrap only. New: kendall_tau_cb() and spearman_rho_cb(), bounds on the two rank correlations the fitted copula implies (the parameter’s bound carried through the measure for a one-parameter family, a delta-method bound on Fisher’s z for the Student-t, or the bootstrap’s). A model’s dictionary says how its covariance was worked out ("covariance_method": "information", "godambe" or "rank"). The warning of a Wald bound that does not exist now names the bootstrap, where it said the copula models had no other bound. Over 500 simulated samples of 100 and of 400 rows (Clayton, Gumbel, Frank) the rank-based 90% intervals covered the true parameter 88.6% to 92.8% of the time and the 95% intervals 93.2% to 96.2%; the bootstrap’s, on 200 censored samples of 100 rows, 92.0% and 96.5% (the parameter) and 85.5% and 96.5% (the joint survival at a point). See “Standard errors and confidence bounds” in Multivariate Modelling with SurPyval.

  • Competing risks: what user tests found missing. FineGrayModel.cb(x, Z, on="cif") bounds a Fine-Gray model’s cumulative incidence (or one minus it, on="sf") by the case bootstrap (n_boot, random_state; clusters resampled whole, strata and weights kept); method="wald" and "lr" refuse, saying why and to use the bootstrap. ParametricCompetingRisks.eliminate(cause, ...) gives the model with failure modes designed out, the causes left keeping their fits (independent causes assumed, as documented), with every function, mean and cb. ParametricCompetingRisks.fit warns, once and with the counts, when a cause has fewer than 10 failures, and FineGray.fit when the cause of interest has fewer than 10 events per coefficient, each saying what to do. The Fine-Gray docs name the cause argument event (they said cause).

  • Test planning: what user tests found missing. demonstration_test_time(reliability, n, failures, mission_time=, shape=) gives each unit’s extended (Weibayes) test length in time, not only in missions: ten units, shape 2, to show 90% over 1000 hours at 90% confidence run 1478 hours each. demonstration_plan takes mission_time to report the test length it finds in time (unit_test_time), and, given n, its refusal now says the test length was searched, the lowest producer’s risk reached, and how many units are enough. mean_ratio_design plans a comparison of two mean lives (exponential, or Weibull with a known common shape) by the exact F test, solving for the power, the events, the units or the detectable ratio; logrank_design’s documentation gives the mean-ratio to hazard-ratio mapping. An AcceleratedTestPlan reports the acceleration factor at each stress and use_test_time, how long the same units would have to run at the use stress for the same precision. The sequential tests print their reject line beside the accept line.

  • The inverse survival function, ``isf``. Every distribution (Weibull.isf(s, alpha, beta)) and every parametric model (model.isf(s)) gives the time at which the survival function is s, scipy’s name for it. It is qf(1 - s) without rounding 1 - s, which qf cannot avoid: below s = 1.1e-16 the quantile is the end of the support, where isf keeps going (isf(sf(t)) gives back t at a survival of 1e-300). It is in closed form for the Weibull, exponential, Rayleigh, both Gumbels, logistic, log-logistic, normal, lognormal, gamma, both betas, uniform and exponentiated Weibull; the others solve log_sf(x) = log(s) (a discrete distribution: the first point with sf(k) <= s). A model’s follows its offset, limited failure population (inf at or below 1 - p) and zero inflation (0 at or above 1 - f0). tests/reference/test_tails.py checks it against 50-digit references from s = 1 to 1e-300.

  • Test planning: one function per comparison design. surpyval.test_planning has logrank_design, cox_design, noninferiority_design, equivalence_design, rmst_design, cure_logrank_design and rate_ratio_design. Each takes the design’s power, size (events, or n with event_probability) and effect, and solves for the one left None: logrank_design(0.5, power=0.8).events is 66, and logrank_design(0.7, n=(200, 200), event_probability=0.3).power is 0.497. The answer is a PowerCalculation, which says what was solved for (solved_for, value) beside the power, events and units, and saves with to_dict(). Giving none or more than one unknown is refused, naming them. New: the power from a number of events, for the log-rank, Cox, non-inferiority and equivalence designs. The numbers are those of the functions they replace, digit for digit. See “Comparing two groups” in Test Planning with SurPyval.

  • Combining, comparing, rescaling and resampling lifetime data. SurpyvalData.concat([a, b, ...]) (also a + b and sum([a, b])) puts the rows of several datasets together, each keeping its counts, weights, event types, states, terminal flags, truncation, attributes, time-varying covariates and readings, sorted as the constructor sorts. Refused, saying what to do: different units, different covariates, ids (or states, or time-varying covariates) on some datasets only, failures without event types beside typed ones, and an item id in more than one dataset (rename the ids first). data == other and data.equals(other, rtol=1e-9) compare two datasets (EventHistoryData too); a dataset is no longer hashable. SurpyvalData.from_dataframe(data.to_dataframe()) is the data again with no column arguments: the names to_dataframe writes are recognised, and it records in df.attrs which columns are covariates and attributes, and the unit. data.rescale_time(factor, unit=None) divides every time (x, the truncation, step-schedule edges, reading ages) by factor, as Parametric.rescale_time moves a model, so the fit of the rescaled data is the rescaled fit. data.resample(random_state=None, size=None) draws units with replacement for a bootstrap: a row counted n is n units and an item’s rows move together, each unit drawn counted by the times it was drawn.

  • A plot of the data itself. SurpyvalData.plot_lifetimes(ax=None, sort="end", max_rows=100) (and surpyval.plotting.plot_lifetimes) draws one line for each unit, the swimmer plot lifelines calls plot_lifetimes: late entry where the line starts, a filled mark for a failure, an open triangle for a censored end, a bracket over an interval, finite right truncation bounds, counts labelled, an item’s rows on one line, event types in colour with a legend, and a note of how many lines max_rows left out. It returns the Axes.

  • A notation for writing survival data as you’d describe it. surpyval.utils.notation: O(10) failed at 10, RC(20) still running at 20, LC(3) failed before 3, IC(5, 10) failed between 5 and 10; 3 * O(10) three alike, and obs / Truncation(tl, tr) the window (tl, tr] the unit was observed in (refused when the observation lies outside it). Observations([...]) collects them, prints them as words, and gives xcnt() (one row per observation) or surpyval_data() for any fitter; Observations.parse("3*10, 20+, <3, [5, 10]") reads the same from text (15- for left censored, too).

  • The notation and SurpyvalData convert both ways, and fitters take it as it is. Weibull.fit(Observations.parse("10, 20+")) (every fitter that takes a SurpyvalData, and life_table, fit_bayes, the software reliability models and the PyMC likelihood). SurpyvalData.from_notation(text or observations, **kwargs) and data.to_notation() (times, censoring, counts and truncation; data with covariates, event types, ids, states, weights, readings or attributes is refused, naming to_observations() or to_dict()). Observations.text() writes text that parse reads back as the same observations; text takes a window after a bar ("12 | (2, 50]") and inf. Observations has == (the same observations in order) and a unit, which reaches the data and the model.

  • Event types, covariates, histories and readings in the notation. Every observation takes event_type= and covariates={name: value} (O(10, event_type="bearing", covariates={"temp": 60})), which become the data’s e and named Z, as SurpyvalData.from_items maps ItemLifetime records; observations that do not share the same covariate names are refused, naming what is missing. to_notation() now keeps named covariates and event types. Item(id, *events, covariates=, readings=, time_varying_covariates=) is one unit’s history (Item("P1", O(120), O(310), RC(1000)) / Truncation(0): the end of watching is RC, late entry / Truncation(tl), 3 * O(120) three failures at once, O(800, terminal=True) the event that ended it, a = 1), checked as an ItemHistory. Items([...]) collects histories: surpyval_data() gives the SurpyvalData with i and a, the primary form, and event_history_data() an EventHistoryData while that class remains; the recurrent fitters, and every fitter that takes a SurpyvalData, take an Items as it is. readings={"vibration": {0: 1.2}} become the data’s Measurements (one unnamed {age: value} series is the joint models’ markers), and a StepSchedule or CovariatePath is passed through for the fits to expand. Items.parse("P1: 120, 310, [400, 450], 1000+ | (0, inf]") reads a history per line; covariates, event types, terminal flags and readings stay in Python, and text() leaves them out. data.to_notation() on data with item ids gives the Items (rows as events, terminal flags, event types, fixed covariates, readings, time-varying covariates and the window), with data.to_notation().surpyval_data() == data; what one history cannot say (rows counting several units, covariates changing between a unit’s rows, gaps in watching, weights, states, attributes) is refused, naming to_dict(). SurpyvalData.from_notation takes an Items.

  • Joint models: which varying path parameters are correlated. JointPH(..., random_effects="diagonal") (and JointAFT) fits the varying path parameters as independent between items, and random_effects=[("a", "b"), ("c",)] correlates those in a block with each other and with none outside it. A correlation left out is 0, not estimated: it has no entry in params, summary() or the saved model, and aic() counts the parameters estimated, so structures compare by aic() on the same data. With five varying parameters the full structure has ten correlations, more than most fleets can pin down. The model keeps the structure as random_effects_structure, and its printout and the summary’s heading say it. The default, "full", is the model as before, number for number. A model with another structure saves as schema 5, which SurPyval 0.28 refuses rather than misread. See “Which path parameters are correlated” in Joint Models.

  • Testing effort and change points for the growth models. surpyval.recurrent.EffortClock(model, effort) (also at the top level) runs any intensity model (GoelOkumoto, YamadaDelayedS, InflectionS, MusaOkumoto, CrowAMSAA, Duane, CoxLewis, HPP) on the testing effort spent instead of time, \(\Lambda(t) = \Lambda_0(W(t))\): with GoelOkumoto, the testing-effort model of Yamada, Ohtera and Narihisa (1986). The effort is a table of amounts per period (EffortTable, or (ends, amounts)) or a WeibullEffort curve (WeibullEffort.fit finds it from a table). ChangePoint(model, tau=None) multiplies the model’s rates by a further parameter, ratio, from the time tau on (for GoelOkumoto, Zhao’s 1993 change-point model); tau is given, or estimated by profile likelihood from one system’s failure times, with change_point_cb for its likelihood-ratio bounds and change_point_test for the test of no change by parametric bootstrap (the chi-squared table does not apply). ChangePoint(HPP, tau) is fitted exactly, as HPP is (the failures over the time observed on each side of tau), from exact failure times; counts in periods and right-truncated data are searched. Both return the ParametricRecurrenceModel the models do, with every answer in time (remaining_faults, time_to_intensity, release_time, the bounds), save and load, and can be given to compare_predictions. Refused, each saying what to do: effort that falls, a failure in a period with no effort, a tau with no failures on one side of it, and a fit that only reaches the model’s limit (no growth on the effort clock, or steady failures either side of the change, where ChangePoint(HPP) is the model; the refusal comes alone, without a warning from the search that ran to that limit). A saved model on a clock has the key clock (the model, and the effort or the time of the change), and a dist that SurPyval 0.28 does not know and so refuses. See “When the testing was not steady” in Software Reliability Growth.

  • The Littlewood-Verrall software reliability model. surpyval.recurrent.LittlewoodVerrall (also at the top level) fits one test campaign’s times between failures: each is exponential with a rate that is itself gamma, with shape alpha and rate psi(i) = beta0 + beta1 i (psi="quadratic" for i**2), so reliability grows on average but a fix may make things worse. It is fitted by maximum likelihood on the gaps’ Pareto likelihood, with the end of testing after the last failure as a c=1 row. The fitted LittlewoodVerrallModel gives the distribution of the time to the next failure (next_failure_sf, next_failure_qf, next_failure_mean, refused where alpha <= 1 makes it infinite) and of the rate now (current_rate, current_rate_qf), random, aic(), covariance() and param_cb (a likelihood-ratio bound for alpha, whose upper end can be inf; Wald bounds for all three). Gaps no more scattered than exponential times have no finite alpha: the fit is refused, saying so and what to fit instead. It can be one of the models of compare_predictions. See “When a fix may not help” in Software Reliability Growth.

  • The Rayleigh defect model, for defects by development phase. surpyval.recurrent.RayleighDefects (also at the top level) is a Poisson process with \(\Lambda(t) = K (1 - e^{-t^2 / (2 c^2)})\): the defects found in each phase of a development (reviews, inspections, test stages) rise to a peak and fall. Fitted to the counts of the phases done so far, it predicts the later phases and what is left for the field. phases_to_data(counts, lengths=None) turns a table of counts by phase into the rows fit takes (phase j as [j - 1, j], or the phases’ lengths on the calendar). Counts that have not yet turned down have no finite total and are refused, saying so. And on every fitted Poisson process, expected_events(start, end) and expected_events_cb give the events expected in a stretch of time (a later phase, a further month of testing) with delta-method bounds. See “Before testing starts” in Software Reliability Growth.

  • WAIC and leave-one-out cross-validation for Bayesian fits. model.waic() and model.loo() of a BayesianParametric estimate the expected log predictive density of a new observation, with its standard error and the effective number of parameters, and surpyval.bayes.compare(fits, criterion="loo") (or "waic") ranks fits to the same data by it, with the standard error of each difference from the paired rows. Every row counts through its own likelihood term (censored, interval, truncated) and a count n is n units. Conjugate fits are in closed form; grid and Laplace fits use the grid’s quadrature, with each row’s share of its leave-one-out posterior at the grid’s edge; fits from draws use Pareto-smoothed importance sampling, with each row’s Pareto k. Each warns, counting the rows, where its estimate is unreliable. LogLikelihood.pointwise gives each row’s log-likelihood. Checked against refitting without each unit, closed forms and ArviZ. See “Comparing fits: WAIC and leave-one-out” in Bayesian Fitting with SurPyval.

  • The Jelinski-Moranda software reliability model. surpyval.recurrent.JelinskiMoranda (also at the top level) fits one test campaign’s failure times, or the times between failures (gaps=True), with the end of testing after the last failure as a c=1 row: the software holds a whole number of faults N, each found at the rate phi. The estimate of N is a whole number. The fitted JelinskiMorandaModel gives the faults left (remaining_faults()), the failure rate now (current_rate()), mtbf(), next_failure_sf, profile_likelihood(N), aic() and likelihood-ratio bounds (param_cb, remaining_faults_cb, current_rate_cb, mtbf_cb); an upper bound of inf on N says that the data do not limit the number of faults. Data that show no reliability growth have no finite N; the fit is refused, with the condition (the failures’ mean time against (n + 1) T / (2 n)) and what to fit instead. Wald and bootstrap bounds are refused with the reason. It reproduces the published fit to the Naval Tactical Data System failures (Jelinski and Moranda 1972). See “A whole number of faults” in Software Reliability Growth.

  • A model on another clock. model.rescale_time(factor) gives the model whose survival function is R(factor * t): a life in operating time put on the calendar (factor=0.25 for a unit that runs a quarter of the time), or a life in another unit (factor=24 from hours to days, with unit="days" for the new label; without unit the label is kept). Every parametric distribution of time has it, with an offset, a limited-failure population and zero inflation, and so do MixtureModel and the point masses. It is the fit to the data in the new unit, found without refitting: a time parameter is divided by factor, a rate multiplied by it, the LogNormal’s mu less log(factor), and shapes, lfp_p and f0 are kept; the covariance follows by the delta method (exactly), the data move to the new unit, so the likelihood-ratio, bootstrap and pivotal bounds are a refit’s, and the log-likelihood rises by log(factor) per exact observation. A model without its data keeps its Wald bounds but refuses neg_ll, aic and bic, saying why. The distributions of counts, the Beta (use the Beta4) and a CustomDistribution refuse, saying what to do. See “Rescaling a model’s time” in Conventions.

  • Which model predicts best. surpyval.recurrent.compare_predictions(x, models, start=10) compares models of one system’s failures by their one-step-ahead predictions (Abdel-Ghaly, Chan and Littlewood 1986): at each failure every model is fitted to the failures before it and its distribution of the time to the next is scored at the time that came. The PredictionComparison it returns has each model’s prequential log-likelihood (and likelihood_ratio(a, b), step by step), the u-plot’s and y-plot’s Kolmogorov distances with the direction of the bias (u_plot, y_plot), a summary() table, a verdict in words and plot("u" | "y" | "ratio"). It takes any of the Poisson-process fitters and JelinskiMoranda. A fit refused at some step makes no prediction there: the step is kept with the reason, the likelihoods are compared on the steps every model predicted, and the table counts the failed steps. See “Which model predicts best?” in Software Reliability Growth.

  • The cheapest time to release. release_time(test_cost, fix_cost, field_cost) on a fitted Poisson process (the software reliability growth models and the other intensity models) gives the testing time that minimises the expected total cost of testing, of the faults fixed in testing and of the faults left for the field (Okumoto and Goel 1980): the time at which the intensity has fallen to test_cost / (field_cost - fix_cost). It returns the time, its cost, and the band of times whose cost is within within (1%) of the least; with reliability= and mission= the release also waits for that target, and life= ends the field’s exposure (needed by a model with no finite number of faults). release_time_cb bounds the time by the delta method or a seeded parametric bootstrap (method="bootstrap"). A model whose intensity never falls that far, and costs with field_cost <= fix_cost, are refused with the reason. See “When to release” in Software Reliability Growth.

  • Remaining faults, mission reliability and the testing needed to reach a target, on every fitted Poisson process (ParametricRecurrenceModel: the software reliability growth models, and CrowAMSAA, Duane, CoxLewis and HPP where the question has an answer). remaining_faults(x) is the faults expected to be left after testing to x (refused, with the reason, for a process whose failures go on without limit); time_to_intensity(target) and time_to_reliability(target, x) are the testing times at which the intensity has fallen to a target and at which a mission of length x succeeds with a target probability (refused where the fitted curve never gets there). Each has confidence bounds: remaining_faults_cb, next_failure_sf_cb (the bounds on next_failure_sf, which is the reliability over a mission), time_to_intensity_cb and time_to_reliability_cb (the last two by inverting the bounds on the curve, so an upper bound can be inf). A new guide, Software Reliability Growth, works through the models, the answers and when not to trust them on the Naval Tactical Data System failures.

  • Software reliability growth models. Four non-homogeneous Poisson processes for faults found and removed during testing, in surpyval.recurrent (and at the top level): GoelOkumoto (\(a (1 - e^{-b t})\)), YamadaDelayedS (\(a (1 - (1 + b t) e^{-b t})\)), InflectionS (Ohba’s, \(a (1 - e^{-b t}) / (1 + \psi e^{-b t})\)) and MusaOkumoto (the logarithmic Poisson model, \(\log(1 + \lambda_0 \theta t) / \theta\)). Each fits failure times of one system or several, or the failures counted in each period of testing (c=2 rows of [start, end] with their counts n), by maximum likelihood or least squares, and returns the ParametricRecurrenceModel the other intensity models do: cif, iif, mtbf, their bounds, param_cb, next_failure_sf, trend_test, aic, simulation, saving and loading. Data that show no reliability growth have no maximum-likelihood estimate (the expected number of faults a runs to infinity), and the fit is refused, saying what was seen and to fit HPP or CrowAMSAA instead. InflectionS takes psi down to -1, so a Goel-Okumoto shape (psi = 0) is inside its range.

  • Torch helpers (``surpyval.torch``): the censored and truncated likelihood as a PyTorch loss, for people who train their own networks. targets(data) (or x=, c=, n=, tl=, ...) turns lifetime data, checked as fit checks it, into the tensors of a Targets; constrain(dist, raw) maps a network’s (N, k) outputs into the distribution’s parameters by name, each inside its range; and nll(dist, target, params, reduction="mean") is the exact negative log-likelihood of failures, right, left and interval censoring, left and right truncation and counts, each parameter a scalar or one value per row. NLLLoss(dist) is the same as a torch.nn.Module. For the Weibull, Exponential, LogNormal, Gamma, LogLogistic, Normal, Gumbel, Logistic and Rayleigh distributions (surpyval.torch.SUPPORTED). In double precision the loss equals the distribution’s own likelihood to 1e-10, with a finite gradient wherever it is finite. PyTorch is not a dependency, not even an optional one: import surpyval does not import it, and the helpers ask you to install it when it is absent. There are no training loops or network architectures.

  • Torch helpers: mixtures, survival curves out and a guide. nll(dist, target, params, mixture=logits) (and NLLLoss) is the likelihood of a mixture of K components of one family per row, the model of Deep Survival Machines, for every kind of censoring and truncation: (N, K) logits give the weights, each parameter is (N, K), (K,) or a scalar, and constrain maps a network’s (N, K, k) outputs. In double precision it equals MixtureModel’s likelihood to 1e-10; with one component it is the loss without a mixture. sf(dist, times, params, mixture=None) gives each row’s survival curve as an (N, T) tensor, for score_predictions and the concordance index, and to_surpyval(dist, params, row=i) turns any row into an ordinary SurPyval model (a MixtureModel for a mixture). The new page Torch with SurPyval trains a mixture network and scores it.

  • Joint models: a lag. JointPH(..., lag=200.0) (and JointAFT) makes the hazard at age t follow the marker’s path at max(t - 200, 0): a reading acts that long later. Every link is shifted; before the lag the path is held at its age-0 value (the slope and the area are 0 there). The cumulative hazard is integrated on each side of the lag. The lag is fixed, not estimated; compare lags by aic(). The model keeps lag, shows it in repr and summary(), saves it and predicts with it; lag=0 (the default) is the model as before, number for number. A lag on the value of a path infinite at age 0 is refused. Checked against R’s JM with a lag on the PBC trial. See “A reading that acts later” in Joint Models.

  • Joint models: exposure that fades. JointPH(Weibull, link="cumulative", weight=("exponential", 0.5)) makes the accumulated exposure count for less the older it is (what was accumulated u ago counts exp(-u / 0.5)), and weight=("window", 1.0) counts only the last 1.0 of it. The plain cumulative link counts an hour of exposure ten years ago like one last week. The scale and the width are in the lifetimes’ unit of time and fixed, not estimated; compare them by aic(). A weight needs the cumulative link and is refused without it. The model keeps weight, shows it in repr and summary(), saves it (schema 5, which SurPyval 0.28 and older refuse rather than predict as if all the exposure counted) and predicts with it; with no weight the model is as before, number for number, and a window wider than every age is the plain cumulative link. See “Exposure that fades” in Joint Models.

  • Competing-risks random survival forests. RandomSurvivalForest.fit (and fit_from_df, with e_col) takes the cause of each failure as e, with split and event as for the tree, and grows every tree as a competing-risks tree for every cause in the data. cif(x, Z, event) averages the trees’ leaf incidences, total_cif sums the causes and sf is the all-cause survival. oob_log_likelihood() scores each out-of-bag failure by the ensemble’s sub-density of its own cause (the competing-risks likelihood), and oob_log_likelihood(event=) and feature_importances(event=) restrict the score to one cause’s cause-specific likelihood, so a feature that changes only one cause’s risk shows up for that cause alone. mortality(x, Z, event=) and score(x, Z, c, e=, event=) give a cause’s mortality and its concordance. Forests save and load with their causes; without e nothing changes. See Machine Learning.

  • The level of a degradation process given that the unit has not failed. level_at(t, y0=, t0=, given_survival=True) of a WienerProcessModel or GammaProcessModel is the distribution of the level at t of a unit that has not reached the threshold since t0: what an inspection finds on a unit still working. For a gamma process it is the increase truncated at the threshold; for a Wiener process the normal level less its reflection in the threshold (the method of images), which also leaves out the paths that crossed and came back. It has sf, ff, df, qf (closed form for the gamma process, a bisection for the Wiener process), random, mean and to_dict (with given_survival and threshold), and works with stress as level_at does. A reading at or past the threshold is refused with given_survival=True. The default, given_survival=False, is unchanged: the level of every path. See Degradation Modelling with SurPyval.

  • Shared frailty for repairable systems. frailty="gamma" (or "lognormal") on CrowAMSAA.fit, Duane.fit, CoxLewis.fit and ProportionalIntensityNHPP.fit (and their fit_from_df and fit_from_recurrent_data) gives each unit an unobserved factor on its intensity, for a fleet whose units differ by more than a Poisson process (or their covariates) allows; cluster= names units that share one. The frailty’s variance theta is estimated with the intensity (the gamma frailty by its closed-form marginal likelihood, the log-normal by quadrature), and the fit is a surpyval.recurrent.SharedFrailtyModel: cif / iif / mcf for the population or for a unit of given frailty, with delta-method bounds; Wald and profile-likelihood param_cb; frailty_test(), the likelihood-ratio test of theta = 0 (a 50:50 mixture of 0 and chi-square(1)); frailties(), each cluster’s predicted frailty with an interval; and forecast (also surpyval.forecast, which takes cluster= for it), whose prediction intervals carry the frailty (negative binomial counts for the gamma frailty). Where theta is estimated at 0 the fit warns and is the plain one. It takes delayed entry and observation windows; counts in intervals, right truncation, how="MSE" and fewer than two clusters are refused, saying what to use. Checked against quadrature of each cluster’s frailty integral, R’s MASS::glm.nb and simulated fleets. See Recurrent Event Modelling with SurPyval.

  • Competing-risks survival trees. SurvivalTree.fit (and fit_from_df, with e_col) takes the cause of each failure as e. The tree then chooses cuts that tell the causes apart – split="cause-specific" (the default), the sum over the causes of the squared cause-specific log-rank statistics, or split="gray", Gray’s two-sample statistic for one nominated cause’s cumulative incidence (event=) – fits a competing-risks model in each leaf (the Aalen-Johansen estimate for kind="non-parametric", one Weibull or Exponential per cause otherwise), and predicts each cause’s cumulative incidence at given covariates with cif(x, Z, event), their sum with total_cif and the all-cause sf, ff, Hf, hf and df. A cause with no failure in a leaf has zero incidence there, which print(tree) says. A tree of depth 0 is the plain competing-risks fit; with one cause the cause-specific rule makes the plain log-rank tree’s cuts. Exact and right-censored times with delayed entry are taken; left and interval censoring, right truncation, selection="ctree" and min_split_gain are refused with causes, each saying what to use. Trees save and load with their causes. Without e nothing changes. See Machine Learning.

  • Relative survival: net survival and excess hazards beyond a population’s own rates. Where units have the event for reasons besides the one studied, and the cause of each event is not recorded, surpyval.RelativeSurvival estimates net survival – the survival were the excess hazard the only one – against the hazards of the units’ own population, held in a surpyval.RateTable (rates by attained age, and optionally calendar year and a stratum such as sex; each unit’s age and the calendar advance along its follow-up, and its expected cumulative hazard is integrated exactly across the bands). method="pohar-perme" (the default) is Pohar Perme’s estimator, consistent for net survival whatever the excess hazard depends on; method="ederer2" the Ederer II relative survival ratio. Both give sf, ff, Hf, pointwise bounds (cb, on the log scale by default or the plain one), a table of the estimate at each time and strict-JSON to_dict / from_dict. surpyval.ExcessHazard fits the excess hazard regression of Estève et al. (1990), \(\lambda_P(t) + \lambda_0(t) e^{\beta' Z}\), additive on the hazard scale, by maximum likelihood: a piecewise-constant baseline excess hazard (one interval by default; breaks gives more), excess hazard ratios with Wald bounds and a summary, the net sf, hf, qf and random of a unit, observed_sf for its all-cause survival, and aliasing and “No finite maximum” as the other regressions have them. Both take exact and right-censored times with counts, from arrays or fit_from_df; delayed entry and interval censoring are refused. Checked against hand-worked values, the Nelson-Aalen estimate (no background hazard), an independent likelihood, and simulations in which Pohar Perme recovers net survival where Ederer II does not. Net survival can rise, and exceed 1, where fewer units fail than the population rates expect; it is reported as it is. See Relative Survival.

  • Censored quantile regression. QuantileRegression models the quantiles of the time to an event directly, log Q(tau | Z) = b0(tau) + b(tau)'Z with coefficients of their own at every level, so a covariate’s effect on the B10 life can differ from its effect on the median, with no proportional hazards or accelerated failure time assumption. Right-censored data are fitted by Peng and Huang’s (2008) martingale estimating equations (method="peng-huang", the default) or Portnoy’s (2003) recursively reweighted quantile regression (method="portnoy"), on a grid of levels (step=0.01), as R’s quantreg::crq fits them. The model’s coefficients(tau), taus / intercepts / coefs (the whole process) and summary(tau) give the effects; qf(p, Z) the B-life of each covariate row, and ff, sf, Hf the step distribution its quantiles make (rearranged where two levels cross). Bounds are case bootstrap percentile intervals: bootstrap_ci(tau), summary(tau, n_boot=...), quantile_cb(p, Z, bound=...) and cb(x, Z, on=...). fit_from_df takes columns or a formula; to_dict / from_dict keep the data, so a restored model still bootstraps. Checked against ordinary quantile regression (no censoring), the Kaplan-Meier and Nelson-Aalen quantiles (no covariates) and the true coefficients of simulated data. See “Semi-Parametric — Censored Quantile Regression” in Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

  • How good are dynamic predictions: accuracy at an age, over a window. surpyval.metrics.dynamic_auc, dynamic_brier and dynamic_calibration (also importable from surpyval) score a model’s chance that a unit still running at an age s fails within the next w, made from what was known at s: a joint model’s readings up to s (never those after), a LandmarkCox’s covariates and last readings then, or the age alone for a distribution or a regression fit. At each age of at, among the units at risk then: the AUC (does a unit that failed in the window get a higher chance than one that did not?), the Brier score (the mean squared error of the chances) and a calibration table (each group’s mean chance beside the share that failed, by Kaplan-Meier, with an interval). Units censored inside the window are handled by inverse-probability-of-censoring weights from the units at risk at s (Rizopoulos 2011; Blanche et al. 2015), the same weights as auc_td and brier_score; with no censoring inside the window the numbers are the plain AUC and mean squared error. A dict of models (a joint model against a Weibull of the ages alone, say) is scored on the same units, with standard errors, intervals and paired comparisons (difference, interval, p-value) from score_predictions. cross_validate=k (with random_state) splits the units into k groups and predicts each from the model refitted without it: give the fitters (WeibullJointPH, Weibull, LandmarkCox or a function of the data). The results, DynamicAccuracy and DynamicCalibration, print what they measure in words and the interval level, and write strict JSON (to_dict / from_dict). Checked by hand-worked examples, against the plain window outcomes, and by a calibration study (200 data sets, 30% censored: mean estimates within Monte Carlo error of the true values). See “How good are the predictions” in Joint Models.

  • Likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds for a parametric competing-risks fit to inspection data. A ParametricCompetingRisks model fitted to left- or interval-censored rows (its causes fitted together) now takes method="lr" and method="bootstrap" on a cause’s net sf, ff and Hf (cb(x, event=k, on="sf", method=...)), as a model fitted a cause at a time does; they were refused. The likelihood-ratio bound profiles the joint likelihood over every cause’s parameters (with one cause it is the univariate fit’s bound, to 1e-5); the bootstrap resamples the units with their windows and refits the causes together (n_boot, random_state; refits kept for an integer seed), the bias-corrected percentile interval. In a simulation of failures found at inspections (n = 300, 200 replicates) the 95% likelihood-ratio bounds on each cause’s net survival covered 92.5% to 96%. Both need the fitted data: a model restored with from_dict refuses them, saying to refit or use method="wald".

  • Joint models: four and five path parameters varying between items, and ``integration=``. A joint model averages each item’s likelihood over the path parameters it could have, on a grid of 7 values of each: 49 nodes for two, 343 for three, and until now no more. varying= now takes up to five names (2,401 nodes an item for four, 16,807 for five), for paths whose shape differs item by item in more than three ways; a sixth is refused, saying what to hold common. The fits take integration="grid" (the full grid) or "pruned" (the grid without its lowest-weight nodes, the far corners that hold less than 1e-9 of its weight between them: 80 of the 2,401 and 1,392 of the 16,807; none in up to three dimensions). The default is the full grid, whatever the number of varying parameters – fits with up to three are unchanged to the last digit – and "pruned" is an option. The model keeps the choice as integration, prints it, saves and restores it (a model saved before reads as "grid"), and predicts on the same kind of grid. With a normal integrand (no marker effect) both grids reproduce the closed form in four and five dimensions to 1e-9 an item, and with a marker effect the pruned log-likelihood is within 1e-6 an item of the full grid’s (3e-10 an item on a fleet read often; estimates of a fleet of 60 within 1e-6 of a standard error). A fit with four varying parameters takes minutes, not seconds, on either grid: the saving in nodes is 3% (8% for five), and the search over the spread’s variances and correlations is most of the time. See “How the integral is done” in Joint Models.

  • Joint models: the links compared in one call. Each joint model fitter has compare_links(data, links=None, metric="aic", ...): it fits the fitter’s model (its baseline, path model and varying path parameters) with each of several links to the same data – by default the value, the slope and the cumulative area alone, and the slope and the area each beside the value – and returns a LinkComparison (surpyval.univariate.joint). Its table ranks the links by AIC, AIC_c or BIC (metric), best first, with each link’s k, log-likelihood, criteria, difference from the best (delta), weight (Akaike weights for AIC), maximum and status; likelihood_ratio_tests() tests each nested pair ("value" against "value + slope", …) by twice the gain in log-likelihood; models holds every fit by its link’s name, and best / best_link the best. Links less than 2 apart are no real preference and the simpler is the best (fewer parameters, then the level before the slope before the area), so by AIC a link one effect richer is chosen only where the likelihood-ratio test of that effect rejects it at the 4.55% level. The table also gives, for a link with another nested in it, the likelihood-ratio test against that one (lr_against, lr_p_value) and each row in words (reads_as: “as good: no real preference”, “worse”, “clearly worse”, with what the test says); verdict says the comparison in plain words (“Risk follows how fast the marker is changing. Adding the level does not improve the fit. …”), and to_dict() gives the verdict, table and tests as strict JSON. The value link is fitted first and the other links start from its path estimates, about a third faster than fitting each alone; a fit from that start that is not a verified maximum is made again from its own start, so each candidate is the maximum its own fit finds (on the Mayo PBC trial the table is that of the four links fitted one at a time). In fleets of 300 items simulated under each link (200 each) the comparison picked the true link 93% (value), 92.5% (slope) and 89.5% (area) of the time, against a target of 90% within the Monte Carlo tolerance; under the value link it chose the value with the slope 4.5% and the value with the area 3.5% of the time, against the test’s 4.55% (tests/calibration/test_link_selection_joint.py). The data and options are those of fit; a marker_reference goes to the links that follow the value only. A fit that is not a verified maximum is shown but neither ranked nor tested, and a link that cannot be fitted is listed with the reason, each said in one warning; a warning every fit gives about the data is given once. A Lloyd-Lipow path is compared without the cumulative links, with a warning. See “Comparing the links” in Joint Models.

  • ``CoxPH`` takes every kind of row, and competing risks. CoxPH.fit (and fit_from_df, fit(data)) now accepts left- and interval-censored rows (c = -1, c = 2, or windows [xl, xr]; xl_col / xr_col), right truncation (tr, tr_col) beside left truncation, and the cause of each failure (e, e_col) for the cause-specific model. Exact and right-censored data, with or without delayed entry, keep the partial likelihood with the same numbers as before (with causes, the partial-likelihood CompetingRisksProportionalHazards). Any left- or interval-censored row, or any right truncation, is fitted by the full likelihood with each cause’s baseline a non-parametric maximum-likelihood estimate on the Turnbull intervals, every baseline and every coefficient in one joint fit, returning a CoxNPMLEModel: per-cause coefficients and hazard ratios with profile-likelihood standard errors, likelihood-ratio and bootstrap intervals (param_cb), each cause’s cumulative incidence cif(x, Z, event), the all-cause sf / ff / Hf, approximate bootstrap bounds on the curves (cb), to_dict / from_dict. Failures with no recorded cause are taken with masked="include". Every Cox model now says how it was fitted in estimator ("partial likelihood" or "NPMLE"), as CompetingRisks does. With one cause the new route is IntervalCoxPH (coefficients to 1e-6), with no covariates the non-parametric estimate of CompetingRisks (cumulative incidences to 1e-6) and, with one cause, Turnbull’s (left and right truncation included). Where every row is right truncated, the data say nothing after the largest truncation time: the fit warns, and its curves are nan there. 90% Wald coverage of the coefficients with interval censoring and delayed entry: see Competing Risks Analysis.

  • ``MultivariateSurpyvalData`` for any number of axes, with names. The data of any model with more than one value per row: x, xl, xr and c are N by D and t N by D by 2 for any D of 2 or more, n one count per row. Optional axis names (names=("hours", "landings")) are used in messages ("Series 1 (landings): ...") and in a fitted model’s results; dimension(d) takes a position or a name; to_dict / to_json / from_dict / from_json (and surpyval.from_json) save and load it, names included. The model decides what the columns mean, and each multivariate fitter says how many axes it takes in n_axes (2 for the copulas).

  • Copula fit takes a MultivariateSurpyvalData as x.

  • The two-clock fit’s data is univariate, with a ``SecondaryClock``. A part that wears on a main clock (hours) and a subordinate one (starts, cycles, landings) has one event per unit, on the main clock, with the second clock read at the same moments. WeibullEquivalence.fit (and every Equivalence fitter) takes x, c, n and tl or t on the main clock, as any univariate fit does, plus x2: an array, or the new SecondaryClock(values, tl=None, name=None) with the second clock’s readings at entry (tl) and its name (the model’s name for the clock). The clock has no censoring: c is the unit’s. Shapes that do not line up are refused saying what is off ("tl was given for 12 units but the secondary clock has no entry reading: set SecondaryClock(..., tl=...)"). SecondaryClock saves and loads with to_dict / to_json / from_dict / from_json (and surpyval.from_dict). fit_from_df reads x_col, c_col, n_col, tl_col and x2_col, tl2_col, x2_name. The numbers are those of 0.28’s fit(x1, x2, ...), unchanged.

  • Interval rows in the two-clock fit. A unit found failed at an inspection (c = 2) is taken, with each clock’s reading at both inspections (N x 2 arrays, or xl_col / xr_col and x2l_col / x2r_col): it contributes \(S(x_l + k\,x_{2,l}) - S(x_r + k\,x_{2,r})\), checked against a brute-force maximisation of the written-out likelihood.

  • A fit that takes one clock refuses x2 (and fit_from_df refuses x2_col, x2l_col, x2r_col, tl2_col and x2_name) with a ValueError pointing to the two-clock fits, in place of Python’s TypeError.

  • ``Hypoexponential.fit``. The sum of exponential stages is fitted to data: Hypoexponential.fit(x, c, n, t, ..., stages=m) estimates the m stage rates by maximum likelihood (or how='MPS', 'MSE', 'MOM') with every kind of censoring and truncation, counts, weights, an offset, a limited failure population and zero inflation, with covariance, every bound and the bootstrap, as for any distribution; fit_from_df, fit_from_surpyval_data and fit(data) take stages too. The number of stages is the caller’s choice (stages is required; a fitted model’s dist.fit refits with its own); compare the AIC of fits with different numbers. The rates are reported slowest stage first. Where the data need fewer stages a rate runs to infinity, and the fit warns “No finite maximum”, saying to fit fewer. fit_bayes refuses it, pointing to fit.

  • Joint models: the unit of each link’s effect. A slope’s or an area’s effect is per unit of the marker and per unit of age, so its size means nothing without both. The joint fits take marker_unit= (the unit the readings are in, a label kept as typed, as unit= is for the ages), and readings given as a Measurements with a unit (units="mm/s") supply it themselves; a different marker_unit beside them is refused. The model keeps it as marker_unit (saved by to_dict), and effect_units names what each effect is per – marker_effect per mm/s, slope_effect per (mm/s)/years, cumulative_effect per (mm/s)·years – with "marker unit" or "time unit" standing in for one not given. The printout shows it on an Effect units line. A label only: nothing is converted, and the fit is unchanged.

  • A fast log-posterior and gradient for samplers. surpyval.bayes.likelihood.log_posterior_and_grad(data, dist, priors) returns f(z) -> (value, gradient) at one point of the free parameters’ unconstrained scale: the posterior fit_bayes uses (to rounding), for every distribution and form it takes, every kind of censoring and truncation and every kind of prior, with the data checked and split once rather than on every call. The gradient is by automatic differentiation, and written out by hand for the Weibull, Exponential, Normal, LogNormal and Gamma; a Weibull with 1,000 rows takes about 35 microseconds a call (scripts/bench_log_posterior.py). It is the groundwork for a gradient-based sampler; fit_bayes is unchanged.

  • Each parameter’s range, public. Every fitted model with with_params – the parametric, mixture and Royston-Parmar models, the regressions (parametric, additive hazards, proportional odds, interval-censored Cox), the parametric competing-risks models, the recurrence, renewal and proportional intensity models, the joint frailty model, the Wiener and gamma degradation processes, the panel-data multi-state models – and the copulas gives model.parameter_bounds: one (low, high) pair per entry of the vector with_params takes (the order of covariance_names), None for an unbounded end. A draw inside the ranges is not refused for being out of range, so a parameter can be drawn on the log or logit scale its range calls for instead of found by trial. Joint constraints (a mixture’s weights summing to 1, a Uniform’s a < b, a Royston-Parmar spline that does not fall) are stated in its docstring.

  • Public homes for two names. surpyval.univariate.joint is now a public namespace (DynamicPrediction, JointModel, LinkComparison, the joint fitters and factories), and conditional_gaps – the time to the next failure from a virtual age, drawn from a uniform – is surpyval.recurrent.conditional_gaps. See Deprecation Policy.

Changed.

  • Small traps from user tests. from_params takes a plain number for every one-parameter distribution (Exponential.from_params(1 / 20000), Rayleigh, Poisson, …); a number, or a list of the wrong length, for a distribution with more parameters is refused naming how many it takes and their names (“Weibull takes 2 parameters (alpha, beta); got 1 number”), where it failed with “object of type ‘float’ has no len()”. A fitted model’s distribution names its distribution (every model is a Parametric), and parameter_roles (on the distribution and the model) says what each parameter does: Gamma’s beta is a rate, Weibull’s a shape. A Turnbull estimate’s printout says Curve : Fleming-Harrington on Turnbull's expected counts, not Estimator : Fleming-Harrington, which read as if that were the method. The data line of a printout counts left and interval censored units among the events (“60 units: 24 events (0 exact, 1 left censored, 23 interval censored), 36 right censored”), where interval data read as “0 events”. from_xrd given fractional counts (such as to_xrd’s Turnbull expected counts) still refuses them, now saying they are estimates, not observations, and to fit the original data. fit_best’s warnings point at the caller’s line, and the one for a candidate set aside says in plain words why and what to do; every other warning with a counted stacklevel now points at the first line outside SurPyval too. The competing-risks models’ standard_errors, covariance and phi, used as a value (np.round(model.standard_errors, 4)), raise a TypeError saying to call them, where numpy’s message did not say.

  • One concordance, one Brier score, one AUC. concordance_index now returns a ConcordanceResult, a float (the index, the same number as before) that carries its standard error se, interval ci, pair counts and influence, and takes weighting=, tau=, alpha_ci= and ci_method= (keyword only) for Uno’s C to a horizon. A regression model’s concordance() returns the same, with alpha_ci= and ci_method=. brier_score and auc_td return a TimeScores, the (times, values) pair they always returned, and integrated_brier_score a Score, a float; each carries the standard errors and the ends of the 1 - alpha_ci intervals (se, lower, upper, from alpha_ci=) that score_predictions gives, and says why where there are none (censoring weights from x_train and c_train, or a missing risk score). They work as numbers wherever the old results did (float, arithmetic, comparisons, numpy, json, unpacking times, bs = ...); a ConcordanceResult now prints as its number, and summary() gives the table its printout used to. score_predictions stays the call for several metrics and models and their paired comparisons.

  • ``DegradationAnalysis`` says which failure times are extrapolated, and can censor units still running. A unit short of the threshold at its last reading, whose path crosses only after it, still fails at the extrapolated crossing by default (the pseudo-failure-time method), and now the summary counts these (“Extrapolated Units”) and the model’s extrapolated marks them. New: running="censor" right censors such units at their last reading instead, and censored_units=[...] censors the units named there (units known to be running, or that failed another way short of the threshold); a listed unit whose path reaches the threshold within its readings is refused, and so is a fit left with no failure, naming running="extrapolate". The bootstrap bounds keep the choice; to_dict saves it. Fits with the defaults are unchanged. See “Units still running at the end of the test” in Degradation Modelling with SurPyval.

  • A non-parametric ``mean()``, ``mean_cb()`` and ``mrl(x)`` warn when they stop at the data. With tau left out they are the area under the estimate up to the largest observed time (the restricted mean, as before). Where units are still at risk past that time (the estimate above zero there), the mean life is not determined by the data, and they now say so: the warning gives the largest time, the survival estimate there and the share of probability past it, and names tau (rmst(tau) for the bounds) and a parametric fit. On ten units with seven running at 1500, mean() is 1300 with the estimate at 0.7. The values are unchanged; mean(tau=) and rmst do not warn. Every estimator (Kaplan-Meier, Nelson-Aalen, Fleming-Harrington, Turnbull) behaves alike.

  • SurpyvalData is the form for several rows per unit; EventHistoryData is being phased out. New code builds a SurpyvalData with i (and a), which every recurrent fitter takes, and nothing new depends on EventHistoryData. It keeps working, with no warning in this release; a deprecation, naming the release that removes it, comes once SurpyvalData does everything it does.

  • The notation keeps SurpyvalData’s rules, checked when an observation is built. A count must be a whole number (2.5 * O(10) is refused, pointing to weights w); an infinite time is refused; an interval must lie inside its window (tl <= lower, upper <= tr; before, any overlap was taken, and SurpyvalData then refused the same row); a suspension must be strictly before its window’s right edge; an interval open at one end is one-sided censoring (IC(5, inf) is RC(5)), as SurpyvalData reads it. The printout says “1 unit”.

  • ``SurpyvalData.to_observations()`` carries weights, the unit, attributes and readings, which from_observations now takes (<kind>_weights, <kind>_attributes, m), and refuses data with terminal flags a or time-varying covariates, naming to_dict(), rather than drop them.

  • A mixture’s residual life is drawn to the last bits, about ten times faster. The renewal models’ draws of the life left at an age (conditional_gaps, used by their simulations) inverted a MixtureModel’s quantile function wherever the cumulative hazard to reach was below 20, which loses about eps * exp(H) of the age found (1e-12 to 2e-11 relative at u = 1e-6) and was itself a root search costing some 1.5 ms a draw. A mixture’s draws now take Newton’s steps on its cumulative hazard throughout, from a bound found from its components: the age found is the root to 1e-13 relative (checked against 50-digit references for two- and three-component Weibull and log-normal mixtures, at ages from 0 to the 0.999 quantile and u from 1e-9 to 1 - 1e-9), in about 0.15 ms. Intentional numerical change: seeded simulations with a mixture lifetime change in the last digits. Draws for every other lifetime are unchanged, bit for bit, except below.

  • A residual-life draw from a lifetime whose cumulative hazard levels off below the amount to reach (a limited-failure population) is inf, an event that never comes, where beyond a cumulative hazard of 20 it came back NaN.

  • The slope link refuses paths whose slope is infinite at age 0. JointPH and JointAFT with link="slope" (alone or in a list) refuse a logarithmic path (slope b / t) and a Lloyd-Lipow path (slope b / t^2) when the fitter is built, and the fit refuses a power path a t^b whose average item’s power is below 1, by the readings or by the fitted estimate. The cumulative hazard starts at age 0, where such a slope makes the failure rate infinite for every item whose slope has the sign of its effect, so a fit could stall at the start or return an effect pushed towards 0 by the quadrature’s nodes rather than by the data. Each refusal says what to use: the links the path can take, or a path whose slope is finite at 0 (LinearPath, QuadraticPath, ExponentialPath). compare_links leaves the slope links out for a logarithmic path, with one warning naming them, and refuses a Lloyd-Lipow path, which can now take only the value, saying there is nothing to compare. The Lloyd-Lipow path’s refusal of the cumulative link no longer suggests the slope.

  • ``Hypoexponential`` takes equal and close rates. Rates no longer have to be distinct: equal rates are the Erlang, and match Gamma with an integer shape to 1e-12. Where the partial-fraction coefficients are large (their absolute values summing to more than 100), the functions come from the matrix exponential of the stages’ generator, computed from non-negative terms only, so they keep their precision: four rates 1e-5 apart gave twice the density and a CDF 18% off at x = 2, where every function is now within 1e-12 of a 150-digit reference. Rates whose coefficients are small give the same numbers as before. moment is a sum of positive terms (moment(2, 0.5, 1.5, 3.0) is 13.555555555555555, the last digit of 122/9 now right).

  • Penalised fits on five more models. Ridge, lasso and elastic-net fits with the objective, standardisation and refusals of the other penalised fits (no covariance, standard errors, bounds or p-values; aic and bic count the effective degrees of freedom; the penalty is saved by to_dict):

    • FineGray.fit_penalised: the subdistribution hazards model, the objective of R’s fastcmprsk::fastCrrp; matches glmnet’s Cox fit on rows carrying the censoring weights to 1e-6 (the PBC data), with strata.

    • AdditiveHazards.fit_penalised: Lin and Ying’s model, its quadratic loss in place of a likelihood (Gorst-Rasmussen and Scheike 2012, R’s ahaz::ahazpen for the lasso); the penalty is put on the coefficients (rates) in the unit of the mean follow-up (model.time_scale), so the fit does not depend on the unit of time. Matches glmnet on the equivalent least-squares problem to 1e-6, and the ridge fit’s closed form. No likelihood, so no aic or bic; penalty_path gives its coefficients and refuses to choose (PenaltyPath.likelihood).

    • ProportionalOdds.fit_penalised: the semi-parametric proportional odds model’s profile likelihood, with delayed entry.

    • Frailty(...).fit_penalised (WeibullFrailty.fit_penalised, …): the parametric shared-frailty models, gamma or log-normal frailty, the frailty variance not penalised; at theta = 0 it is the penalised proportional hazards fit.

    • fit_tvc_penalised and fit_tvc_timeline_penalised of the parametric PH, PO and AFT families: time-varying covariates, N and the standardisation over the subjects, as CoxPH.fit_tvc_penalised, so splitting a subject’s rows does not change the fit. The parametric additive hazards models refuse (a penalty on their rates would depend on the unit of time).

    diagnose() refuses each of these penalised models, as it does a penalised Cox model.

  • Analytic two-stage bounds for accelerated degradation. DegradationModel.cb(x, Z) with method="analytic" (the default) and life_parameter_covariance() now work for a model fitted with stress covariates Z and for a step-stress (acceleration="clock") model fitted with population_method="moments"; both raised NotImplementedError and pointed to the bootstrap. The covariate (ADT) bound applies the generated-regressor correction to the regression life fit, each unit’s pseudo-time variance entering at its own stress; with paths that fit their readings exactly it is life_model.cb’s. The step-stress bound takes the joint least-squares covariance of the clock and every unit’s path, so the pseudo failure times are correlated through the shared clock, and the bound under a stress carries the uncertainty of both the life parameters and gamma; life_parameter_covariance() returns the life parameters followed by gamma. In closed form, with no refitting: a fraction of a second where a 200-resample bootstrap takes about ten. In 100 simulated step-stress tests the analytic standard error of gamma was within 3% of the spread of the estimates. A population_method="reml" step-stress model still refuses the analytic bound (its mixed-model clock’s covariance is not derived) and points to method="bootstrap".

  • An accelerated survival part for the joint models. JointAFT(Weibull, path_model, varying=, link=), ready-made as WeibullJointAFT (a straight line), beside JointPH: the marker speeds up the item’s ageing instead of multiplying its hazard. By age \(t\) an item has used up the effective age \(A(t) = \int_0^t \exp(\gamma' z + \zeta_v (m(s) - r) + \zeta_s m'(s))\, ds\), and its survival is the Weibull’s at that age, so life used at a high reading is not given back when the reading falls (the cumulative-exposure model of step-stress tests, with the reading as the stress). The same data, path models, varying, hazard_covariates / path_covariates, marker_reference, fit / fit_from_df, parameter names, predict and DynamicPrediction; marker_effect is the log of how many times faster an item ages per unit. Links "value" and "slope"; "cumulative" is refused, saying why. Every kind of item (failures, right, left and interval censoring, left and right truncation) is fitted, its likelihood checked against a dense-grid integral to within 1e-5 an item; with a marker that never changes the fit is JointPH’s with every effect divided by beta. The fitted JointModel says which survival part it has in survival ("PH" or "AFT"), its kind, printout and summary headings. See Joint Models.

  • An accelerated joint model saves as schema 5, which SurPyval 0.28 and older refuse with a request to upgrade rather than read it as a proportional hazards model. Every other file keeps its schema; a joint model saved before has no "survival" and loads as proportional hazards.

  • Joint models: the quick two-stage fit, for a first look and for comparison. fit(..., how="two-stage") (and fit_from_df) on any joint fitter, JointPH or JointAFT, fits each item’s path to its readings alone (pulled towards the fleet’s average where it has few readings), then the survival part with each item’s predicted path taken as a known covariate: a fraction of a second, where the joint fit takes seconds to minutes. It is exactly where the joint fit starts its search, now returned as a JointModel of its own with how == "two-stage" and maximum == "not applicable": the same parameters, predictions, predict / DynamicPrediction and accuracy measures. It is approximate, and says so in its printout (the Fit line), its summary() headings and its prediction’s printout and to_dict ("how"): its estimates are biased, its survival part’s standard errors (and its prediction bands) are too small, and its path part has none (nan). It has no likelihood of the whole model, so neg_ll(), log_likelihood, aic(), aic_c(), bic() and compare_links refuse it, pointing to the accuracy measures. A simulation study on the joint model’s fleets (200 a path) found its marker effect within 5% with monthly readings, but its intervals covering the truth 80% to 97% of the time (the joint fit’s 93% to 98%), and 8% low, covering 80.5%, with readings every six months; its spread between items was far off for curved paths. See “A quick first look: the two-stage fit” in Joint Models.

  • A two-stage joint model saves as schema 5, which SurPyval 0.28 and older refuse rather than present it as the joint likelihood’s fit.

  • A joint model with a lag, or with four or five varying path parameters, saves as schema 5, which SurPyval 0.28 and older refuse with a request to upgrade. Before, 0.28 read a lagged model and predicted as if there were no lag, and failed with a KeyError at the first prediction of a model with more than three varying parameters. A joint model with no lag and at most three varying parameters keeps its schema.

  • FineGray, CompetingRisksProportionalHazards and ParametricCompetingRisksRegression refuse left- and interval-censored rows with a message naming what takes them (CoxPH.fit(x, Z, c=c, e=e) with covariates, CompetingRisks or ParametricCompetingRisks without), in place of “Left or interval censoring not implemented with Competing Risks”. pseudo_cif refuses such rows (and two-column x) saying the same.

  • CoxPH.fit no longer refuses left- or interval-censored rows (it fits them by the full likelihood, above), and its fit_from_df’s x_col is optional (give xl_col and xr_col instead).

  • A copula given data with other than two series now raises a ValueError saying it takes exactly two axes (it was a NotImplementedError), and MultivariateSurpyvalData refuses data with one value per row, pointing to SurpyvalData (it was accepted and refused by every model that reads it).

  • The two-clock fit’s fit_from_df names its columns as the univariate fits do (x_col and x2_col, tl_col and tl2_col).

  • Four of diagnose()’s refusals are now worded as permanent, not as checks still to come, and each names what to use instead: a discrete distribution (compare discrete fits by aic() and sf with KaplanMeier.fit), a distribution whose fitter lacks the shared optimiser (its sf beside KaplanMeier.fit, and aic()), a parametric regression with a link other than exp(beta'Z) (refit with PH(dist) or AFT(dist) and diagnose that), and a parametric proportional odds or additive hazards model fitted to left- or interval-censored or right-truncated data (diagnose the PH and AFT fits of the same data, compare by aic()). The last now points to those fits rather than only to likelihood_ratio_test(), which tests whether the covariates matter, not whether their effects stay constant. Each still raises NotImplementedError.

  • Development: more copied code shared. The weighting of the Aalen-Johansen incidence increments by the survival just before each time is one pair of helpers, survival_before and aalen_johansen_iif (which now take one curve per row as well as one curve), read by the non-parametric incidence and its variances, the restricted mean time lost, Gray’s test and the pseudo-observations. The HPP and proportional-intensity HPP likelihoods take their Poisson-count sums from one poisson_count_sums and their right-truncation terms from the NHPP’s log_one_minus_exp. The two degradation bootstraps (the two-stage one and the destructive one) count their refits with one RefitTally. The Cox start-stop fits (plain, weighted and penalised) check their row weights and mark their models through one helper each, and the parametric PH, AH, PO and AFT start-stop fits keep their rows and mark their models through start_stop_rows and mark_tvc_fit. The parametric regression fitters (PH, AFT, PO, additive hazards and accelerated life) share one base class, RegressionFitter (the distribution, the baseline functions each family reads, and the likelihood), and the PH, AFT and PO fitters one fit through LogLinearRegressionFitter. Fitted numbers, printouts, messages and warnings are bit-identical, checked with the refactor snapshot.

  • Development: one set of scales for the non-parametric intervals. The pointwise bounds (bound_type ‘exp’, ‘log’, ‘logit’, ‘arcsine’ and ‘normal’), the bands, sf_diff’s transforms and the non-parametric cumulative incidence’s log(-log) bound all take their transform, its delta-method scale and its inverse from one table. Some bounds and sf_diff statistics move in their last digit or two (within 1e-12 relative), from the order of the arithmetic.

  • Likelihood-ratio bounds are taken exactly onto the region’s boundary. The searches took a point up to 1e-6 of deviance outside the likelihood region, or as far inside, as on its boundary, and the bound was the function’s value there. Each answer is now moved onto the boundary from where its search ended (back onto it where it is outside, along the gradient or along whichever single parameter loses least; then out along the function’s gradient; then along the boundary to where the function is most extreme), so a bound is the function’s value at a point of the region. A Uniform’s bands, which stopped up to 3e-9 inside its region, are its extremes to rounding (checked against the corners of the region, a triangle); a NegativeBinomial’s agree to 3e-14 with the extremes found slice by slice (1e-11 where the extreme is its Poisson limit, approached only as r -> inf), on every platform: the searches stop on the boundary up to 1e-6 along it from the extreme, which left its sf(2) upper bound 2e-12 short on arm64. Its 95% sf(8) lower bound, which was 3e-8 beyond the extreme of that limit, is a point of the region 3e-9 short of it: down that valley 1 - p cannot be resolved in doubles finely enough to go further (one ulp of p there is 1.2e-7 of sf(8), which a step back along the gradient alone lost or not as the platform’s rounding fell: 6e-8 short on x86-64 Linux, 1.2e-7 on arm64). Where the step back onto the boundary would lose an ExpoWeibull’s narrowing valley, the answer is kept as found. Other likelihood-ratio bounds move in their last digits.

  • Faster likelihood-ratio bounds where the region runs down an edge valley. The check that a search’s answer is the extreme stops at the first of its two searches that finds the region going further (the one from the estimate now goes first: the one from beside a slice’s extreme far down a NegativeBinomial’s valley took up to 0.9 s to find nothing); an answer from the probes down the valleys that checks out and is as far out as every point of the region known is taken without the further searches from the estimate and the walks’ tips, which found the same extreme; the walks out to a parameter’s bounds at several levels solve the steps they share once (each level’s bounds are the same to the bit); and the NegativeBinomial’s likelihood evaluates its log-gamma ratios in plain numpy where nothing is traced (18% faster an evaluation, the same to the bit). The conformance registry’s likelihood-ratio sweeps take 58 s rather than 150 s for the NegativeBinomial and 399 s rather than 549 s for the ExpoWeibull (one process, the same machine).

Deprecated.

  • 39 classes at the top level of surpyval that a call returns rather than a user types: base fitters, fitted models, test results and plots.
