They live in their subpackages, for type hints and isinstance: surpyval.univariate.regression (AFTFitter, AalenAdditiveModel, AdditiveHazardsFitter, AdditiveHazardsModel, BuckleyJamesModel, CoefficientPlot, CoxFrailtyFitter, CoxFrailtyModel, CoxMixedEffectsFitter, CoxMixedEffectsModel, CoxNPMLEModel, DistributionalFitter, DistributionalRegressionModel, FrailtyFitter, FrailtyModel, IntervalCoxPHModel, MixtureCureFitter, MixtureCureModel, ParameterSubstitutionFitter, ParametricRegressionModel, ProportionalOddsFitter, ProportionalOddsModel, PseudoRegressionResult, QuantileRegressionModel, SemiParametricRegressionModel, ZeroInflatedFitter, ZeroInflatedModel), surpyval.univariate.nonparametric (IntervalLogRankResult, LogRankResult, MaxComboResult, MaxStatResult, NonParametricPlot, PairwiseLogRankResult, PermutationLogRankResult, TrendLogRankResult), surpyval.univariate.parametric (DiscretizedFitter, LikelihoodContourPlot, RoystonParmarModel) and surpyval.univariate.joint (JointModel). surpyval.<name> gives the same class, with a FutureWarning naming its subpackage, until v0.30; dir(surpyval) and from surpyval import * no longer list them. The distributional, mixture-cure and zero-inflated regressions’ base fitters and models, and PseudoRegressionResult, are newly importable from surpyval.univariate.regression. The base fitters a model is built from by hand (ProportionalHazardsFitter), MixtureModel, and the two-clock fits’ EquivalenceFitter and EquivalenceModel stay at the top level.

  • fit_from_surpyval_data (the parametric distributions) and fit_from_recurrent_data (every recurrent fitter): fit takes the data object itself, Weibull.fit(data) or CrowAMSAA.fit(data), with the same options. Each old name gives the same fit to the last digit, with a FutureWarning saying to call fit(data), and is removed in v0.30.

  • Internal steps that surpyval.univariate.nonparametric and surpyval.utils exposed as public names. From the non-parametric namespace: the lower-case estimators kaplan_meier, nelson_aalen, fleming_harrington and turnbull (use the fitters, KaplanMeier.fit and the rest), greenwood_variance, nelson_aalen_variance and fleming_harrington_variance (the fitters’ cb), rank_adjust, canonical_heuristic, FIT_FUNCS, VAR_FUNCS and PLOTTING_METHODS. From surpyval.utils: coerce_xcnt_x, format_truncation, group_xcnt, xcnt_sort and resolve_cr_censoring, which SurpyvalData runs. Each still works, with a FutureWarning saying what to use, and is removed in v0.30. surpyval.utils keeps round_sig, is_missing_event, missing_events, normalise_unit and same_unit, and surpyval.pymc all of its names.

  • surpyval.metrics.concordance_estimate (and surpyval.concordance_estimate) is concordance_index, which now gives the standard error and interval (alpha_ci= for alpha), and a regression model’s concordance_estimate() is its concordance(). Each gives the same numbers, with a FutureWarning, and is removed in v0.30.

  • The renewal fitters’ fit_from_parameters (GeneralizedRenewal, GeneralizedOneRenewal, ARA and ARI) is from_params, the name every other family uses for a model built from given parameters. The old name gives the same model, with a FutureWarning naming from_params, and is removed in v0.30.

  • The 21 test-planning functions that each solved one design for one unknown: logrank_events, logrank_sample_size, logrank_power, cox_events, cox_sample_size, cox_power, cox_detectable, noninferiority_events, noninferiority_sample_size, noninferiority_power, equivalence_events, equivalence_sample_size, equivalence_power, rmst_sample_size, rmst_power, cure_logrank_sample_size, cure_logrank_events, cure_logrank_power, rate_ratio_power, rate_ratio_detectable and rate_ratio_exposure. Each still works, with a FutureWarning naming the design function call that replaces it (logrank_events(0.5) is logrank_design(0.5, power=0.8).events), and is removed in v0.30. Note that the design functions take power with no default.

  • EquivalenceFitter.fit’s keyword x1 (use x), tl as a pair per unit of both clocks’ entry ages (give tl the main clock’s and SecondaryClock(x2, tl=...) the second’s), and fit_from_df’s x_cols and tl_cols (use x_col and x2_col, tl_col and tl2_col): each warns, gives the same numbers, and is removed in v0.30.

  • Development: REMOVED_IN is "0.30" (for the names deprecated in 0.29, which now pass it) and REMOVED_IN_NEXT "0.31".

Fixed.

  • A joint fit whose likelihood rises without limit along a hazard coefficient says so. A level of a hazard covariate with no failures runs its coefficient off to infinity; the search could stop on the rise and pass the checks of a maximum, depending on the platform, and the fit returned with no warning. The fit now applies Newton’s test along each hazard coefficient’s profile (as the regressions do) and, where the likelihood still rises, warns that no verified maximum was reached, naming the covariate.

  • A Bayesian predictive quantile in the far upper tail is solved to the last digits of the time. The search on the log of the time stopped within 1e-15 of it, which near a time of 1 (a Beta’s upper edge) left the time up to nine doubles out and moved a tail probability of 1e-12 there by up to 1e-7 of itself.

  • A joint model’s ``cb`` failed where a path parameter was common to all items (JointPH(Weibull, QuadraticPath, varying=("a", "b")), say): the bound differentiates the prediction through the common parameters’ means in forward mode, for which the path had no rule, and raised NotImplementedError. It now gives the delta-method bound, as for a path whose parameters all vary.

  • The distribution functions keep their digits further into the tails. A Rayleigh’s ff and Hf with a small sigma lost 1e-12 of their value where x**2 went subnormal (now (x / sigma)**2 / 2); a Beta’s log density with a large shape lost 1e-11 to log(1 - x) (now log1p) and 3e-13 to scipy’s betaln (now the cancellation-free form the incomplete beta already used), and its quantile below the smallest normal double 2e-10 at alpha = 1e-3 (so seeded draws of such a Beta move in their last digits); a normal or lognormal hazard between 1 and 100 standard deviations lost up to 1e-13 to a difference of logs (now from erfcx); and the log of a gamma or beta probability within 0.1 of 1 is taken from its complement (it lost up to 2e-13 between 0.9 and 0.999). The tails reference test now holds each function to 1e-12 (from 1e-8), or 64 ulps of its inputs’ sensitivity where that is larger. The discrete distributions at large parameters, and the gamma density at shape 1e3, are not yet within it (errors up to 3e-9): they are listed in it as known failures under #1300.

  • ``SurpyvalData.from_observations`` with ids paired ids with the wrong times where the rows were sorted (any data without covariates or event types): observed=[5, 1], observed_ids=["a", "b"] gave “a” the time 1. The rows now stay in the order of the lists.

  • SurpyvalData.from_dataframe(..., attribute_cols=...) without ids, event types or covariates sorted the rows after reading the attributes, so a row could carry another row’s attributes; the rows now stay in the frame’s order. Slicing data without ids (data[rows]) now keeps the time-varying covariates of the rows kept, renumbered, rather than dropping them.

  • The PyMC helpers’ likelihood (surpyval.pymc.log_likelihood and censored_likelihood) had a NaN gradient for a row whose truncation or interval had a bound so far in a tail that the probability beyond it rounds to 0 (a Weibull tl=1e-170, say), though its value was right; PyMC’s sampler needs the gradient. Such a bound is now taken as its limit, as fit takes it, and the gradient is finite.

  • RenewalModel.with_params refuses a lifetime (or ARI baseline) parameter at or outside its range, and any value that is not finite, naming each and saying to draw inside parameter_bounds. An ARI model took a negative scale or shape without a word and predicted nan.

  • JelinskiMoranda.fit and LittlewoodVerrall.fit given a SurpyvalData (or the notation’s Observations or Items) dropped what they have no place for without a word: the rows of several units were read as one campaign, and covariates, event types, truncation and weights were ignored. Each is now refused, saying what to do (fit each unit on its own, or data.without(...)); data of one unit, or with no units, fits as before. WeibullEffort.fit given event data now refuses it, naming EffortClock.

Documentation.

  • Competing Risks SurPyval Modelling named Gray’s test’s and FineGray’s cause argument cause; it is event. It now says the Fine-Gray baseline (and phi) is at covariates 0 unless fitted with center=True. Regression Modelling with SurPyval says Cox coefficients are named coef_0, … for an array Z (pass a DataFrame, Z_cols or a formula to name them), and maps fit_tvc’s xl, xr and c to R’s start, stop and status.

  • Choosing a Model, a new page linked from the start of the documentation and from the Quickstart: Choosing a Model goes from the data to a model by yes-or-no questions, each with two answers, in three stages (the shape of the problem, how to write each unit’s record, and what is asked), says how the need to extrapolate decides between a parametric and a non-parametric model, and ends with a table of situations and the calls that handle them. The bundled agent skill follows the same questions (.claude/skills/surpyval/references/choosing-a-model.md).

  • The coverage quoted for the bootstrap bounds of limited-failure and zero-inflated models (method="bootstrap") in Parametric SurPyval Modelling is remeasured with the current bootstrap (the old figures predated v0.27’s reading of the bounds at their levels): 90% intervals 88.8% on average, 95% ones 94.0%, at their level for a limited failure population with lfp_p well below 1 and one to three points short for a zero-inflated model and with lfp_p at 1. 500 refits in place of 200 give the same, so the default n_boot stays; the study is scripts/studies/lfp_zi_bootstrap/draws.py. Nothing computed changes.

  • The coverage of the delta-method bounds on state occupation probabilities of ParametricMultiState and ParametricMultiStateRegression (cb) is measured, for common states and for one occupied 1% to 5% of the time (scripts/studies/multistate_occupancy; Multi-State Models gives the figures). At 300 and 1000 units the default bounds hold their level throughout; at 100 units, with 10 to 35 observed moves out of the rare state, those involving it are two to four points short. A logit scale and a bootstrap by parameter draws were measured beside them and neither does better where it matters, so the default (bound_type="exp") stays and nothing computed changes. A cut-down version of the study joins the calibration suite.

v0.28 (14 November 2026)

Highlights.

  • The life at one usage rate. EquivalenceModel.at_usage(rate) turns a life measured on two clocks (hours and starts, say) into an ordinary life model in hours for a unit used at one steady rate, with bounds that carry the uncertainty in the exchange between the clocks. Anything that takes a life model, such as a block of a reliability block diagram, can take it.

  • Pooling rates across sources. surpyval.pooled_rate combines event counts and exposures (or events out of trials) from several sources that really differ, giving the average across them, an honest range for a new source like them, and each source’s estimate pulled towards the others, instead of one over-precise number from adding everything into one pot.

  • Unit labels you can compare. surpyval.utils.normalise_unit and surpyval.utils.same_unit are public, so tools that combine models can check that they are in one unit ("h", "hrs" and "hours" agree).

  • Two wrong numbers fixed. The joint frailty model’s expected count of repeat events far past the terminal ages, and likelihood-ratio bounds where the profile likelihood levels off: those now say the bound is open (infinite) instead of giving a meaningless finite end.

  • Fast Bayesian predictive curves. A Bayesian fit on a grid of tens of thousands of points gives its predictive sf, hf and the rest in microseconds after a table built in under a second, within 1e-6 of the exact sum, so calculators that ask for many values take a second, not minutes.

  • Two old names removed: check_ph (use diagnose()) and AalenAdditive’s coef_penalty (use penalizer).

Upgrading from 0.27.

  • Removed names. Each now raises the error Python would (an AttributeError or a TypeError) naming the replacement and the release (see Removed):

    • check_ph, deprecated in 0.26: the Cox model’s (and every semi-parametric model’s) check_ph() method and proportional_hazards.diagnostics.check_ph. Use model.diagnose(transform=...), whose tables["proportional_hazards"] is the same table, number for number;

    • AalenAdditive’s coef_penalty (argument of fit and fit_from_df, and model attribute), deprecated in 0.27: use penalizer. Models saved with the old key still load.

  • Numbers that change on purpose. Each is described, with the old and new values, under Fixed below:

    • JointFrailtyModel.mcf far past the terminal event’s ages now rises to its limit and stays there (3.6829 on a 60-unit fit, where it was 5.47 at 1e6 times the terminal scale and 1.5e-4 at 1e8 times). At the ages of the data it is unchanged (to 5e-15; 7e-11 for a steep recurrent shape);

    • likelihood-ratio bounds (param_cb(method="lr")) where the profile likelihood levels off below the critical value are now open, -inf or inf with a warning, instead of a spurious finite end (the joint frailty model’s alpha on that fit: (-inf, inf), was (-1.6e31, 9.3e6)). This applies to the joint frailty, shared-frailty, proportional odds and interval-censored Cox models and the parametric regressions. A bound the search cannot settle in 60 steps is nan. Bounds where the profile does reach the critical value are unchanged on every test fit;

    • a likelihood-ratio lower bound at the edge of the parameter space is the edge itself: the joint frailty model’s theta lower bound is 0, where it was 2.2e-308.

  • Warnings you may see. An open likelihood-ratio bound comes with a warning saying which end is open and why.

Added.

  • The unit-label helpers are public: surpyval.utils.normalise_unit (a label as a model stores it) and surpyval.utils.same_unit (whether two labels name the same unit, read with pint, so "h", "hrs" and "hours" agree). Tools that combine models can check they are in one unit. See the Units section of Conventions.

  • EquivalenceModel.at_usage(rate) gives the life of a unit used at one constant rate (the second clock’s units per unit of the first, such as starts per hour) as a plain life model on the first clock, LifeAtUsage: sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf, random(size, random_state=), mean (and mean(tau=)), rmst, cb and quantile_cb, each the model’s *_at_usage at that rate, with bounds that include the uncertainty in k. Tools that take a univariate life (a block of a reliability block diagram) can take it as one. See Equivalent Time Scales.

  • Competing risks with failures found at inspections, without a model. CompetingRisks.fit (and fit_from_df, fit(data)) now takes left- and interval-censored rows (c = -1, c = 2, or windows [xl, xr]) and estimates each cause’s cumulative incidence by the non-parametric maximum-likelihood estimate of Hudgens, Satten and Longini (2001): cif, the all-cause sf / ff / Hf, innermost_intervals, case-bootstrap bounds (cb(..., n_boot=, random_state=)), plot, to_dict. Failures whose cause was not recorded are taken with masked="include". Data with only exact and right-censored rows keep the Aalen-Johansen estimate, with the same numbers as before; the fitted model’s estimator says which was used ("Aalen-Johansen" or "NPMLE"). With exact times the NPMLE is the Aalen-Johansen estimate (to 1e-8), with one cause Turnbull’s. What needs each failure’s time (a cause’s net survival, hf, df, iif, rmtl, set_support, the stacked plot, weights, delayed entry) is refused for such data, saying what to use. See Competing Risks SurPyval Modelling.

  • Gray’s test for failures found at inspections. gray_test now takes left- and interval-censored rows (and masked causes with masked="include"): Gray’s test on data completed by multiple imputation from the pooled non-parametric estimate (refitted to a bootstrap sample for each imputation), combined by Rubin’s rules with Li, Raghunathan and Rubin’s F reference (n_imputations, random_state). On exact and right-censored data it is Gray’s test exactly, as before. Its size with the groups inspected on different schedules was 0.033 at the 5% level (300 replicates). The result is still the named tuple (statistic, df, p_value, cause, groups), now with method, n_imputations, df_denominator and relative_increase as attributes and a to_dict.

  • surpyval.pooled_rate(events, exposure, kind=...) pools event counts from several sources (sites, hospitals, studies, fleets) that may each have their own true rate: the two-stage (hierarchical) gamma-Poisson model for events in a time at risk (kind="rate") and beta-binomial model for events out of a number of trials (kind="probability"). Its PooledRate result gives the population (between-source) distribution as a Gamma or Beta with its parameters, the average across sources with its interval, the range for a new source like these (the predictive interval), each source’s own (Jeffreys) and shrunk estimate with intervals, Pearson’s heterogeneity test with \(I^2\), the one-pot estimate for comparison, update(events, exposure) for a new source’s own data, the assumptions in words, and to_dict / from_dict. method="Bayes" (default: a weak prior, the posterior on a grid) or "MLE" (marginal maximum likelihood with profile-likelihood and parametric-bootstrap intervals). Below min_sources (default 4) it gives no population, with a warning, and shows the sources side by side. See Pooling Rates Across Sources.

  • A Bayesian fit’s predictive curve is fast where its posterior has many points. Each value of the posterior predictive (sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, and through them qf, cs and mrl) was a sum over every point of the posterior, about 37,500 for a grid of two free parameters, so a calculation that asks for many values took minutes (in one application an optimal replacement age took about 40 s and a failure-finding search over 6 minutes on such a fit). A posterior of more than 2,000 points now tabulates its predictive cumulative hazard once, on first use: summed exactly at a few hundred times placed adaptively and read between them by a Hermite cubic in log H against log t with the exact slopes. Every stretch is checked against the full sum at two points; the far tails, and any stretch that cannot be brought within the tolerance (near the points’ own offsets, for example), use the full sum, so nothing is extrapolated. sf, ff and Hf are within 1e-6 of the full sum, relative, and hf and df (the curve’s slope) within 1e-5 (at most 4e-7 and 8e-6 on the posteriors tested: Weibull grids, an exponential of rate 1e-9, offsets, a limited failure population, zero inflation), and the curve is still a proper distribution (df the slope of ff, qf the inverse of ff). On a 37,538-point grid the table takes 0.7 s; then sf and hf at 1,000 times take under a millisecond (2.0 s before), 2,000 single-time calls of each 0.13 s (3.7 s), and an optimal-replacement search 0.07 s (1.2 s). model.predictive_table = False gives the full sum everywhere. See “Many points: a table” in Bayesian Fitting with SurPyval.

Changed.

  • A Bayesian fit of more than 2,000 posterior points gives predictive values from the table above, so they move from the full sum’s by less than 1e-6 relative in sf, ff and Hf and 1e-5 in hf and df. The 12 November rule for the tails (a small ff keeps its digits) holds there to that relative accuracy rather than to a rounding; beyond the tabulated range (failure or survival probabilities below about 1e-10) it is the full sum, as before. Fits of fewer points, the closed forms, mean, random and the credible intervals are unchanged.

Removed.

  • check_ph, deprecated in v0.26: SemiParametricRegressionModel.check_ph (CoxPH and the other semi-parametric models) and surpyval.univariate.regression.proportional_hazards.diagnostics.check_ph. Use model.diagnose(transform=...): its tables["proportional_hazards"] is the table check_ph returned, and diagnostics.zph_table / zph_score_test give it directly. The old names raise an AttributeError that names diagnose().

  • AalenAdditive’s coef_penalty, deprecated in v0.27 (the argument of fit and fit_from_df and the model attribute): use penalizer. The old argument raises a TypeError and the attribute an AttributeError, each naming penalizer. A model saved with the old coef_penalty key still loads.

Fixed.

  • A Bayesian fit’s qf with an offset and a limited failure population, or zero inflation, no longer fails to bracket. For example p of 0.04 with an offset of 20 and a share failing of 0.8 raised ValueError: f(a) and f(b) must have different signs (and so did any array of probabilities containing such a value): the root was sought on the log of time between ends whose values were computed on time itself, and exp(log(t)) is not t to the last bit, so an end that sat on the root could change sign. The ends are taken again on the log scale, and an end with the other end’s sign there is the root to a rounding. With a limited failure population the share that ever fails is now worked out once per fit, not at every qf call.

  • A Bayesian fit’s qf(0) with offsets or zero inflation (a wrong number). Where the posterior points each have their own offset, or the fit is zero-inflated, BayesianParametric.qf(0) returned the posterior median offset (19.76 on one fit), above qf(0.01): a B0 life later than the B1 life. It is now where the predictive life starts: 0 with zero inflation, otherwise the smallest offset across the posterior points. qf never decreases in p, and ff(qf(p)) is p above any mass at 0. qf of any p above 0 is unchanged.

  • The joint frailty model’s mcf far past the terminal event (a wrong number; an intentional numerical change there only). JointFrailtyModel.mcf, the expected count of recurrent events by an age with the terminal event stopping them, went wrong at ages far beyond the terminal event’s: on a 60-unit fit it was 3.682 at 1e4 times its terminal scale, 5.47 at 1e6 times and 1.5e-4 at 1e8 times, for a count whose limit is 3.683. Past the terminal ages every unit has stopped having events, so the count must rise to a limit and stay there. The integral over age was a fixed 64-point rule over [0, x], whose nodes all but missed the ages where events happen once x is far beyond them. It is now integrated over the log of age on panels that do not depend on x, with the frailty average in log space, and stops once the integrand has died away: the count never decreases with age and reaches its limit (3.6829 on that fit, at any age from about 100 times the scale; checked against adaptive quadrature to 1e-10 and by simulation). At the ages of the data the values are unchanged (to 5e-15; 7e-11 for a steep recurrent shape, where the old rule was the less accurate). sf, ff, Hf, hf and df were already right there (now tested against quadrature far out).

  • Likelihood-ratio bounds on a flat profile (a wrong number). The joint frailty model’s param_cb(method="lr") reported a finite bound where the profile likelihood never reaches the critical value: on a 60-unit fit whose profile of alpha levels off at a deviance of 2.96, the 95% interval was (-1.6e31, 9.3e6) and the 99% one (-1.6e31, inf), or on x86-64 Linux (-4e12, inf) and (-inf, 1.6e31) by interpreter, the 99% interval not containing the 95% one; each call took one to twenty minutes. Those ends were where the searches could no longer solve the likelihood, not crossings. The search is the one the shared-frailty, proportional odds and interval-censored Cox models and the parametric regressions use for param_cb(method="lr"). Each side is now first probed two and four Wald half-widths out; where the profile is still below the critical value there, it is walked out (steps growing by 1.6, at most 60) until it reaches the critical value, inside which the bound is searched for as before, or levels off (flat to 1e-6 a step, too little to reach the critical value before the end of the range): that end is open, -inf or inf, with a warning saying so. The alpha interval above is now (-inf, inf) at both levels, in about 2 seconds; a one-sided 95% bound, whose critical value (2.71) is below the plateau, is finite. Every other bound of those models’ test fits is unchanged. A lower bound at the edge of the space is the edge itself: the joint frailty model’s theta lower bound of 2.2e-308 is now 0.

v0.27 (13 November 2026)

Highlights.

  • Multi-state models, surpyval.multistate: units that move between several states (working, degraded, failed; healthy, ill, dead). Non-parametric (MultiState, Aalen-Johansen), Cox (MultiStateProportionalHazards), parametric with either clock (ParametricMultiState, ParametricMultiStateRegression, with clock="reset" for semi-Markov models), and PanelMultiState for states seen only at visits or inspections, with the expected length of stay in each state. See Multi-State Models.

  • Landmark analysis and dynamic prediction, landmark: the chance of the event in the next window for a unit that has lasted to now, given what is known about it now. See Landmark Analysis.

  • One data object for everything, SurpyvalData: beside x, c, n, t and the weights w, it now takes the unit i with several rows per unit, the state s and the state moved into e, the terminal flag a (the event that ended a unit’s history for good), x mixed with xl/xr row by row, and readings over time (Measurements, data.m). The multi-state, recurrent, degradation and joint fits all take it, so CrowAMSAA.fit(data) works as Weibull.fit(data) does.

  • Panel counts: recurrent events seen only as the number found at each inspection (PanelCountMCF, PanelCountRegression).

  • More regression and recurrent models: mixed-effects Cox (CoxMixedEffects) and the log-normal frailty, Cox regression for interval-censored data (IntervalCoxPH), mixture-cure and zero-inflated regression, parametric competing-risks regression, stratified and clustered Fine-Gray, the joint frailty model of repeat events and a terminal event (JointFrailty), Andersen-Gill, Prentice-Williams-Peterson and Wei-Lin-Weissfeld, and equivalent time scales (Equivalence: one life on two clocks, such as hours and starts).

  • Comparing groups and reporting: adjusted survival curves for groups not assigned at random, exposure (person-years) tables, four more tests in the log-rank family, the restricted mean time lost to a cause, and more confidence-interval types for the non-parametric curves.

  • The survival tree and random survival forest are stable, as surpyval.ml (surpyval.beta.ml still imports them, with a warning).

Upgrading from 0.26. No name is removed in this release (0.26 deprecated only check_ph, which goes in 0.28), and the new arguments are all optional. What can look different:

  • Numbers that change on purpose. Each is described, with examples of the old and new values, under Changed or Fixed below:

    • the bootstrap bounds of a fit by rank regression (MPP), MPS, MSE or the method of moments now refit each resample by that method, not by maximum likelihood (a 95% bound on an MPP Weibull shape moved from [0.82, 2.32] to [0.88, 2.70] on ten lifetimes);

    • every bootstrap bound (parametric, regression, non-parametric bootstrap_cb, degradation and Buckley-James) reads its bounds at the levels asked, so it is a little wider and holds its level;

    • zero-inflated fits read a [0, t] interval, and a truncation at 0, as including the units dead on arrival (f0 can be larger);

    • Fine-Gray standard errors are the robust (sandwich) ones by default, as R’s crr reports them; robust=False gives the old ones;

    • a distributional regression’s coefficients on a scale or a location change sign (a positive coefficient now means a shorter life, as in the AFT and PH models); the fitted model and its predictions are the same, and a model saved by 0.26 is converted when it loads;

    • hess_inv of a weighted parametric fit is the inverse Hessian (it held the robust covariance); covariance() is unchanged;

    • penalised Cox on start-stop data counts subjects, not rows, so the same penalizer shrinks the same however the follow-up is split;

    • random of a Bayesian fit gives different lives for the same seed (the distribution of the draws is unchanged);

    • joint models that stopped at a correlation of 1 now reach the maximum;

    • fits, standard errors and bounds that moved, or failed, when the times were written in another unit (the repairable-system models and every other family that takes finite differences) now give the same model in any unit (changes in the sixth or seventh digit in ordinary units);

    • smaller corrections: a penalised fit that stopped short now searches again; clustered standard errors of a distributional regression with rows not in time order; likelihood-ratio bounds on a flattening profile; Aalen’s constant-effects test and its last event time; ProportionalIntensityNHPP’s start on data the item records refuse; Bayesian fits’ tails and upper quantiles; the parametric regressions’ quantiles in closed form (at rounding level); the renewal models’ simulated draws (at rounding level).

  • Warnings you may see. Arguments that, given by position, were silently read as something else now warn with a FutureWarning (see Deprecated); AalenAdditive’s coef_penalty is now penalizer (the old name works, with a warning, until 0.28); and surpyval.beta.ml warns at its import.

  • Saved files. Weighted models, models with coefficient signs and data with states are saved as schema 4, which 0.26 refuses to read rather than misread them. Files saved by 0.26 load in 0.27.

  • Labels. Unit labels are kept exactly as typed ("hrs" stays "hrs", not pint’s "hour").

Added.

  • Landmark analysis and dynamic prediction (van Houwelingen 2007; van Houwelingen and Putter 2011): landmark(life, at, horizon) derives the landmark data of a SurpyvalData – the units still at risk at each landmark L, entered at L, their covariates as known then (the last value at or before L of time-varying covariates and measurements) and their follow-up cut at L + horizon – as another SurpyvalData, stacked over several landmarks with L (and, with interactions=True, each covariate times L) as covariates. LandmarkCox fits a Cox model at one landmark or a supermodel over several (effects polynomial in the landmark, or any basis given; a baseline per landmark or one pooled baseline), with robust standard errors clustered on the unit, and gives the dynamic prediction P(T <= s + w | T > s, Z(s)) (predict, sf/ff/Hf from s, table for landmarks by covariate profiles) with robust bounds (cb, the infinitesimal jackknife over units), the effects at each landmark (beta, beta_cb), summary and to_dict / from_dict. landmark_kaplan_meier gives the survival from a landmark by group. Checked against R dynpred and survival (coxph(... + cluster(id))) to about 1e-10. Guide: Landmark Analysis.

  • Several rows per unit, and the terminal flag a: a unit (i) may have several rows without states, stretches of its own clock in time order (covariate stretches still running at x, or repeated events), and SurpyvalData(..., a=...) (from_dataframe(a_col=...), data.a) marks the event that ended a unit’s history for good. An event row with no a is terminal on its unit’s last row and not before (data.a_inferred marks those rows); a = 1 on a running row, a row after a terminal one and overlapping or out-of-order rows are refused, naming the rows. a is carried by indexing, reshapes, DataFrames and JSON ("schema": 4), shown in the repr and summary() (“units: 2 (1 ended for good, 1 still running)”), and given to a fit with an a argument. Fits of one row per unit, to_xrd and life_table refuse data whose units have several rows, naming fit_tvc or the recurrent models; n_items counts units. Data without a and with one row per unit is unchanged. A repeated id without states, refused before, is now a unit with several rows.

  • x with xl and xr: the three may now be given together (SurpyvalData, SurpyvalData.from_dataframe and every fit_from_df with x_col, xl_col and xr_col), read row by row as an exact time in x or a range in xl and xr, the other blank (None, NaN or pandas’ NA). A range is read by its bounds as a [xl, xr] row is, and a c given must agree with it. A row giving both is left out of every per-row argument, with a warning naming it; a row giving neither is refused. Only x, or only xl and xr, is read as before. See Conventions.

  • Measurements in the data model: Measurements holds readings taken on units over their lives, on their own timeline (one measurement, or several named ones such as vibration and temperature, each with an optional unit label), built from {i: {x: value}}, {name: {i: {x: value}}} or a long DataFrame (Measurements.from_dataframe), and written by to_dataframe and to_dict. SurpyvalData(..., i=..., m=...) and SurpyvalData.from_dataframe(..., m=...) attach them, linked to the rows by the unit ids (a unit with readings but no rows is warned of). data.m and data.markers are one store: data with one unnamed measurement (the joint models’ markers) behaves, prints and saves exactly as before. Indexing and every reshape keep the readings of the units kept; without("m") (or "measurements") leaves them out; with_measurement(name) keeps one, which the joint models then fit; data with several measurements is refused by a fit until one is chosen. Readings are per unit: where a unit has several rows they are kept while any of its rows is, and a fit that takes markers refuses such units rather than hand the readings to each row; reshapes of such data keep the readings by unit. extend_running and update of data with marker readings, which took its records for event histories and failed, now work. See Conventions.

  • States in the data model: SurpyvalData(..., s=...) takes the state each row’s unit was in during the row (from its entry tl to x), with e the state it moved into at x and i the unit, so one unit has a row for each stay. c is read from e where it is left out (a blank e: still in the state), and a c that disagrees with e is refused, naming the rows. Without s every row starts from the one initial state and nothing changes: ordinary survival and competing-risks data are that case. i is the new name of ids, which stays as its other name (one argument, one list). The states are carried by indexing and every reshape, shown in the repr and summary(), read by from_dataframe(s_col=...) and written by to_dataframe, to_dict and to_json (data with states is "schema": 4). Fits that are not multi-state, to_xrd and life_table refuse data in more than one state, naming the multi-state models and data[data.s == state]; data in one state fits exactly as without s. Without c, a row given as a range (xl, xr) takes its flag from its bounds, and e must agree. See Conventions.

  • The multi-state models fit a SurpyvalData: MultiState.fit(data, transitions=tm), and likewise MultiStateProportionalHazards, ParametricMultiState and ParametricMultiStateRegression (which take the data’s covariates with their names), take x, e, s (as state), tl, i, n and the unit from the data, with the same result as from the arrays. Data without s starts every row from the one initial state (the one state of transitions nothing moves into, or "event-free"), so competing-risks data fits as it is. Interval- and left-censored rows, weights, right truncation, time-varying covariates, measurements, masked causes and data without s whose units have several rows are refused, naming the rows or the fix; the terminal flag a is ignored (the transitions say which states absorb). fit also takes s= as another name for state=, and fit_from_df s_col= for state_col= (give one). The panel models (PanelMultiState, PanelMultiStateRegression), whose s is the state seen at a visit, take arrays and refuse a SurpyvalData in words. See Multi-State Models.

  • Recurrent fits from a SurpyvalData: every recurrent model’s fit (HPP, CrowAMSAA, Duane, CoxLewis, NonParametricCounting, the renewal models, the proportional-intensity and recurrent Cox models and the cause-specific models) takes a SurpyvalData with units i: CrowAMSAA.fit(data). Each unit’s rows are read as its history (x its age at each row, c = 1 the end of its record), a row starting (tl) after the previous one ended as a gap (windows), and covariates that change within a unit are fitted by the model’s fit_tvc; the fit is that of the same arrays. A terminal event (a = 1) is fitted as an event followed by the end of the unit’s observation, and the model’s new notes (shown in its repr) say so, and where a was inferred. Every recurrent fit_from_df takes a_col for the same notes. EventHistoryData and handle_xicn are unchanged. The joint frailty model reads a as its terminal event: JointFrailty.fit(data) and JointFrailty.fit_from_df(..., a_col=...) (in place of terminal_col) fit as the arrays with terminal, with a note where a was inferred; PanelCountMCF and PanelCountRegression take arrays of visits and counts and refuse a SurpyvalData in words.

  • Degradation and joint fits from measurements: DegradationAnalysis, WienerProcess and GammaProcess take their readings as a Measurements (fit(m, threshold=...)), or a SurpyvalData holding them as data.m (its covariates Z are each unit’s stress), in place of the arrays x, y and i, and give the arrays’ fit exactly; their fit_from_df also names the readings’ column m_col (y_col is its other name, unchanged). The joint models (WeibullJointPH, JointPH(...)) take a Measurements as markers (or its other name m), matched to the life rows by unit: beside arrays with i=, beside a SurpyvalData without readings, or in fit_from_df(..., i_col=..., m=...). Several measurements are refused until one is chosen with with_measurement(name), now also a method of Measurements. See Degradation Modelling with SurPyval and Joint Models.

  • Panel counts: recurrent events seen only as the number found at each inspection, each unit inspected at its own times (failures found at each check of a machine, new tumours at each clinic visit). PanelCountMCF (also at the top level) estimates the mean cumulative function without assuming a process: the maximum likelihood estimator under a Poisson working model (Wellner and Zhang 2000; the default) or the maximum pseudo-likelihood estimator, the isotonic regression of the cumulative counts (Sun and Kalbfleisch 1995). PanelCountRegression fits the proportional means model E[N(t) | Z] = Lambda0(t) exp(beta'Z) with the baseline unspecified, by the pseudo-likelihood (how="pseudo", the default; R spef’s "MPL", matched on simulated panel counts) or the likelihood (how="MLE", the default of PanelCountMCF; Wellner and Zhang 2007). Where a covariate separates the units that counted events from those that did not, so the coefficient has no finite estimate, the fit says “No finite maximum” and is not converged, by either method. Both are consistent when the counts are not Poisson; mcf_cb, param_cb and standard_errors are bootstraps over units. fit_from_df, to_dict / from_dict, aliased covariates as the other regressions. The parametric intensity models (CrowAMSAA, CoxLewis, ProportionalIntensityNHPP, …) now take a count of 0 on an interval-counted row (c=2 or c=-1), so they fit panel counts too; a 0 on an exact-event or end-of-observation row is still refused.

  • The joint frailty model of recurrent events and a terminal event, JointFrailty (surpyval.recurrent, and at the top level), with JointFrailtyModel: items with repeated events (repairs, readmissions) whose history ends in an event that depends on them (scrapping, death). Each item’s frailty u multiplies its recurrent intensity and, as u ** alpha, its terminal hazard (Liu, Wolfe and Huang 2004; Rondeau et al. 2007); gamma or log-normal frailty, Weibull baselines (the recurrent one the power-law intensity), on the item’s age (time_scale="calendar") or, for the recurrences, the time since the last event ("gap"), with delayed entry (tl) on the calendar scale. The terminal event is given by terminal=1 on the row (c=1) that closes an item’s history. Fitted by maximum marginal likelihood, the frailty integrated out by a trapezoid rule over each item’s integrand, accurate to rounding; theta, alpha, beta, gamma, summary(), Wald and profile-likelihood param_cb, frailty_tests() (no frailty, against an even mixture of chi-square on one and two degrees of freedom; and alpha = 0), each item’s predicted frailty (frailties), cif, iif, mcf (the expected count, the terminal event stopping it) and the terminal event’s sf, ff, hf, Hf and df, for the population or for one item’s frailty, with cif_cb, iif_cb, mcf_cb and sf_cb; random and from_params; to_dict / from_dict. Checked against R frailtypack 3.8.2.

  • Semi-Markov (“clock reset”) parametric multi-state models: ParametricMultiState.fit(..., clock="reset") and ParametricMultiStateRegression.fit(..., clock="reset") (and their fit_from_df), where each transition’s hazard is a function of the time spent in the current state (the time since a repair, a relapse). Each transition is fitted on the durations x - tl. The occupation and transition probabilities come from the renewal equations, solved by convolution on a grid refined until they settle (about 1e-6), with or without recovery (a cycle); cb gives delta-method bounds as on the forward clock. A distribution that does not live on (0, inf), and a prediction from a later start without from_state, are refused with the reason.

  • The expected length of stay in each state for both clocks of the parametric multi-state models: length_of_stay(x, state, ...), length_of_stay_se and length_of_stay_cb (delta method on the logit of the fraction of x - s spent in the state). Checked against R flexsurv (totlos.fs, totlos.simfs).

  • Mixed-effects Cox regression, CoxMixedEffects (R’s coxme): a Cox model whose log hazard has Gaussian random effects, a random intercept per group of one or more grouping factors, nested (wards in hospitals) or crossed (batches and machines), and random slopes, correlated with the intercept or not. Terms are given as groups=, as RandomEffect(groups, slopes=[...]) objects, or in fit_from_df in the bar notation (random_effects="(1 + trt | centre) + (1 | hospital/ward)"). Fitted by maximum likelihood as coxme fits it: the coefficients and random effects maximise the penalised partial likelihood, the variances its Laplace approximation to the integrated partial likelihood. Efron or Breslow ties, counts, late entry and strata as in CoxPH. Reports Wald intervals on the fixed coefficients, variance_components() with profile-likelihood intervals (variance_cb()), the predicted random effects, lr_test() against the Cox model (a boundary-aware chi-square mixture), coxme’s integrated, penalised and null log-likelihoods, and predictions averaged over the random effects (the default, as CoxFrailty), for an observed group, or with the random effects at 0 (marginal=False). Checked against coxme 2.2.22 on the kidney, lung and a nested/crossed/random-slope data set. Guide: Shared Frailty Models.

  • CoxFrailty.fit(..., family="lognormal"): the log-normal shared frailty with a Cox baseline (coxme’s (1 | group)), beside the gamma frailty.

  • Stratified and clustered Fine-Gray regression. FineGray.fit(..., strata=...) gives each stratum its own baseline subdistribution hazard and its own censoring distribution, with shared coefficients (Zhou, Latouche, Rocha and Fine, 2011), or, with strata_censoring="common", one censoring distribution for every stratum (for many small strata); cif/sf then take stratum=. cluster=... keeps the estimates and makes the robust standard errors allow for dependent units within a cluster (Zhou, Fine, Latouche and Labopin, 2012). Both combine with each other and with weights; fit_from_df takes strata_col and cluster_col; to_dict/from_dict keep each stratum’s baseline. Checked against R crrSC 1.1.2 (crrs, crrc) on simulated data, to 1e-7. The diagnostics refuse a fit with strata or clusters, with what to do instead.

  • The restricted mean time lost (RMTL) to a cause of failure: the area under the cause’s cumulative incidence up to a horizon tau, the average time of the first tau lost to that cause. CompetingRisks.rmtl(event, tau) gives it exactly for the step estimate, with a delta-method standard error (with one cause it is tau less KaplanMeier.rmst, with the same standard error) and a normal interval; ParametricCompetingRisks.rmtl(event, tau) from the fitted distributions, with a delta-method interval on the logit of rmtl / tau; and surpyval.rmtl_diff(model_a, model_b, event, tau) compares two groups (difference, its interval and z-test, and the ratio with its interval), as rmst_diff does for survival. Checked against R survival 3.8.12, cmprsk 2.2.12, survRM2 1.0.4 and GFDrmtl 0.1.0.

  • More pointwise confidence-interval types for the non-parametric survival estimates (Kaplan-Meier, Nelson-Aalen, Fleming-Harrington, Turnbull, and the survival of CompetingRisks): cb(bound_type=...) now also takes 'log' (the default of R’s survfit), 'logit', 'arcsine' (arcsine-square-root), 'peto' (Peto’s variance) and 'rothman' (Rothman’s Wilson-type interval), beside 'exp' (log(-log), still the default) and 'normal'. quantile_cb and plot take them too. Checked against R survival 3.8.12 (survfit(conf.type=...)) and km.ci 0.5.6 to rounding.

  • The Cox model for interval-censored data, IntervalCoxPH (model IntervalCoxPHModel): the covariates multiply the hazard, S(x | Z) = S0(x) ** exp(beta'Z), and the baseline is a non-parametric maximum-likelihood estimate with mass only on the Turnbull intervals of the pooled data, fitted jointly with the coefficients (the model of R’s icenReg::ic_sp(model = "ph"), whose coefficients, log-likelihood and curves it matches). Takes exact, right-, left- and interval-censored rows (x as [left, right] pairs), counts and left truncation; fit_from_df reads intervals from xl_col and xr_col. Standard errors from the profile likelihood (Murphy and van der Vaart 2000); param_cb with Wald, profile likelihood-ratio (method="lr") and case-bootstrap (method="bootstrap") intervals, and covariance(method= "bootstrap"). sf, ff, Hf, hf, df, qf, baseline_sf, random, with_params, summary, to_dict / from_dict. cb on the curves, right truncation and diagnose() refuse, saying what to use instead. CoxPH still refuses interval-censored rows. Guide: Interval-Censored Cox Regression.

  • MultiStateProportionalHazards can share a covariate’s effect among some transitions only: shared={"age": [("healthy", "dead"), ("ill", "dead")]} gives age one coefficient on the two transitions into death and its own on the others (several groups are a list of such lists; transitions may also be named "healthy -> dead"). The list form, shared=["age"], still shares it among every transition. A new proportional_baselines option takes transitions whose baseline hazards are proportional: they share one baseline (the first’s) and the log of each other’s ratio to it is one more coefficient ("baseline: ill -> dead vs healthy -> dead"). Both are R mstate’s general expanded design, one stratified Cox model of the stacked data; the predictions’ standard errors carry the shared parameters’ covariance across transitions. Checked against mstate 0.3.3 on the MGUS data and a simulated model with recovery (coefficients, standard errors, log partial likelihood and probtrans’s probabilities and standard errors). For two transitions sharing a baseline, the standard errors use the covariance \(\phi_h \phi_g\) times the baseline’s variance; msfit uses \(\phi_h^2\), which depends on the order of the transitions, so the standard errors differ from mstate’s there (by about 7% to 13% in the checks). Saved models gain the keys shared_groups and baseline_groups when the options are used.

  • Pivotal bounds for probability-plotting fits: cb, quantile_cb and param_cb take method="pivotal" on a model fitted with how="MPP" (rank regression) of the Weibull, LogNormal, LogLogistic, Normal, Logistic, Gumbel, GumbelLEV or Exponential. The fitted line’s error, measured in units of its own slope, has a distribution free of the parameters; it is simulated from n_sim standard samples (9999 by default) of the same size and rank pattern, fitted by the same regression, and inverted for bounds on the parameters, the quantiles (B-lives) and sf / ff / Hf (Lawless 2003, section 5.1; the Monte Carlo pivotal bounds of Abernethy’s New Weibull Handbook). Exact for complete and type II censored samples up to Monte Carlo error: over 1000 samples of 5, 10 and 20, 90% bounds covered 88.2% to 91.9%, where the MLE’s Wald bounds covered 64% to 89% (calibration/test_coverage_pivotal.py). Seeded by random_state; to_dict now records an MPP fit’s plotting options ("mpp_options"), so a model saved with_data=True gives the same bounds. Refused, with what to use instead, for other methods and families, offsets, left- or interval-censored and truncated data. The fits agree exactly with R’s WeibullR, whose pivotal-rr bounds are constructed differently (see Parametric SurPyval Modelling).

  • Parametric.rba(basis="median"): Abernethy’s reduced bias adjustment of a maximum-likelihood fit, the Weibull shape multiplied by C4^3.5 (median-unbiased; basis="mean": C4^6) or the LogNormal or Normal sigma by sqrt(r / (r - 1)) / C4, for r failures; opt-in, returning the adjusted model (bias_adjustment says what was applied). The factors agree with R WeibullR’s rba to 1e-12.

  • Four more tests in the log-rank family, each with a result object, to_dict and a plain-words section in Non-Parametric SurPyval Modelling, checked against R:

    • maxcombo_logrank: the max-combo test of two groups, the largest of several Fleming-Harrington weighted log-rank statistics (by default FH(0, 0), FH(0, 1), FH(1, 0) and FH(1, 1)), with a p-value from their joint normal distribution, so it allows for picking the best weighting; two- or one-sided, each component’s z and the correlation matrix reported; strata, tl and t0 as for logrank. For delayed, fading or crossing effects. Matches R’s nph::logrank.maxtest.

    • trend_logrank: the log-rank test for trend across ordered groups (Tarone), one degree of freedom, with default (1, …, k) or own scores, two- or one-sided, and every option of logrank (weightings, strata, tl, t0, sampling weights). Matches the trend test computed from R’s survdiff.

    • permutation_logrank: the (weighted, stratified) log-rank test with an exact p-value (all relabellings of the units, when there are at most max_exact) or a seeded Monte Carlo one with its standard error. The docs say when it is valid (the same censoring in every group) and when to use logrank instead. Matches R’s coin::logrank_test.

    • maxstat_logrank: the maximally selected log-rank statistic, the cut-point of a continuous covariate that best separates survival, with a p-value corrected for the search (the exact Gauss p-value by default; Lausen’s 1994 bound, Lausen and Schumacher’s 1992 approximation or a permutation p-value on request). The naive p-value at the best cut is reported only to show that it is not valid, and the docs point to regression on the covariate itself. Matches R’s maxstat::maxstat.test.

  • Multi-state models for panel data, PanelMultiState and PanelMultiStateRegression (also at the top level): units whose state is seen only at visits (clinic visits, inspections, survey waves), so that each move happened at an unknown time between two visits. A continuous-time Markov model with a constant intensity for each allowed move, fitted by maximum likelihood from the states seen (the likelihood of R msm: products of \(\exp(Q t)\) over the gaps, by the forward recursion). Data are one row per visit (x, s, i, and fit_from_df with x_col, s_col, i_col); a visit may see a set of states (censored), a death may be timed exactly (exact_entry) and a move may be seen as it happened (obstype="exact"). Covariates act on the log intensities, per transition or shared, and may change between visits; pci lets the intensities change at given times. intensity_matrix, transition_probabilities, occupancy, occupancy_se and cb (delta-method bounds from the exact derivatives of the matrix exponential), mean_sojourn and sojourn_cb, param_cb and summary (Wald bounds, intensity ratios), a fit that warns where an intensity runs to 0 (no finite maximum), and to_dict / from_dict. Checked against R msm 1.9: log-likelihoods to 1e-12, intensities, standard errors and bounds to about 1e-6. Misclassified states (hidden Markov models) are not built. See Multi-State Models.

  • Exposure (person-years) tables, person_years(x, c, n, tl, factors=, timescales=, rates=, per=, alpha_ci=), as R’s survival::pyears: the total time at risk, the events and the units in each cell of fixed factors crossed with time bands that each unit moves through while followed (attained age, calendar period, time since entry: R’s tcut), with each cell’s event rate (per per units of time) and its exact Garwood bounds. rate_ratio(cells, reference) gives the ratio of two cells’ rates with its exact conditional bounds and test (R’s poisson.test); rates= (one rate or a table by some of the dimensions) gives expected events and the observed to expected ratio (standardised incidence or mortality ratio) with exact bounds; margins(by) adds the table up; time outside every band is reported in offtable. The PersonYears result has to_dict / from_dict. Also poisson_rate_bounds(events, exposure), the exact bounds of one rate. Left and interval censored rows are refused with the fix. Checked against pyears and poisson.test on mgus2 (cells exact). Guide: the “Exposure (person-years) tables” section of Non-Parametric SurPyval Modelling.

  • Sample size and power for four designs the plain log-rank calculation does not answer, in surpyval.test_planning: a Cox model’s coefficient for a continuous covariate or one correlated with the others (cox_events, cox_sample_size, cox_power, cox_detectable; Hsieh and Lavori 2000, variance inflated by 1 / (1 - R^2)); non-inferiority and equivalence of a hazard ratio (noninferiority_events, noninferiority_sample_size, noninferiority_power, equivalence_events, equivalence_sample_size, equivalence_power); a difference in restricted mean survival time between two groups with given survival curves, uniform entry, follow-up and dropout, the variance of each Kaplan-Meier RMST computed from the curves (rmst_sample_size, rmst_power); and a log-rank test when some units are cured, from the test’s mean and variance under the two mixture-cure curves (cure_logrank_sample_size, cure_logrank_events, cure_logrank_power). Guide: the section “When the plain log-rank calculation is wrong” in Test Planning with SurPyval.

  • Equivalent time scales, Equivalence(Weibull) (and WeibullEquivalence, LogNormalEquivalence, LogLogisticEquivalence, GammaEquivalence, ExponentialEquivalence): one life measured on two clocks (hours and starts, say) combined into one age x1 + k x2, with k >= 0, what one unit of the second clock is worth on the first, estimated by maximum likelihood together with the distribution on the combined clock. The likelihood is the first clock’s, each failure carrying the clock-rate factor 1 + k * rate (an accelerated failure time model with acceleration 1 + k * rate, Duchesne and Lawless 2000); fitting the distribution to x1 + k x2 without it pulls k towards 0. Takes failures, units still running, left-censored units, counts and late entry (a pair of ages). param_cb("k") (Wald, or the profile likelihood with method="lr"), k_lr_test() (k = 0 on its boundary: half the chi-square p-value), equivalent(x1, x2), the distribution’s functions and cb on the combined clock, and the life along a usage path (sf_at_usage, qf_at_usage for B-lives, cb_at_usage, quantile_cb_at_usage, with bounds that include k’s uncertainty), random, to_dict / from_dict and a plain reading of k in the repr. Guide: Equivalent Time Scales.

  • Parametric multi-state models, ParametricMultiState (a distribution for each transition, Weibull by default, or a different one per transition) and ParametricMultiStateRegression (a parametric regression for each transition, WeibullPH by default, or any of the PH, AFT and other parametric regressions), also at the top level. Each transition is fitted to the spells in its ‘from’ state, the others censored and each spell left truncated at its start (the clock goes forward: a Markov model). transition_probabilities solves the Kolmogorov forward equations by product integration with fourth-order Magnus steps on an adaptive grid, to about 1e-8 per row; occupancy, occupancy_se and cb (delta-method bounds over every transition’s parameters), cumulative_hazard and hazard. The curves are smooth and extend past the data. clock="reset" (semi-Markov) is refused with the reason. Checked against R flexsurv 2.3.2 (pmatrix.fs): the fits’ log-likelihoods agree, and with flexsurv’s parameters the transition probabilities agree to 1e-11; with one transient state the occupation probabilities are ParametricCompetingRisks’ cumulative incidences.

  • Multi-state models, surpyval.multistate (MultiState, MultiStateProportionalHazards and TransitionMatrix also at the top level), for units that move between several states (healthy, ill, dead; working, degraded, failed). TransitionMatrix declares the states and the allowed transitions (with illness_death, competing_risks, progressive and from_matrix). The data are spells, one row per stay in a state (x, e the state entered or missing if censored, state, tl its start, i the unit, n), with to_stacked / from_stacked for R mstate’s layout of one row per possible transition. MultiState is the Aalen-Johansen estimate: transition_probabilities(x, s) (the matrix \(P(s, t)\)), occupancy(x, state, s, from_state), cumulative_hazard, occupancy_se and cb with the Greenwood-type and Aalen-type variances of mstate and the infinitesimal jackknife of survfit, a stacked plot, delayed entry and tied times. MultiStateProportionalHazards is a Cox model of each transition, fitted as one stratified Cox model of the stacked data, with each covariate’s effect per transition or shared by all of them; occupancy and transition_probabilities for given covariates, with standard errors and bounds that include the coefficients’ uncertainty (mstate’s msfit and probtrans), and it warns where the predicted hazards of leaving a state add up to more than 1. Every estimate and variance equals R’s (survival 3.8.12, mstate 0.3.3) to rounding on the MGUS data and a simulated illness-death model with recovery; with one transient state the estimate is CompetingRisks’ cumulative incidence, and with one transition the Kaplan-Meier estimate with Greenwood’s variance. Not yet built: semi-Markov models and states seen only at inspections. datasets.load_mgus2 adds the MGUS data (spells=True gives its illness-death spells). See Multi-State Models.

  • Adjusted survival curves for groups that were not assigned at random (two suppliers on different duty, treated and untreated patients). direct_adjustment(model, group, levels, Z, w, covariates, robust, cluster) takes a fitted regression that has the group among its covariates, predicts every unit’s survival curve with the group set to each level in turn, and averages over the sample (standardisation, or g-computation). It returns AdjustedCurves: sf, ff and cb of a level’s adjusted curve, sf_diff and rmst_diff (the adjusted difference between two levels in survival at a time and in restricted mean survival time, each with a standard error, interval and test), rmst and plot. The variances are built for the parametric regression families (the delta method through the parameters’ covariance) and CoxPH (the baseline’s variance and the coefficients’, as in CoxPH.cb), plus, by default, the spread of the units’ predictions (covariates="sampled"; "fixed" leaves it out for a reference population). The group is a column position, a column name or a formula’s variable (with the DataFrame as Z, so interactions with the group are rebuilt). Any other model with sf(x, Z) gives the curves, and its bounds refuse with what to use; a stratified Cox model is refused. Checked against R: the averaged survfit(coxph, newdata) curves and riskRegression::ate’s risks to 1e-6, and a survreg delta method by hand to 1e-3. weight_diagnostics(w, group, Z, extreme, smd) checks a set of weights brought to a weighted comparison (KaplanMeier.fit(..., w=) with sf_diff and rmst_diff): each group’s effective sample size, its largest weight’s share and the number of extreme weights, the standardised mean difference of each covariate before and after weighting with the ratio of the weighted variances, and flags, plain sentences for anything outside the usual rules. No propensity model is fitted. New guide: Adjusted Survival Curves.

  • Regression for repeat events without a baseline shape: AndersenGill, PrenticeWilliamsPeterson and WeiLinWeissfeld (surpyval.recurrent, and at the top level), the semi-parametric relatives of the proportional-intensity models. Andersen-Gill has one unspecified baseline intensity for every event (the coefficient is a log rate ratio); Prentice-Williams-Peterson has a baseline per event number and puts an item at risk of its k-th event only after its (k - 1)-th, on the item’s age (time_scale="total", the default) or on the time since its last event (time_scale="gap"); Wei-Lin-Weissfeld models the time from the start to each event number marginally. Each is the Cox partial likelihood on its own layout of the rows, fitted by CoxPH (its tie handling, aliasing and check of the maximum; no second likelihood), and each reports the robust (sandwich) covariance with every item a cluster as covariance() and standard_errors(), with the model-based one as naive_covariance() and both in summary(). Fits: fit(x, Z, i, c) and fit_from_df from an event log, where the covariates on a row are those in force up to its time; fit_tvc(i, xl, xr, c, Z) and fit_tvc_from_df from start-stop rows (delayed entry, gaps, covariates that change between events) for the first two; max_events models an item’s first few events only. The model, a RecurrentCoxModel, gives cif(x, Z) (for Andersen-Gill the expected number of events; with stratum the cumulative hazard of that event number), sf for the gap-time and marginal models, plot, diagnose (the Cox fit’s), neg_ll / aic / bic, and to_dict / from_dict; cox is the underlying Cox model. Coefficients, both covariances, the likelihood and the cumulative baseline equal R’s coxph(... + cluster(id)) on the bladder data in the matching layouts (bladder2 for Andersen-Gill and both Prentice-Williams-Peterson forms, bladder for Wei-Lin-Weissfeld). Not offered, each a refusal that says what to use: robust bounds on the curve (cif_cb), simulation, weights, penalised fits, and counted or left-censored rows. See Recurrent Event Regression Analysis (what each model assumes about a repeat event, in words) and Recurrent Event Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

  • The names of the regression families have a public home, surpyval.univariate.regression.kinds: PROPORTIONAL_HAZARD, ACCELERATED_FAILURE_TIME, PROPORTIONAL_ODDS, ADDITIVE_HAZARD, ACCELERATED_LIFE and DISTRIBUTIONAL, the values a fitted parametric regression model’s kind takes, and two groups of them, TIME_SCALING (the covariates rescale time) and HAZARD_BASED (the covariates act on the hazard), so model.kind in kinds.TIME_SCALING replaces a comparison with a string literal. The strings are unchanged.

  • Regressions are fitted on continuously varying covariates: a ramp-stress test, a thermal cycle, a planned mission or dose profile. An item record whose time_varying_covariates are a CovariatePath used to be refused by every fit; now each path is cut into steps and the model fitted to them by its fit_tvc, with the steps halved until no estimate moves by more than 1% of its standard error. The fitted model holds path_steps: the steps in each stretch of a path at the end, the rows fitted, the largest move of an estimate at the last halving (in standard errors), the tolerance and whether it was met; a fit that still moves after eight halvings, or would need more than two million rows, returns its last fit with one warning. Every fitter that takes time-varying covariates from item records does so: proportional hazards, proportional odds, additive hazards, Cox and accelerated failure time (cumulative exposure). The new CovariatePath.to_steps(t_max, steps=8, start=None) gives the steps as a StepSchedule: each stretch between the path’s breakpoints in steps equal steps at the midpoint value, a flat stretch one step, so a flat path is fitted as the constant covariate and a path made of steps exactly as fit_tvc fits those steps. In the fit, the step a failure falls in ends with the path’s value at the failure. On a baseline defined below 0 an item with a path needs its left_truncation. The path must be external (planned, not read from the item): a measured signal belongs in a joint model. See “Fitting on a continuous path” in Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

  • Joint models: what the hazard follows of the marker’s path is a choice, JointPH(Weibull, path_model, link=...). "value" (the default, as before: risk follows the level), "slope" (risk follows how fast the marker is changing, the path’s rate of change) or "cumulative" (risk follows the accumulated exposure, the area under the path from age 0), or a list of them, each with an effect of its own: marker_effect, slope_effect, cumulative_effect. link=["value", "slope"] asks whether, at a given level, a rising marker is at more risk than a steady one. Every part of the joint model works with every link: the data (failures, right, left and interval censoring, truncation), the covariates in each part, any path model, sf, ff, cb, predict, summary and to_dict/from_dict (a model saved before follows the value). With the slope or the area alone the Weibull alpha is that of an item at a slope and an area of 0, and marker_reference is refused; a Lloyd-Lipow path, whose area from age 0 is not finite, is refused for the cumulative link. On the Mayo PBC trial the four models agree with R’s JM to within 0.15 standard errors of every estimate. The degradation path models gain slope(x, *params), the path’s rate of change, and slope_jacobian: analytic for the built-in paths (and through a LinkedPathModel), central differences for a PathModel of one’s own that does not give them. No numbers change: a fit with the default link is the same to the last digit. See “What the hazard follows: the link” in Joint Models.

  • Parametric competing-risks regression: ParametricCompetingRisksRegression (surpyval.univariate.competing_risks, and at the top level). Every cause of failure gets its own parametric regression of its hazard on the covariates (model=WeibullPH by default; any parametric regression fitter, such as ExponentialPH, WeibullAFT, LogNormalAFT or LogLogisticPO, for every cause or one per cause in a {cause: fitter} dict), and the model gives each cause’s cumulative incidence at any covariate row as a smooth curve that carries on past the last observation, which the cause-specific Cox model’s step estimate cannot. The likelihood of cause-specific hazard models factorises over the causes, so each cause is its fitter’s own fit with the other causes’ failures censored, kept in models[cause]; nothing is assumed about how the causes depend on each other. Fits: fit(x, Z, e, c, n, tl, model, init) (right censoring, counts, delayed entry; a DataFrame Z names the coefficients; fit(data) takes a SurpyvalData) and fit_from_df (Z_cols or formula). With Z after the times and paired with them as in every regression: cif(x, Z, event), iif, probability_of_cause(Z, event); hf, Hf, sf, ff and df of the first failure of any cause, or with event=k the cause’s net ones; qf(p, Z) and mean(Z) of the whole unit’s life; random(size, Z, random_state). params, parameter_names ("<cause>: <name>"), covariance() (block-diagonal over the causes), standard_errors() and summary() (the causes’ regression tables stacked); neg_ll, log_likelihood, aic, aic_c and bic of the whole model (BIC’s sample size the failures of any cause). cb(x, Z, event, on, alpha_ci, bound): delta-method Wald bounds on the cumulative incidence (logit scale) and on the all-cause sf, ff and Hf (log cumulative hazard scale); one cause’s net bounds are its own model’s, likelihood-ratio and bootstrap included. to_dict / from_dict keep every prediction, bound and table. Refused, each saying what to use: left- and interval-censored rows (ParametricCompetingRisks, without covariates), weights, likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds on the cumulative incidence and the all-cause functions, diagnose() on the whole model (each cause’s own, models[cause].diagnose()), and a fitter that is not a parametric regression (CompetingRisksProportionalHazards for Cox). Checked against R flexsurv: each cause’s flexsurvreg(dist = "weibullPH") fit and the cumulative incidences of pmatrix.fs on the competing-risks multi-state model, at given covariate rows; its incidences also match the Aalen-Johansen product integral of its own fitted hazards on a fine grid (to 1e-6), and on Weibull data the cause-specific Cox model’s incidences lie inside its 95% bands. It shares the cause-by-cause assembly (the incidence integral, the Aalen-Johansen step, random draws, the block-diagonal covariance, the information-criterion terms and the Wald bounds) with ParametricCompetingRisks and CompetingRisksProportionalHazards in one internal module; no number of either changes. See “Parametric Competing-Risks Regression” in Competing Risks SurPyval Modelling.

  • Zero-inflated regression: ZeroInflated(latency, incidence, covariates, links) and the prebuilt WeibullZeroInflated, LogNormalZeroInflated, LogLogisticZeroInflated, GammaZeroInflated and ExponentialZeroInflated. A share of the units fails at time 0 (dead on arrival), and covariates act both on that share (f0, through a logit, probit or complementary log-log link) and on the life of the units that work (the latency, a distribution with covariates on its parameters, on the scale by default): F(t | z) = f0(z) + (1 - f0(z)) F_u(t | z). It is the zero-inflated fit (zi=True) with covariates, and reduces to it without them. Where every row says whether its unit was dead on arrival, the fit is two stages, a binary regression and the latency’s regression on the units that worked, which is the joint maximum with a block-diagonal covariance; left censoring, an interval starting at 0 or right truncation without late entry couple the parts, and both are fitted together (method="auto", "two-stage" or "joint"; model.fit_route says which). Late entries say nothing about f0. An interval starting at 0 includes the units dead on arrival. ZeroInflatedModel adds doa_probability(Z) and susceptible=True on sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf and mean for the life of a unit that worked, with the family’s fit_from_df (formulas={"f0": ..., "alpha": ...}), fit_penalised, bounds, random, to_dict and from_dict. New guide: Zero-Inflated Regression.

  • Mixture-cure regression: MixtureCure(latency, incidence, covariates, links) and the prebuilt WeibullMixtureCure, LogNormalMixtureCure, LogLogisticMixtureCure, GammaMixtureCure and ExponentialMixtureCure. A fraction of the units never fails (sound parts, cured patients), and covariates act both on the probability of ever failing (the incidence, lfp_p, through a logit, probit or complementary log-log link) and on the life of the units that do fail (the latency, a distribution with covariates on its parameters, on the scale by default as in an AFT model): S(t | z) = 1 - pi(z) + pi(z) S_u(t | z). Both parts are fitted together by maximum likelihood with every censoring, truncation, count and weight; it is the limited-failure fit (lfp=True) with covariates, and reduces to it exactly without them. The model is a member of the distributional regressions and has their fit, fit_from_df (formulas={"lfp_p": ..., "alpha": ...}), fit_penalised, bounds (cb, param_cb, parameter_cb; Wald, likelihood-ratio and bootstrap), summary, random, to_dict and from_dict. MixtureCureModel adds susceptible_probability(Z), cure_probability(Z), cure_given_survival(x, Z) (the chance that a unit still running at x never fails), susceptible=True on sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf and mean for the latency alone, and follow_up(), Maller and Zhou’s check that the units were followed long enough to show a plateau. The likelihood-ratio bound on a quantile, quantile_cb(p, Z, method="lr"), has an infinite upper end where the likelihood region allows a susceptible probability at or below p. Data with no cured fraction end in the “No finite maximum” warning, naming lfp_p and saying to fit the latency alone. Checked against R’s flexsurvcure (Weibull, log-normal and log-logistic latencies; logit, probit and loglog links; late entry): log-likelihoods to 1e-3, estimates to 5e-3 on the link scale, standard errors to 1%. The distributional regressions’ links gain "logit", "probit" and "cloglog" for a parameter in (0, 1). New guide: Mixture-Cure Regression.

  • Repeat events with failure modes and covariates: CauseSpecificProportionalIntensity (surpyval.recurrent, and at the top level), the regression counterpart of CauseSpecificNHPP. Every event type (failure mode) has its own baseline intensity and its own covariate coefficients, so a covariate can raise one mode’s rate and leave another’s alone. The modes of a marked Poisson process are independent, so each is the single-mode proportional-intensity fit (ProportionalIntensityHPP for baseline=HPP, else ProportionalIntensityNHPP with Duane, CrowAMSAA or CoxLewis) of its own events over every item’s whole observation window, kept in models[event]; there is no second likelihood. Fits: fit(x, Z, i, c, n, e, tl, tr, baseline, init) and fit_from_df (e_col) for fixed covariates, and fit_tvc, fit_tvc_timeline and their _from_df forms for covariates that change over time (the single-mode fits’ rows, plus the mode e of each failure). Per mode, with the mode as event after Z: cif, iif, cif_cb, iif_cb, and cif_tvc, iif_tvc, cb_tvc along a schedule, each the mode’s own model’s. Totals over the modes: total_cif, total_iif, total_cif_tvc, total_iif_tvc, with bounds total_cif_cb, total_iif_cb and total_cb_tvc that add the modes’ delta-method variances and form the bounds on the log scale, as CauseSpecificNHPP’s totals, so a one-mode model’s total bounds are that mode’s. coefficients() is the table of every (mode, covariate): the coefficient, the rate ratio exp(coef), the standard error, Wald intervals for both, z and p; summary() stacks the modes’ parameter tables. neg_ll, aic, bic and aic_c are those of the whole model (sums over the modes); to_dict / from_dict keep every prediction and each mode’s covariance, so a restored model gives the same bounds and tables. One aliasing warning covers the fits of all modes. Not carried over yet, each refusing with what to use instead: diagnose, residuals, cramer_von_mises, trend_test, plot, the simulation methods and mcf (call them on models[event]), forecast and surpyval.forecast, growth and the MTBF methods; counts of failures (c = 2) and right truncation; bounds other than Wald’s. See “Several failure modes, each with its own covariate effects” in Recurrent Event Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

  • Repairable systems with several failure modes, on CauseSpecificNHPP (one intensity model per event type). Each mode’s bounds through the model, with the mode as event: cif_cb, iif_cb, mtbf and mtbf_cb, the mode’s own model’s (method="crow" included). The totals over the modes with bounds: total_iif and total_mtbf beside total_cif, and total_cif_cb, total_iif_cb and total_mtbf_cb, which add the modes’ delta-method variances (the modes of a marked Poisson process are independent) and form the bounds on the log scale, so a one-mode model’s total bounds are that mode’s. Growth per mode: growth() returns a table with a row per mode holding its trend parameter (beta of CrowAMSAA and CoxLewis, alpha of Duane) with its interval, the Wald test that it is at its no-trend value and the conclusion ("increasing", "decreasing" or "none"), the mode’s intensity and MTBF at the end of observation with bounds, and its share of the total intensity; a model fitted with dist=HPP is refused, saying which dist to refit with. Forecasts: forecast(age, horizon, n, limit, alpha_ci, event) gives the expected number of events of one type, or of every type, over a time ahead with its Poisson prediction interval, and surpyval.forecast takes the model (every type). summary() stacks the modes’ parameter tables. to_dict now keeps each mode’s parameter covariance and the end of observation, so a restored model gives the same Wald bounds, growth() and summary(), and the same forecasts for given ages; what needs the data (a forecast of the fitted items, method="crow", plot, the likelihood) is refused as before, and a dict saved by an older version loads as before. The coverage of the total bounds is studied in tests/calibration/test_coverage_recurrent.py (two modes on 10 systems, 1000 replicates: 0.943 to 0.961 against 0.95).

  • Covariates that change over time in the recurrent-event regressions: ProportionalIntensityHPP and ProportionalIntensityNHPP gain fit_tvc (start-stop rows i, xl, xr, c, Z, n), fit_tvc_timeline and their _from_df forms, with the names and data shapes of the life regressions’ time-varying fits. Each row is an interval of an item’s history over which its covariates hold one value; the covariates in force multiply the intensity then (no memory of earlier values). Any row may end in a failure (c = 0), a row may hold a count of failures (c = 2 with n), an item may enter late and may have gaps. With one covariate value per item the fit is that of fit; cutting a row in two changes nothing. The fitted ProportionalIntensityModel gains cif_tvc, iif_tvc and cb_tvc (on="cif" or "iif"): the expected number of events, the intensity and their delta-method bounds along a StepSchedule (or Z rows with xl), from the origin or, with given, from an age; a schedule that never changes gives cif, iif, cif_cb and iif_cb exactly. summary, covariance, param_cb, the information criteria, to_dict / from_dict and pickle work as for any fit. Not available for such a fit, each refusing with what to do instead: residuals, cramer_von_mises, trend_test, diagnose and plot; simulation and mcf along a schedule (they take one covariate vector); a continuously varying CovariatePath; left-censored counts (c = -1; give a c = 2 row) and right truncation. See “Covariates that change over time” in Recurrent Event Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

  • A published Deprecation Policy, linked from the documentation’s home page and from Contributing: what is public, how a renamed or removed name is deprecated (a warning for at least one release naming the replacement), the hint it gives once removed, what may change without notice (names starting with an underscore, surpyval.beta, the last digits of a result), and how releases before 1.0 behave.
