A new test, surpyval/tests/test_public_surface.py, keeps a list of the public names (546 today) and fails when one disappears without a deprecation or a new one is not yet listed; python -m surpyval.tests.test_public_surface --update regenerates the list.

  • diagnose() for distributional regressions (WeibullDistributional and every Distributional(dist)), which refused before: the Cox-Snell residuals on exponential paper with an AIC screen against the other prebuilt distributions fitted with the same covariates (distribution), the likelihood-ratio test of a quadratic term for each covariate on each parameter that holds it, drawn as score residuals (functional_form), and one-step dfbeta per coefficient (influence); a parameter column says which parameter a row is about. Every censoring and truncation is supported; weighted and penalised fits are refused, saying what to use. Checked against flexsurv (the quadratic-term statistics and AICs to 1e-6, the Cox-Snell residuals to 1e-4, with delayed entry too) and gamlss’s normalised quantile residuals (1e-5); the size and power study is tests/calibration/test_size_distributional_diagnostics.py.

  • ParametricCompetingRisks.fit takes left-censored (c = -1) and interval-censored (c = 2) rows with their cause – failures found at an inspection – each contributing \(\mathrm{CIF}_k(x_r) - \mathrm{CIF}_k(x_l)\) (over \(S(t_l)\) with entry). Such rows tie the causes together, so with any of them the causes are fitted jointly by maximum likelihood, and covariance() is the inverse of the joint Hessian, with terms between causes, which every cb (cif, sf, ff, Hf) and standard_errors use; fit_from_df takes the windows as xl_col/xr_col. Data without such rows fit cause by cause exactly as before. The non-parametric CompetingRisks still refuses them, now naming ParametricCompetingRisks. Saved with to_dict, a joint fit keeps its covariance between causes under "joint" and is stamped schema 4, which SurPyval 0.26 and older refuse with a request to upgrade rather than load it without those terms; every other ParametricCompetingRisks save is unchanged.

  • Delayed entry (left truncation) in the cause-specific Cox model: CompetingRisksProportionalHazards.fit(x, Z, e, tl=entry) (and fit_from_df(..., tl_col=), fit_penalised(..., tl=), and fit(data) for a SurpyvalData with entry times) fits each cause’s CoxPH with the entry-adjusted risk sets, so the coefficients, the baselines and the cumulative incidences count an item at risk only once it has entered. Checked against R’s coxph(Surv(tl, x, cause == k) ~ ...) per cause and the multi-state survfit on two data sets to 1e-6 (reference_r_competing_entry.R); with no entry after the first time the fit is the one without tl, to the last bit. FineGray, model="Fine-Gray" and gray_test refuse such entry times with a message naming the cause-specific model and the Aalen-Johansen estimate (they used to say only that the fit takes no left truncation, or not take tl at all).

  • Delayed entry (left truncation) in the non-parametric competing-risks estimate: CompetingRisks.fit(..., tl=) and fit_from_df(..., tl_col=) count a unit at risk only between its entry and its exit (tl < t <= x), and CompetingRisks.fit(data) now passes a SurpyvalData’s entry times through instead of refusing them. The bounds carry over (Aalen’s variance, and the robust one with weights). The cumulative incidence and the robust standard errors match R’s survfit(Surv(entry, x, factor(e)) ~ 1) to 1e-10 on the PBC trial on the age scale; a fit with every entry before the first time is bit-identical to before. Right truncation is still refused.

  • Parametric.with_params takes the full vector of covariance()’s rows, in the order of covariance_names (the distribution’s parameters, then lfp_p and f0), so a draw from the covariance of a limited-failure or zero-inflated fit maps straight back to a model; the short vector of the distribution’s parameters works as before. The offset is with_params(params, gamma=...) (kept when not given), and lfp_p=/f0= go with the short vector, as MixtureModel’s w=. A drawn lfp_p above 1 or f0 below 0 is refused with what to do. New Parametric.bootstrap(n_boot, random_state) returns the refits behind the method="bootstrap" bounds (the same refits for the same seed) as a ParametricBootstrap: the refitted models, their parameters in covariance_names order, each offset fit’s gamma and the count of failed refits, with to_dict. A short section on carrying a fit’s uncertainty forward is on the parametric modelling page.

  • diagnose() of a parametric proportional hazards or accelerated failure time model fitted to time-varying covariates (fit_tvc, fit_tvc_timeline and their _from_df forms), which refused before. Each unit’s residual is the sum over its rows: a PH unit’s Cox-Snell residual adds its rows’ cumulative-hazard increments H(stop | Z_row) - H(start | Z_row), an AFT unit’s standardised residual is its accumulated age. The likelihood-ratio tests use the fit’s own likelihood; influence and outliers name units by their identifiers; the functional-form plot is per row; common_shape tests factors that keep one level within each unit; calibration is not made. A weighted fit_tvc model refuses, saying what to do. Checked against R’s flexsurvreg(Surv(start, stop, event) ~ ...) on the Stanford heart data, against the ordinary fit for constant covariates, and by a seeded simulation (scripts/studies/tvc_diagnose_power.py).

  • diagnose() for Bayesian fits (fit_bayes, by the grid, the Laplace approximation or a closed form, and from_draws with data): posterior predictive checks under the observed censoring and truncation (a realised Anderson-Darling discrepancy and the failures in time bins), the maximum-likelihood fit’s goodness-of-fit tests, a prior-data conflict check (Box’s prior predictive check in its normal form) and the grid’s accuracy (a finer grid, or the grid for a Laplace fit). Before, it refused, pointing to model.mle.diagnose().

  • covariance() and standard_errors() of a fitted Bernoulli, FixedEventProbability or Binomial: the variance of p, \(\hat p (1 - \hat p) / N\) from the events and trials (a Binomial’s known n has a zero row and column), for code that propagates it; nan with no events or only events, where the formula’s 0 would claim p is known. Models restored from older dicts get it from their saved counts. param_cb("p", method="jeffreys") adds the Jeffreys interval (Beta(k + 1/2, N - k + 1/2) quantiles) beside the exact Clopper-Pearson default. Checked against R’s binom.test, qbeta and binom::binom.confint to 1e-10; the coverage study (scripts/studies/probability_coverage.py) is on the Bernoulli page.

  • ParametricCompetingRisks carries its parameters’ uncertainty: params and parameter_names ("<cause>: <name>"), covariance_names, covariance() (the causes’ covariances on the diagonal, exact since the likelihood factorises by cause, lfp_p and f0 rows included) and standard_errors(); with_params(params) rebuilds the model from a vector in that order (or the shorter params), so draws from the covariance can be propagated; and cb(x, event=None, on="cif") gives Wald bounds on each cause’s cumulative incidence (logit scale) and on the all-cause sf, ff and Hf (one bound on log H), with a cause’s net functions bounded by its own model (likelihood-ratio and bootstrap too). Per-cause fits and the cumulative incidence match R’s flexsurv (estimates to 1e-6, covariance to 1e-4, CIF to 1e-6); a 1000-replicate study covers 0.936 to 0.962 at 95% (scripts/studies/parametric_competing_risks_cb_coverage.py).

  • ParametricCompetingRisks gives the lifetime of the whole unit (its first failure from any cause): df(x), the all-cause density \(S(t)\sum_k h_k(t)\); mean(), the all-cause MTTF by quadrature (inf with a cure fraction unless defective=True, as Parametric.mean); and qf(p), the all-cause quantile (B10 is qf(0.1)) by root finding on the cumulative hazard, precise in the upper tail and inf above a cure ceiling. sf, ff, df and qf take event=k for cause k’s net function (its own model), as CompetingRisks.sf(x, event) does. Checked against closed forms (exponential causes, Weibull causes with a common shape, two LogLogistic causes) to 1e-10.

  • life_models.GeneralLinear: the linear life model for any number of covariates, \(L(Z) = a + \beta' Z\) (Linear for several, as GeneralLogLinear is the log-linear one). On the mu of Normal, Logistic or Gumbel the covariates shift the distribution, so the fit does not depend on where zero is (a shift of the data moves a alone): AcceleratedLife(Normal, life_models.GeneralLinear) is R’s survreg(..., dist = "gaussian") on the times themselves (also "logistic" and "extreme"), matched to 1e-5 with the same signs. A positive coefficient means a later life, as in every life model. It names its coefficients by the columns, saves and loads, and flags aliased columns as GeneralLogLinear does.

  • Documentation: CustomDistribution recipes for the generalised gamma and the generalised F in Prentice’s parameterisations, as R’s flexsurv writes them (gengamma: mu, sigma, Q; genf: mu, sigma, Q, P), in “Parametric SurPyval Modelling”. The generalised gamma holds the Weibull (Q = 1), the lognormal (Q = 0, exact through fixed) and the gamma (Q = sigma), so one fit tests all three by likelihood ratio; it fits every kind of censoring and truncation. Both recipes, and AFT fits on them, match flexsurvreg on lung (log-likelihoods to 1e-6, estimates to a hundredth of a standard error, standard errors to 1e-3); inverse Gaussian AFT and PH fits match a likelihood written with scipy.stats.invgauss. The tests run the recipe cells from the page itself.

  • The degradation level of WienerProcessModel and GammaProcessModel: level_at(t, Z, y0=, t0=) is the distribution of the level at time t, from new or from a reading y0 at an age t0 (a ProcessLevel with sf, ff, df, qf, random, mean and to_dict; normal for a Wiener process, y0 plus a gamma variable for a gamma process, on the stress clock with Z), and random_path(times, size, Z, random_state=, y0=, t0=) draws the levels at several times from independent increments, for simulating inspections against a preventive limit. Matches scipy’s normal and gamma to 1e-12; for the gamma process level_at(t).ff(threshold) is sf(t) exactly. Both models also gain with_params(params), a model rebuilt from a flat vector in the order of covariance_names (no covariance or likelihood), so draws from covariance() become models; the spread of ff over such draws matches the delta-method standard error of cb to within 1%. GammaProcessModel now refuses a non-positive alpha or beta and WienerProcessModel a non-finite mu.

  • Turnbull.fit(..., w=): the Turnbull estimate with sampling weights, for interval and left censored and truncated data. The estimate is the weighted non-parametric MLE (each row counts n w in the EM; checked against R’s icenReg::ic_np(..., weights = w) to 1e-8), unchanged by the scale of the weights and equal to the weighted Kaplan-Meier on right censored data with turnbull_estimator="Kaplan-Meier". Its bounds are the weighted case bootstrap, bootstrap_cb(x, random_state=seed) (95% coverage 0.93 to 0.95 in a simulation of informative sampling); cb, quantile_cb, the bounds of rmst and sf_diff refuse it, naming bootstrap_cb. A weighted probability plot of interval censored or truncated data now uses the weighted Turnbull positions.

  • Time-varying coefficients in the Cox model: CoxPH.fit(..., time_interaction={column: g}) (and fit_from_df) gives a covariate the coefficient \(\beta + \gamma g(t)\), with g "t", "log" or any function of time, by splitting the rows at the event times. The coefficient table names the interactions (karno:log(t)); time_varying_effect() gives \(\beta(t)\) with Wald bounds, with plot(); sf, Hf and the other predictions at fixed covariates apply \(\beta(t)\) at each time, and phi, the concordance, diagnose() and to_dict refuse. Matches R’s coxph(..., tt = function(x, t, ...) x * g(t)) on veteran and lung (Efron and Breslow ties, strata, weights) to 1e-6, and diagnose()’s advice for a continuous covariate that fails the proportional-hazards test now names it.

  • The restricted mean survival time of the parametric models: rmst(tau) (the RMST, its delta-method standard error and 95% interval, in the form of the non-parametric models’ rmst), rmst_cb(tau) (Wald, likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds, at one horizon or several) and mean(tau=tau) (the point). Exact for the Exponential, Weibull, Gamma and LogNormal, by quadrature otherwise; offsets, limited failure populations and zero inflation included. The parametric regression models have rmst(tau, Z), rmst_cb(tau, Z) (Wald and bootstrap) and rmst_diff(tau, Z_a, Z_b), and surpyval.rmst_diff compares parametric fits as well as non-parametric ones. Checked against R (survreg and integrate with the delta method by hand, and flexsurv’s summary(type="rmst")) on lung and ovarian.

  • CompetingRisks.fit(..., w=) and fit_from_df(..., w_col=): the Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence of data with sampling or inverse-probability weights, with the robust (infinitesimal jackknife) variance behind every cb (the cumulative incidence, and sf, ff and Hf), the effective sample size in the printout and schema-4 dictionaries. Checked against R’s survfit(Surv(x, factor(e)) ~ 1, weights = w) (pstate and std.err, ties included) to 1e-10. gray_test(..., w=) refuses, saying what to use instead.

  • CoxPH.fit_firth: the Cox model with Firth’s penalty (Heinze and Schemper 2001), half the log determinant of the information added to the partial log-likelihood, so the estimates stay finite where a covariate separates the events from the survivors (a monotone likelihood). With the coefficients’ standard errors, profile penalised-likelihood intervals and p-values (Wald ones with profile=False) in model.firth and summary(), and the penalised likelihood-ratio test from likelihood_ratio_test(). aic(), bic() and aic_c() refuse (FirthRefusal): the penalised likelihood does not compare models, so refit with CoxPH.fit for them or use the penalised test; the printout says so. Breslow ties; delayed entry (start-stop rows), counts and strata. Checked against R’s coxphf on six data sets (coefficients and standard errors to 1e-6, bounds to 1e-5). The “No finite maximum” warning of a Cox fit now names it.

  • Uno’s concordance index and standard errors for C: surpyval.metrics.concordance_estimate(x, c, risk, weighting="uno", tau=...) gives Harrell’s or Uno’s inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted C, optionally only over the pairs whose event is at or before a horizon tau, with its infinitesimal-jackknife standard error and a normal or logit confidence interval; compare_concordance tests the difference between two scores’ C on the same subjects, with the covariance of the two. Every regression model gains concordance_estimate() and concordance(weighting=, tau=). They reproduce R’s survival::concordance (timewt = "n" and "n/G2", ymax, and two fits’ var) on lung and veteran to 1e-10 for C and a relative 1e-8 for the variances, and survC1::Est.Cval for Uno’s C to 1e-7. concordance_index is unchanged.

  • surpyval.metrics.score_predictions: the Brier score, integrated Brier score and time-dependent AUC with standard errors and confidence intervals from their IPCW influence functions (the censoring estimate’s variability included), and, for several models scored on the same subjects, the paired difference between each pair with its interval and p-value. Returns a PredictionScores result with to_dict. Checked against R’s riskRegression::Score(se.fit = TRUE) (scores, standard errors, intervals, contrasts and p-values) and timeROC(iid = TRUE) with compare to 1e-9 on two synthetic sets (one with tied times) and Cox models of veteran. brier_score, integrated_brier_score and auc_td are unchanged.

  • e= and cause= on brier_score, integrated_brier_score, auc_td and score_predictions: the Brier score, integrated Brier score and time-dependent AUC of one cause with competing risks, scoring predicted cumulative incidences, with standard errors, intervals and model comparisons. A subject with a competing event counts as never having the cause; controls="cause_free" (default) or "event_free" chooses the AUC’s controls (timeROC’s AUC_2 and AUC_1). Checked against riskRegression::Score(cause = k, se.fit = TRUE) and timeROC(cause = k, iid = TRUE) to 1e-9 on a synthetic set with tied times (both causes) and the PBC trial (death, transplant competing). c may be left out when e is given; an unknown cause, or cause without e, is refused.

  • Pseudo-observations and regression on them: pseudo_survival, pseudo_rmst and pseudo_cif give the jackknife (leave-one-out) pseudo-values of the Kaplan-Meier survival at chosen times, of the restricted mean survival time to tau and of a cause’s Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence; pseudo_regression (and pseudo_regression_from_df) fits survival-probability (cloglog or logit link), RMST (identity or log) and cumulative-incidence (cloglog or logit) regressions to them by estimating equations with robust (sandwich) standard errors, returning a PseudoRegressionResult (coef, se, ci, p, summary(), predict, predict_cb, to_dict()). A positive coefficient means a shorter life: the survival models are on 1 - S(t) and the RMST model is g(RMST) = a - b'Z. Checked against R’s pseudo (pseudosurv, pseudomean, pseudoci, to 1e-8) and geepack::geeglm with an independence working model (coefficients and robust standard errors, to 1e-6) on lung, ovarian, the PBC trial and a seeded competing-risks set. Guide: Pseudo-Observations.

  • Confidence bounds on a Cox model’s predicted curve: SemiParametricRegressionModel.cb(x, Z) bounds the predicted sf, ff or Hf at covariates Z, with the variance of the baseline and of the coefficients (Tsiatis 1981, Link 1984: R’s survfit(fit, newdata) std.err), under Efron’s or Breslow’s ties, with case weights (the robust covariance), for stratified fits (stratum=) and for start-stop data. bound_type takes R’s conf.type names: "log-log" (the default, the same scale as the Kaplan-Meier, Nelson-Aalen and Aalen bounds, so curves on one chart get bounds by the same rule), "log" (R’s default; pass it to match R’s survfit printout) or "plain". On each scale the bounds agree with R survival 3.8.12 to about 1e-9 on lung, ovarian and heart (scripts/reference/reference_r_cox_curve.R). plot_partial_effects(plot_bounds=True) now draws them for a Cox model, which refused before. The conformance bound sweeps include them. A model restored by from_dict (which does not keep its data) and a penalised fit refuse them.

  • surpyval.recurrent.mcf_diff: compares two groups’ mean cumulative functions, each fitted with NonParametricCounting.fit. It returns an MCFDiffResult with the difference of the MCFs at each time and its pointwise confidence bounds (diff, diff_cb, plot; the sum of the groups’ Lawless-Nadeau robust variances), and the pseudo-score tests of Cook, Lawless and Nadeau (1996) of whether the groups’ event rates differ, with constant and linear weights and a robust (default) or Poisson variance. Late entry and gapped observation are taken as the MCF takes them. Checked against R’s reda::mcfDiff and reda::mcfDiff.test on two seeded data sets (agreement about 1e-14).

  • interval_logrank: log-rank and Wilcoxon-type tests of groups of interval-censored data (any mix of exact, right, left and interval-censored rows, as x/c, a two-column x or xl/xr). Each unit is scored from the Turnbull estimate of the pooled data, with Sun’s log-rank scores (the default), Finkelstein’s, or the Wilcoxon-type scores, and the score sums are compared by their permutation distribution: a chi-squared p-value, or a Monte Carlo permutation one (method="permutation", seeded by random_state). Returns an IntervalLogRankResult with to_dict(). Matches R’s interval::ictest(..., method = "pclt") to 1e-8 on the breast cosmesis data and on simulated three-group data. Truncated data are refused. logrank given left or interval-censored data, or a two-column x, now says to use it; its results are unchanged.

  • Parametric.likelihood_contour(alpha_ci, n_points): the joint likelihood-ratio confidence region of a fit’s two parameters, the contour where the log-likelihood is half the chi-squared (two degrees of freedom) critical value below its maximum, found by root finding along rays from the estimate, with each parameter’s exact extremes over the region (bounds). It returns a LikelihoodContour with to_dict(). surpyval.plot_likelihood_contour draws one or more fits’ contours at one or several levels, with the estimates marked, to compare two samples. Models with other than two fitted parameters, offset, limited-failure and zero-inflated models, and weighted fits are refused with a message saying what to use. Checked against WeibullR’s MLEcontour and the profile likelihood solved in base R.

  • CrowAMSAA.projection(..., bias_corrected=True): False uses the plain maximum-likelihood shapes in the demonstrated intensity and in the rate of new BD modes, as the worked example of MIL-HDBK-189C (section 6.3.3.8) does (demonstrated MTBF 7.71, projected 10.82 on its 56-failure data), where MIL-HDBK-00189A and the default use the bias-corrected shapes (7.85 and 11.29). The default and its numbers are unchanged; GrowthProjection.bias_corrected records the choice. Both examples and the handbook’s test-find-test example (14.81 and 15.13) are pinned by tests.

  • Documented, and pinned by tests, how counts n and weights w compare with writing the rows out as copies in logrank (every weighting, Fleming-Harrington included) and pairwise_logrank: counts match the copies to rounding, weights give the same numerator but the robust variance, so a smaller statistic. No numerical change.

  • Reference checks: the actuarial life table against KMsurv::lifetab column by column; the survival of a weighted Cox model against R’s survfit(coxph(..., weights = w)), with Efron’s and Breslow’s ties and with late entry; a published distributional regression (the PET film accelerated life test of Mazucheli, Louzada-Neto and Achcar 2003, with covariates on the Weibull shape) to every printed digit and against flexsurv; and the robust covariance of Royston-Parmar and distributional fits, with and without clusters, against the sandwich written out by hand.

  • Bootstrap bounds (method="bootstrap" on cb, quantile_cb and param_cb) for limited-failure and zero-inflated models, with or without an offset, which refused before; param_cb bounds lfp_p and f0 too. The refits are of the same model (lfp=, zi=, offset=, fixed=), drawn from it as the plain models’ are; a unit drawn as never failing is censored at the last time in the data where its drawn censoring time is beyond it; and a refit that puts lfp_p or f0 on its edge counts there, so an interval can reach the edge. The intervals are BCa, with the jackknife’s acceleration (the model refitted without each unit in turn); the plain and offset models’ bootstrap intervals are unchanged. The conformance bound sweeps include them, and a calibration study checks their coverage.

  • Bootstrap bounds for weighted fits: method="bootstrap" on cb, param_cb and quantile_cb (and mrl_cb of a distribution) of a parametric distribution or a parametric regression (PH, AFT, PO, additive hazards, accelerated life) fitted with sampling weights w, which 0.26 refused, is the case bootstrap: the units are resampled with their weights and the weighted model refitted. A seed gives the same bounds at any scale of the weights. Likelihood-ratio bounds still refuse weighted fits.

  • CoxPH.fit_from_df takes w_col (lifelines’ weights_col), which 0.26 refused: the same fit as CoxPH.fit(..., w=), with the weights of rows dropped for a missing covariate dropped with them.

  • CoxPH.fit_tvc takes weights w (one per interval row) and fit_tvc_from_df takes w_col: the weighted partial likelihood of start-stop data, with the robust covariance clustered by subject (R’s coxph(Surv(start, stop, event) ~ ..., weights = w, robust = TRUE, id = id)). Not with strata yet.

  • logrank and pairwise_logrank take sampling weights w (0.26 gave Python’s TypeError): weighted numbers at risk and of events, with the design-based variance, R’s robust score test coxph(..., weights = w, robust = TRUE, ties = "breslow")$rscore. Every weighting, strata, tl and t0 take weights; the result reports weighted and does not depend on the scale of w.

  • A stratified Cox model (CoxPH.fit(..., strata=) and fit_tvc(..., strata=)) now has what an unstratified one has, where each was refused before: compute_residuals (martingale, deviance, score, dfbeta, Schoenfeld and scaled Schoenfeld, each within its stratum’s risk sets), the proportional-hazards test, diagnose() (its calibration curve predicting each row from its own stratum), the robust (sandwich) standard errors, to_dict / to_json (one baseline per stratum; such a file is schema 4, which an older SurPyval refuses rather than reading the first stratum’s baseline as the model’s), and concordance(), which pools the pairs within each stratum as R’s concordance does and takes strata= to score new data. All agree with R’s survival (residuals, cox.zph, coxph(robust = TRUE), concordance) to 1e-6 on the lung data stratified by sex and the start-stop heart data stratified by surgery (scripts/reference/reference_r_stratified_cox.R).

  • random(size, Z, random_state=) on the accelerated failure time models (WeibullAFT, LogNormalAFT and the others) and the parametric proportional odds models (WeibullPO, …), which raised NotImplementedError, and on the Cox model (CoxPH, with stratum= for a stratified fit) and the Aalen additive model, which had none. Each draw is an exact inverse-transform draw at its covariate row. The Cox and Aalen models draw from their step survival curves: a draw is an event time, or inf beyond the last time the curve is estimated at, as often as sf there says. A new conformance property checks, for every regression with random, that 20,000 draws at one row are within the 0.1% Kolmogorov-Smirnov band of its sf, and the seed properties now cover the regressions.

  • likelihood_ratio_test() on a distributional regression (WeibullDistributional and the others), which 0.26 refused. With no argument it is the global test: twice the gain in log-likelihood over the distribution fitted alone, on one degree of freedom per estimated coefficient over every parameter. likelihood_ratio_test(parameter="beta") tests one parameter’s covariates (does the shape depend on the load?), against the fit with that parameter’s coefficients at 0 and the others refitted. Aliased coefficients and those held at 0 are not counted; a coefficient held at another value is refused, saying what to do. The result is the dictionary the other regressions’ tests return.

  • Weighted Data says which robust formula the standard errors use (HC0, with no small-sample factor; R’s survey package multiplies by sqrt(n / (n - 1)), 0.5% at 100 units and 5% at 10), that counts n are frequency weights, and, with a worked example, why a weighted Cox model with tied failure times gives a different answer under Efron’s ties for one subject of weight 3 than for three identical copies (use n for repeated identical units, w for survey and importance weights). No numbers change.

  • Weights w in the competing-risks regressions: CompetingRisksProportionalHazards.fit(..., w=) (cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray), FineGray.fit(..., w=) and their fit_from_df(..., w_col=). Cause-specific Cox is the weighted CoxPH per cause, R’s coxph(Surv(x, e == k) ~ z, weights = w, robust = TRUE). Fine-Gray multiplies the weights into its censoring weights and estimates the censoring distribution from the weighted Kaplan-Meier (so whole-number weights give the counted fit exactly; R’s finegray leaves its censoring distribution unweighted), with the robust covariance clustered by unit, Fine and Gray’s with each unit’s influence (the part through the censoring distribution included) times its weight, so w = 1 gives the unweighted fit’s. Checked against R (coefficients 1e-8; standard errors 1e-6 against coxph(..., weights = fgwt * w, cluster = id) with the censoring term taken out, as coxph holds the censoring distribution fixed; the term itself against its definition). The information criteria, the diagnostics and the penalised fit refuse weighted fits.

  • AalenAdditive.fit(..., w=) and fit_from_df(..., w_col=): Aalen’s additive hazards model with sampling weights. Each increment of the cumulative effects B(t) is a weighted least-squares fit, and every standard error and bound (summary, cumulative_coefficients_cb, cb, plot) uses the robust variance, the sum of the units’ squared influences, which does not depend on the scale of the weights. Matches R’s timereg::aalen(..., weights = w, robust = 1) (cum and robvar.cum, to 1e-12), with and without delayed entry. Whole-number weights give the estimate of the same counts exactly. constant_effects_test() refuses a weighted fit; the model shows its effective sample size and saves as schema 4.

  • Weights w for distributional regression (WeibullDistributional.fit(..., w=w) and every Distributional fitter) and Royston-Parmar regression (RoystonParmarPH, RoystonParmarPO, RoystonParmarRegression), with w_col in fit_from_df: weighted estimates, the robust (sandwich) covariance, Wald and case-bootstrap bounds; likelihood-ratio bounds and tests and the information criteria refuse. Checked against R’s flexsurvreg and flexsurvspline with weights (estimates to 1e-5, robust standard errors from a hand sandwich to 1e-4). Royston-Parmar’s knots are placed on the event times counted by n, not weighted. A Royston-Parmar left truncation at 0 is now read as none: it made the fit unverified and a weighted fit’s covariance nan.

  • Sampling weights w in penalised fits: CoxPH.fit_penalised, CoxPH.fit_tvc_penalised and the parametric PH, AFT and PO fit_penalised, which refused them. The objective is the weighted log-likelihood over \(N_w = \sum n w\) plus the penalty, with the covariates standardised by their n w-weighted standard deviations, so rescaling the weights changes nothing. The Cox fit matches R’s glmnet(..., family = "cox", weights = w) to 1e-6 (ridge, lasso and elastic net, Breslow and Efron, with and without delayed entry); the parametric fits are checked against their optimality conditions. No standard errors, and aic/bic refused, as for every weighted fit; penalty_path of weighted fits keeps the coefficients and refuses choosing by AIC or BIC. A parametric penalised fit with a delayed entry at 0 is now "verified" (it was left “unverified” by a nan second derivative; the estimates do not change).

  • covariance_names on every parametric fit (Weibull.fit and the rest): the name of each row of covariance(), in its order. It is the distribution’s parameters, then lfp_p for lfp=True and f0 for zi=True (['alpha', 'beta', 'lfp_p', 'f0']), so the third row of a limited-failure fit’s covariance is no longer a guess. A parameter fixed at fit time keeps its (zero) row. An offset gamma has no row: the covariance holds it at its estimate, since a Wald standard error for a threshold is unreliable (in a simulation of n = 200 Weibull fits its 95% interval covered the true offset 89% of the time at shape 3.5, 76% at shape 1.5, and the Hessian did not exist below shape 1; scripts/studies/offset_gamma_wald.py); param_cb("gamma") has the likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds. parameter_names, hess_inv (the distribution’s block only) and the saved dictionary are unchanged.

  • diagnose() for Aalen’s additive hazards model (AalenAdditive), which refused before. constant_effects reports, per covariate, the model’s constant_effects_test() (timereg::aalen’s Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, with n_boot resampled processes and random_state), with the cumulative coefficients and their bands as plots; its rows never fail, since the model allows effects that change, and the advice points to AdditiveHazards when none does. non_negative_hazard tests whether any observed unit’s estimated cumulative hazard falls (a negative hazard), by the largest fall in standard errors against the falls of the resampled processes, and advises CoxPH when one does. The statistics match timereg 2.0.7 to 1e-8 where both anchor the line at the same time. In simulations (tests/calibration/test_diagnose_aalen.py) the constant-effects rows rejected 3-3.5% of constant effects at the 5% level with 300 units, the falling-hazard test none of 200 data sets with positive hazards and 90% of those with negative fitted hazards; the power against an effect of 0.5 falling to 0.1 was 0.34 with 500 units. Weighted fits are refused.

  • Regressions as plain life models, and their parameter uncertainty carried along. model.at(Z) is the lifetime distribution of a unit with one covariate row (LifeAtCovariates, at the top level too, as the other result classes are): sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf, random, mean, rmst and cb taking times only, each exactly the regression’s at Z, on every parametric regression, CoxPH (with stratum=) and the semi-parametric proportional odds and additive hazards models; random(n) is qf(U), as Parametric.random. with_params(params), covariance_names and _estimates() on the parametric regressions (PH, AFT, PO, AH, accelerated life, Royston-Parmar, distributional) and the semi-parametric ProportionalOdds and AdditiveHazards models: a model at a flat parameter vector in the order of covariance()’s rows, keeping the formula, centre and fixed parameters, without data or covariance (the semi-parametric baseline is re-estimated at the new coefficients). At R’s estimate a Weibull AFT and PH at fixed covariates match flexsurv’s summary(newdata=) and survreg’s predicted quantiles to 1e-9. The semi-parametric ProportionalOdds and AdditiveHazards models gain random(size, Z).

  • RoystonParmarModel.with_params(params): the same spline (knots, scale, unit) at other coefficients, given in the order of the new covariance_names (gamma_0, gamma_1, …), so a draw from covariance() becomes a model and the coefficients’ uncertainty can be propagated. The model returned has no data or covariance: cb, standard_errors, neg_ll and the information criteria refuse on it. Coefficients whose spline falls somewhere in log time (a decreasing cumulative hazard) are refused with the time where it does. Checked against flexsurv’s psurvspline family at given coefficients on all three scales to 1e-12; the 2.5% and 97.5% points of sf over 4000 draws match the Wald band of cb to 0.0013.

  • Recurrent models can be stepped forward one failure at a time. RenewalModel (GeneralizedRenewal, GeneralizedOneRenewal, ARA, ARI) gains next_failure_qf(p), the inverse of next_failure_sf (on the cumulative hazard, so the upper tail keeps its digits), next_failure_random(size) (next_failure_qf at uniform draws), states() (the units’ states, from the fitted items, an age or known failures) and advance(states, x), the state after a failure at x and its repair by the fitted rule (failed=False to run on); the four next-failure methods take states=. A loop of draws and advances reproduces time_terminated_simulation and count_terminated_simulation in distribution (seeded two-sample tests on counts and event times, every family). ParametricRecurrenceModel (HPP, CrowAMSAA, Duane, CoxLewis) has the same next_failure_sf, next_failure_hf, next_failure_qf and next_failure_random from an age. Both kinds gain covariance_names and with_params(params), the same model at a flat parameter vector in that order (a draw from covariance()); draws through it spread as the delta method says (within 5%).

  • ParametricCompetingRisks.diagnose(), which refused before. Cause by cause, it tests the Cox-Snell residuals of the cause’s distribution (its cumulative hazard over each unit’s time at risk, from entry, with the other causes censored) against the unit exponential, by the univariate distributions’ bootstrap goodness-of-fit tests; screens the univariate alternatives by AIC; and tests the largest gap between the model’s cumulative incidence and the Aalen-Johansen estimate (CompetingRisks.fit) by parametric bootstrap (n_boot=, random_state=), drawn with the Aalen-Johansen band. The advice says which cause to refit with which distribution (dist={cause: ...}, or from_fitted), or to use the non-parametric estimate. With delayed entry (tl) the incidence is compared with the Aalen-Johansen estimate that takes the entry times, the model’s incidence conditioned on surviving to the first entry as the estimate is, and each resample draws a unit’s latent times beyond its entry. A model fitted to left- or interval-censored rows is refused with its own message (its causes are fitted jointly and keep no data; it says to compare distributions by AIC and the all-cause survival with the Turnbull estimate) rather than the message for a model restored with from_dict. With every unit entering late (200 replicates of n = 100 at 10%) the right models were rejected 3-11% of the time. Size and power: tests/calibration/test_size_parametric_competing_risks_diagnostics.py (200 replicates of n = 100 at 10%: the right models rejected 7-10.5% of the time; a wrong distribution for one cause was flagged for that cause 80% of the time and for the right cause 5.5%).

  • A calibration study of the plain models’ bootstrap bounds (tests/calibration/test_coverage_bootstrap.py): Weibull and LogNormal, about 30% right censored, at 30, 100 and 300 units, on param_cb, cb(sf) and quantile_cb at 90% and 95% (200 replicates of 200 refits a design). Its first run found the intervals about a point short at every sample size, which led to the fix below; with it, averaged over each size’s 16 bounds, they cover 0.880 / 0.930 at 30 units, 0.891 / 0.947 at 100 and 0.888 / 0.946 at 300 (90% / 95%; LogNormal at 100 units over the first 160 of its 200 replicates). One 30-unit design (LogNormal) still has a bound outside its tolerance and is marked as a known shortfall (a strict xfail, with the numbers in the reason).

  • The calibration runs end with a “pooled calibration coverage” section: each study’s mean coverage over its bounds at each level, the gap from nominal and the count below it. It is a report only; nothing passes or fails on it, and no seed, replicate count or tolerance changed.

  • Group-sequential designs in surpyval.test_planning: a comparison looked at a few planned times, stopping early for efficacy or futility while keeping its level. logrank_group_sequential(hazard_ratio, looks, power) gives the boundaries at each look, the maximum and expected events (the single-analysis events of logrank_events times the inflation factor), the units (with event_probability) and the hazard ratio on each boundary; group_sequential_design gives the same for any normal test statistic on the information scale, and boundary_crossing the chances of crossing any boundaries. Efficacy boundaries: O’Brien-Fleming, Pocock, Wang-Tsiatis and Haybittle-Peto, or Lan-DeMets alpha spending (O’Brien-Fleming-type, Pocock-type, Hwang-Shih-DeCani, Kim-DeMets); one- or two-sided; futility boundaries by beta spending, binding or non-binding. The designs report the critical values and nominal p-values, the alpha and beta spent, the inflation factor, the stopping probabilities and expected information under both hypotheses; update re-computes a spending design at the information the looks came at; decide, the stage-wise p_value, the median-unbiased estimate with its interval (hazard_ratio_estimate for the log-rank design) and repeated_interval analyse a study. Computed by recursive numerical integration (Jennison and Turnbull 2000, chapter 19), not simulation; checked against R’s gsDesign 3.11.0 and rpact 4.4.0 (to about 1e-6) and Jennison and Turnbull’s tables, and by simulated log-rank studies. to_dict / from_dict. Guide: Test Planning with SurPyval.

Changed.

  • Unit labels are kept exactly as typed wherever they are shown or saved: Measurements(..., units={"vibration": "mm/s"}) prints, plots and saves "mm/s" (not pint’s "millimeter / second"), and a model’s unit="hrs" stays "hrs" (it was stored as "hour"), as do the data classes’ unit. pint still reads the labels where they are compared (the data’s and the fit’s, a dataset’s records, combined data), so "h" and "hours" still agree; the new surpyval.utils.units.same_unit does it. Axes show the label as typed ("Time (hrs)"). Files saved with pint’s names load as before.

  • The bootstrap bounds of an MPP, MPS, MSE or MOM fit refit by that method (an intentional change of numbers). param_cb(..., method="bootstrap") and bootstrap() refitted every resample by maximum likelihood, whatever the model was fitted by, so the bound on, say, a rank-regression shape was the spread of the maximum-likelihood shape, centred by the share of those refits below the rank-regression estimate. They now refit with the model’s own how (and an MPP fit’s plotting options). On ten Weibull lifetimes the 95% bound on an MPP shape of 1.43 moved from [0.82, 2.32] to [0.88, 2.70].

  • Zero-inflated fits: a row “failed by t” includes the units dead on arrival (an intentional change of numbers). In a univariate fit(..., zi=True) an interval starting at 0, [0, t], was read as “after 0 and by t”, leaving out the mass f0 at 0, while left censoring at t included it. Both now contribute f0 + (p - f0) F(t), the likelihood of zero-inflated data with such rows (Moulton and Halsey 1995, Biometrics 51(4); Braekers and Grouwels 2016, Comm. Stat. Theory Methods 45(7); Grouwels 2015, PhD thesis, section 2.1) and the rule of ZeroInflated, whose fit without covariates is now the univariate fit on the same rows, without rewriting them. A left truncation at 0 is now no truncation (it divided by 1 - f0); a late entry at tl > 0 is unchanged. ``f0`` can be larger on data with left-censored or ``[0, t]`` rows: on 100 units, 10 failed at 0 and 7 found failed at an inspection at 2 recorded as [0, 2], a Weibull’s f0 went from 0.100 to 0.150 and its scale from 10.27 to 10.97, the same as with those rows left censored at 2. Bayesian fits (fit_bayes) use the same likelihood. Fits with no [0, t] row and no truncation at 0 are unchanged to the last digit, left censoring and intervals that open above 0 included.

  • What 1.0 will promise is now written down. Deprecation Policy says that from 1.0 SurPyval follows semantic versioning (no breaking change to the public interface before 2.0), that a deprecated public name keeps working, with a warning, for at least two minor releases and at least six months, whichever is later, and what a 1.x release may still change (corrected numbers, the oldest supported Python or numpy). The rules before 1.0 are unchanged. The dictionary to_dict writes is documented key by key, for every class, on Saving and Loading Models (The saved-model dictionary), and a test keeps the page and the code in step: from 1.0 keys may be added but are not renamed or removed. The conventions page documents on="R" and on="F" as accepted spellings of "sf" and "ff". Custom distributions are written with autograd.numpy, and the policy now says that is part of the interface. No change to any result.

  • The recurrent models’ standard errors are steadier under a change of time unit (an intentional numerical change, in the seventh digit or beyond). The finite-difference Hessian behind the Poisson-process, proportional-intensity, cause-specific and renewal models’ covariances (scale_free_hessian) stepped each direction by 1e-3 of a standard deviation. With times in hours or seconds the negative log-likelihood is in the thousands, and rounding then cost the Hessian about its seventh digit, so the same data in another unit gave bounds that differed by up to 1.4e-6. It now steps by 3e-3 and cancels one more term of the difference’s error (four step sizes, not three). The largest relative difference between a generalised renewal model’s standard errors fitted in months and in another unit (the test data of the unit checks):

    Unit

    Before

    After

    hours

    9.4e-8

    2.1e-8

    seconds

    3.9e-7

    6.1e-8

    years

    2.4e-7

    6.3e-9

    Against the closed-form Hessian of a power-law process, the standard errors are within 2e-9 from years to hours as before and within 4.4e-7 in seconds (8.3e-9 before). Example: a generalised renewal model in hours, standard errors of [q, alpha, beta] 4.482161218522, 132.8835862844, 0.09875842148647 before and 4.482161306947, 132.8835700725, 0.09875843998802 now; CrowAMSAA on the same repair fleet in hours, 4657.449597614 and 0.2461119034716 before, 4657.449566626 and 0.2461119023258 now.

  • The quantiles of the parametric regressions are computed in closed form (an intentional numerical change, at rounding level). qf(p, Z) of the proportional hazards, accelerated failure time and proportional odds models with the log-linear link, on a Weibull, Exponential, Gumbel, Logistic, LogLogistic, Normal, LogNormal or Gamma baseline, and of the additive hazards model on an Exponential baseline, is now the baseline’s own inverse at a target moved by the covariates (for proportional hazards \(H_0^{-1}(-\log(1 - p)\, e^{-\beta' Z})\)) instead of a numerical search on the model’s cumulative hazard. A custom link, the accelerated life and distributional models, the additive hazards model on another baseline and any other baseline keep the search, unchanged. The quantiles move by rounding: on the 28 parametric regressions of the conformance suite at probabilities from 1e-12 to 1 - 1e-12, by at most 1.4e-14 relative (4.6e-13 absolute); both agree with a 50-digit reference to within 2e-14 relative. For the WeibullPH example in qf’s docstring, qf(0.9, [0]) was 15.502628026657936 and is 15.502628026657938. The Wald bounds on a quantile (quantile_cb) move by at most 7e-10 relative, through their numerical gradient. It is about 20 to 50 times as fast: qf at 39 points takes 0.1 to 0.2 ms instead of 1 to 6 ms, and, since ParametricCompetingRisksRegression.cif integrates over a cause’s quantiles, its cif at 12 times takes 0.17 s instead of 0.74 s, and cb(..., on="cif") 2.2 s instead of 13.9 s, with the same incidences and bounds within 1e-11 relative. The parametric bootstrap’s draws use the same closed form.

  • Fine-Gray standard errors are the robust ones by default (an intentional numerical change). FineGray (and CompetingRisksProportionalHazards with model="Fine-Gray") reported model-based standard errors: the inverse information of the weighted partial likelihood, which takes the censoring weights as known (R cmprsk::crr’s invinf). covariance(), standard_errors(), p_values, summary() (its standard errors, Wald intervals, z and p) and the printout now use the robust (sandwich) variance Fine and Gray derived, which adds each unit’s influence on the estimate, the part through the estimated censoring distribution included: the variance crr reports (its var) and prints, reproduced to about 1e-7 (relative) on eight stored crr fits, with ties between events of both causes and censorings, with counts (crr given each row n times) and with no censoring. The coefficients, the likelihood, the baseline and every prediction are unchanged. The model-based variance stays available, under the name the other regressions use for the choice: covariance(robust=False), standard_errors(robust=False) and summary(robust=False); the model-based p-values are the p column of summary(robust=False). The reason for the change of default (design principle 15): the model-based variance is not the variance of this estimator, whose weights are estimated and whose risk sets repeat units; the robust one is the method’s own and the reference software’s.

    The robust standard errors are mostly smaller than the model-based ones, but not always: on the stored crr fits, 17 of 22 coefficients get a smaller standard error. The numbers that change, standard errors model-based → robust (every Wald interval, z and p moves with them):

    • the competing reference data, cause 1 (group, z): 0.33147, 0.16439 → 0.30823, 0.15600; p 0.0172, 0.4443 → 0.0104, 0.4202;

    • the same, cause 2: 0.44598, 0.24453 → 0.43318, 0.20337; p 0.0355, 0.3282 → 0.0304, 0.2397;

    • PBC, death (drug, age, log_bili, female): 0.17603, 0.00818, 0.08971, 0.23463 → 0.17584, 0.00959, 0.09410, 0.26680;

    • the docstring examples: the censored one’s variance (FineGrayModel.covariance) 0.04419 → 0.04333, and the standard error in FineGrayModel.summary’s (no censoring) 0.1741 → 0.1727.

    Over the stored crr fits the robust standard errors are from 25% smaller to 17% larger than the model-based ones (the larger ones are all for death in PBC: age, log_bili and female, and age and female again with the times rounded to half years). In a simulation from the model (n = 200, 47% censored, 1000 replicates) the 95% Wald intervals covered the two coefficients 94.3% and 93.2% of the time with the robust variance and 94.8% and 94.3% with the model-based one.

    What else follows:

    • A saved model’s dict holds both: "covariance" (and "se", "p_values") the robust one, as covariance(), and "model_covariance". A dict saved by 0.26 or earlier holds only the model-based covariance, and the robust one cannot be rebuilt without the data: it loads with its predictions and covariance(robust=False) as they were, while covariance(), standard_errors() and summary() refuse, saying to ask for robust=False or refit, and p_values is nan (the model-based ones are in summary(robust=False)).

    • A fit with weights w gets the same term for the censoring distribution, with sampling weights: every sum (the censoring Kaplan-Meier and its at-risk counts included) weighted, and each unit’s influence its weight times the unweighted one. So a fit with w = 1 reports exactly the unweighted standard errors, and scaling every weight changes nothing. Before, a weighted fit held the censoring distribution fixed (R’s coxph on finegray’s data), and w = 1 gave slightly different standard errors from no w. On the weighted reference data the standard errors move from 0.53324, 0.26389 to 0.53366, 0.26592 (cause 1) and from 0.84097, 0.46078 to 0.84041, 0.46074 (cause 2). A weighted fit has no model-based covariance: robust=False is refused.

    • Where a coefficient runs off (a fit that warns “No finite maximum”), the robust covariance of the other coefficients can be nan too, where a risk set’s sum underflows.

    • FineGrayModel.p_values is computed in the tail (2 * norm.sf), as summary()’s, so a p-value below 1e-16 is no longer 0.

  • random of a Bayesian fit (BayesianParametric.random) takes one uniform number per life, where it took two (one to pick a posterior point and one for the life). The number picks a point by the posterior’s cumulative weights, and its place within that point’s share is the probability for the point’s own quantile; a closed-form predictive (an Exponential with a Gamma prior, a Normal with a Normal prior on its mean) uses its quantile directly. On a grid the life is drawn at the grid point, not at a point jittered within its cell, so the draws follow exactly the distribution sf, ff and qf describe. This is an intentional change to results: the same seed gives different lives than before. For example, a Weibull fit to 3 failures and 37 survivors with the default grid, random(3, random_state=1), was [2596.0, 33586.3, 10561.4] and is now [2240.2, 30592.9, 18897.8]; an Exponential with a Gamma(2, 500) prior on 100, 250 and 400 hours was [783.8, 51.0, 250.5] and is now [192.8, 1029.9, 39.5]. The distribution of the draws is unchanged.

  • A saved single-process repairable model keeps its bounds. to_dict / to_json of a maximum-likelihood HPP, CrowAMSAA, Duane or CoxLewis fit (ParametricRecurrenceModel) and of a proportional-intensity fit (ProportionalIntensityModel) now store the parameter covariance ("covariance"), and the restored model computes covariance(), standard_errors(), summary(), param_cb and the Wald bounds (cif_cb, iif_cb, mtbf_cb, cb_tvc) from it, equal to the fit’s. The renewal models (GeneralizedRenewal, GeneralizedOneRenewal, ARA, ARI) do the same for covariance(), standard_errors(), the Wald param_cb and summary(); with the repair parameter on the edge of its range, its interval (a profile-likelihood one) and so summary() need the data and are refused, saying so. Before, a restored model refused them, while a restored CauseSpecificNHPP or CauseSpecificProportionalIntensity (whose causes are these same models) gave them. What needs the data is still refused, with a message that says what is and is not available: the likelihood and the information criteria, the diagnostics, plot, Crow’s exact bounds, the profile-likelihood intervals and the repair test. The entry is optional on reading (the schema is unchanged): a dictionary saved by an earlier version loads as before and refuses the bounds, saying it holds no covariance; a model with no likelihood (from_params, how="MSE") and a penalised fit save null. No fitted number changes.

  • Bootstrap refits with no finite maximum are always reported. A resample can leave the likelihood with no finite maximum: no failures, fewer distinct failure times than parameters, or a covariate group with no failures. Every bootstrap that refits resamples (method="bootstrap" on the parametric models, the parametric regressions including cb_tvc and distributional regression, a competing-risks cause’s net bounds, DegradationAnalysis and DestructiveDegradation, and Parametric.bootstrap) now treats them one way: a refit that returns with no finite maximum is kept at the estimate it reached, so that it counts toward the end of the bounds it ran to (as before); a resample the fit refuses because its likelihood has no maximum at all is left out (as before, but no longer counted as an ordinary failure); and both are said in one BootstrapRefitWarning (surpyval.utils.no_maximum), with how many of how many, what was done with them and what to do, whenever there is at least one. Before, they were said only above 2% of the refits, the degradation bootstraps did not count them at all, and DestructiveDegradation.cb repeated each refit’s own warning (30 warnings for 30 refits of noise-free readings; now one). The counts are on the warning (no_maximum, no_estimate, unverified, failed, n_boot) and on Parametric.bootstrap()’s result (no_estimate, new, beside no_maximum and failed). The fit’s refusals of such data raise NoFiniteMaximumError, a ValueError. The bounds themselves do not change: on 13 checks across every path (normal data and data with such refits) they are identical to the bit. Example: a Weibull fitted to 3 failures among 10 units, cb([2, 5], method="bootstrap", n_boot=200, random_state=1), gives the same bounds as before ([0.6917, 0.9934] at 2) and now says that 26 of the 200 resamples had fewer than two distinct failure times and were left out. The goodness-of-fit reports (univariate and competing-risks incidence) add a note with the count of their refits with no finite maximum.

  • The renewal models’ simulations (GeneralizedRenewal, GeneralizedOneRenewal, ARA) draw a failure at a large virtual age (a cumulative hazard past 20) by Newton’s method on the cumulative hazard with the hazard rate, kept inside a bracket, in place of bracketing and regula falsi: about 3 evaluations of the lifetime’s Hf and hf per draw where it took 12 to 15 of Hf, and 2 to 5 times faster per draw (a two-Weibull mixture lifetime 5 times). The draws agree with the old ones and with 50-digit roots to rounding (1e-13), but are not bit for bit the same. MixtureModel.Hf and hf are computed from each component’s Hf and hf (one call each; the hazard is the components’ hazards weighted by their share of the survivors), and stay precise out to a cumulative hazard of 700.

  • The survival tree and random survival forest are stable: surpyval.beta.ml is now surpyval.ml (from surpyval.ml import SurvivalTree, RandomSurvivalForest), with the stability promise, deprecation cycle and conformance checks of the rest of the package; the models themselves, their fits and their numbers are unchanged. The old name still imports them, with a FutureWarning at the import, until the first release on or after 12 April 2027 (the day the top-level data-format functions go), and a tree or forest saved by 0.26 (to_json, to_dict or a pickle) still loads. The beta tier, surpyval.beta, is empty.

  • The sign of a distributional regression’s coefficients is reversed on scale and location parameters (WeibullDistributional and every Distributional(dist)). In 0.26 every coefficient took its link’s sign, as R’s gamlss and flexsurvreg do, so a positive coefficient on a Weibull’s scale meant a longer life: the opposite of SurPyval’s AFT and PH models. Now each coefficient follows SurPyval’s sign, that of the AFT models: a positive coefficient means a shorter life. The fitted model, its predictions and its bounds are the same; only the reported coefficients of the parameters below change sign, and with them their bounds, fixed= and init= values and formulas you write with them.

    • A scale (alpha of a Weibull, log-logistic or ExpoWeibull, sigma of a Rayleigh), a location (mu of a LogNormal, Normal, Gumbel, GumbelLEV or Logistic) and a shape whose increase makes every life longer (a Gamma’s alpha, an ExpoWeibull’s mu, a Beta’s alpha): the sign is reversed, alpha(z) = alpha e^{-b'z}, mu(z) = mu - b'z. Covariates on the scale alone now give exactly the AFT model’s coefficients, sign included.

    • A rate (an Exponential’s failure_rate, a Gamma’s beta) and a Beta’s beta (both shorten lives as they rise), and a shape or spread with no direction of its own (a Weibull’s beta, every sigma of a location-scale distribution): unchanged.

    model.coefficient_signs gives each parameter’s sign. Before and after, on the bearings of Distributional Regression, whose scale falls with load:

    model = surv.WeibullDistributional.fit_from_df(
    bearings, x_col="hours", c_col="censored", Z_cols=["load"]
)
model.params[2:]   # alpha_load, beta_load
# 0.26: [-0.3978, 0.2695]  (alpha(z) = alpha e^{+b z})
# 0.27: [ 0.3978, 0.2695]  (alpha(z) = alpha e^{-b z}, as WeibullAFT)
model.qf(0.1, loads)  # the same in both: [350.0, 359.3, 333.6, 287.0]

    A model saved by 0.26 (to_dict, to_json or pickle) is converted when it is loaded: its coefficients, covariance and fixed values take the new sign and it predicts exactly as it did. A model saved now carries its signs ("coefficient_signs") and is stamped schema 4, which 0.26 refuses with a request to upgrade rather than reading the coefficients with the old sign. R’s gamlss and flexsurvreg coefficients on a scale or a location are SurPyval’s with the sign changed.

    Only the distributional model changes: no proportional odds model and no Royston-Parmar model changes sign. Royston-Parmar regression is unchanged: on the hazard scale its coefficients already had the PH sign (a positive one shortens life), and on the odds scale the sign of every SurPyval PO model (a positive one multiplies the survival odds, so lengthens life; flexsurv’s odds-scale coefficients are these negated). df=1 on the odds scale is now checked to give PO(LogLogistic)’s coefficients.

  • robust_p_values(cluster=None) on the parametric regressions: the Wald p-values on the robust standard errors, the p column of summary(robust=True).

  • Robust is all or none on the parametric regressions. In 0.26 summary(robust=True) showed robust (sandwich) standard errors while cb, param_cb and p_values kept the model-based covariance, so one coefficient could show two uncertainties. Now cb, quantile_cb and param_cb take robust=True and cluster, as summary does, and robust_p_values() gives the p-values, all on the robust covariance: param_cb(name, robust=True) is the interval in summary(robust=True), and robust_p_values() its p. What has no robust form refuses with a message rather than mix: robust=True with method="lr" or "bootstrap" (they use no covariance), cluster without robust=True, and, as before, a model restored from a dict (no data for the sandwich), a penalised fit and a fit_tvc model. Without robust=True nothing changes: every bound and p_values stay model-based (with weights w that covariance is already the robust one).

  • ``hess_inv`` is always the inverse Hessian. In 0.26 a parametric model fitted with weights w (Weibull.fit(x, c, w=w) and the others) held the robust (sandwich) covariance in hess_inv. Now hess_inv is the inverse Hessian of the weighted log-likelihood with the weights as given (R’s survreg(..., robust = TRUE)$naive.var), as its name says, and the robust covariance is covariance() (and standard_errors()), as it already was. Every bound, band, plot and summary inside SurPyval reads covariance(), so a weighted fit’s bounds are unchanged; unweighted fits are unchanged (the two matrices are the same there). If you read hess_inv for a variance, read covariance() instead: on a weighted fit hess_inv is now the smaller, model-based matrix, which is not the variance of the estimate. A weighted model’s dictionary stores each matrix under its own name: "hess_inv" is the inverse Hessian and "covariance" the robust covariance. A weighted model saved by 0.26 loads with its robust bounds and no hess_inv (it saved the robust covariance as "hess_inv" and did not save the inverse Hessian).

  • Weighted models saved by 0.27 cannot be loaded by 0.26. Every model fitted with weights w (the parametric distributions and regressions, Cox and its penalised and competing-risks forms, the distributional and Royston-Parmar regressions, Aalen’s additive model, the non-parametric estimates including Turnbull, and the Aalen-Johansen CompetingRisks) is saved as schema 4 (to_dict, to_json), which 0.26 refuses with a request to upgrade rather than read the inverse Hessian, now under "hess_inv", as the robust covariance. Weighted SurpyvalData stays schema 3, and unweighted models save as before. 0.27 still reads every weighted model 0.26 saved, with the same bounds.

  • Penalised fits on more models: ridge, lasso and elastic net (fit_penalised(..., penalizer, l1_ratio, standardise)) on RoystonParmarPH / RoystonParmarPO (the PH or PO family on the spline baseline), on the Cox model with time-varying covariates (CoxPH.fit_tvc_penalised and CoxPH.fit_tvc_timeline_penalised), on the cause-specific competing-risks Cox model (CompetingRisksProportionalHazards.fit_penalised, one penalised Cox fit per cause), on ProportionalIntensityHPP and on the distributional regressions (WeibullDistributional.fit_penalised and the others, with a penalty per parameter’s coefficients). Each has the refusals of CoxPH.fit_penalised (no covariance, bounds or tests; weights refused) and counts its effective degrees of freedom in aic and bic. The Cox, cause-specific and HPP fits agree with R’s glmnet to six digits; the distributional fit on a Weibull’s scale alone is WeibullAFT.fit_penalised, coefficient for coefficient.

  • penalty_path(fit_penalised, *data, l1_ratio=..., n_penalties=20, min_ratio=1e-3): the coefficient path of any penalised fit, over glmnet’s default path of penalties (its largest penalty and the coefficients along it agree with glmnet’s), with each fit’s effective degrees of freedom, AIC and BIC; best("bic") or best("aic") chooses the penalty, table() lists the path and plot() draws it.

  • The penalised regression guide and the fit_penalised docstrings now say that standardise=True divides by standard deviations with divisor N (glmnet’s), not N - 1 (lifelines’), why, how large the difference is (a factor of \(\sqrt{N / (N - 1)}\)), and how to reproduce a lifelines fit. No change in behaviour.

  • Penalised Cox on start-stop data counts subjects, not rows: CoxPH.fit_tvc_penalised and fit_tvc_timeline_penalised divide the partial likelihood by the number of subjects and standardise the covariates over the subjects (each subject’s covariate averaged over its follow-up), so splitting the same follow-up into more rows no longer changes how hard a penalizer shrinks. In 0.26 the way to fit start-stop rows was CoxPH.fit_penalised(stop, Z, tl=start), which counts rows (as glmnet); with no ids it still does, unchanged, and the guide now points start-stop data to fit_tvc_penalised.

  • Refusals no longer send users to issue numbers: the diagnose() refusals of models whose checks are not built yet, and a few other messages, said “tracked in #NNN” (issues that are now closed). Each now says what to use instead: a parametric competing-risks model points to each cause’s models[cause].diagnose(), Buckley-James and distributional regressions to a PH or AFT fit’s diagnose(), and so on.

  • diagnose() on an AalenAdditiveModel or a BayesianParametric was an AttributeError; it now refuses with NotImplementedError, pointing to constant_effects_test() and model.mle.diagnose().

  • fit_bayes(..., w=...) and fit_bayes_from_df(..., w_col=...) were Python’s TypeError; they now raise a ValueError naming the method and the argument, why, and what to use instead (the weighted maximum-likelihood fit, or counts n).

  • The printout of a limited-failure fit whose lfp_p lands at its bound of 1 (within 1e-5) now says so and what to do: the data show no sign of units that never fail, so fit without lfp=True.

  • Documented two results that surprised readers: a competing-risks model’s all-cause ff follows how (Nelson-Aalen by default) and so is below the sum of the cumulative incidences unless fitted with how="Kaplan-Meier"; and NonParametric.cs with the default step estimate holds its last value past the data, while the interpolated forms give nan there.

Deprecated.

  • Arguments that, given by position, were silently read as something else now warn, with a FutureWarning (shown wherever the call is made) that says what the value was taken as and the keyword to use. Nothing else changes: each call returns exactly what it did before, and the arguments stay positional (making them keyword-only, or refusing the call, would be a breaking change, which waits for 2.0). Passing the argument by name silences the warning.

    • The recurrent fits’ item ids. CrowAMSAA, Duane, CoxLewis, HPP, NonParametricCounting, ARA, ARI, GeneralizedRenewal, GeneralizedOneRenewal, CauseSpecificMCF and CauseSpecificNHPP take the item ids i second, where every other fit(x, c, n, t) takes the censoring flags, so CrowAMSAA.fit(x, c) read the flags as two items with nothing censored: on x = [5, 12, 20, 31, 45, 60, 80], c = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1] it gives alpha 19.99 and beta 1.00, where fit(x, c=c) gives 7.63 and 0.76. The same holds after Z in ProportionalIntensityHPP, ProportionalIntensityNHPP, AndersenGill, PrenticeWilliamsPeterson, WeiLinWeissfeld and CauseSpecificProportionalIntensity (fit, fit_penalised), and for i_col in every recurrent fit_from_df. The ids stay a positional data argument (fit(x, i, c) is unchanged), so the warning fires only for the call that cannot be told apart: i given by position, no c, and values of 0s and 1s. Name the argument (c= or i=).

    • Parametric.mean(defective, tau) and ParametricCompetingRisks.mean(defective): mean(5) took the 5 as defective and ignored it (6.524 on a Weibull fitted to 3, ..., 10), where a non-parametric model’s mean(5) is the mean restricted to 5 (mean(tau=5) is 4.671). Pass defective by name.

    • Parametric.mean_cb(alpha_ci, ...): a non-parametric model’s mean_cb takes tau first. Pass alpha_ci by name.

    • Parametric.random(size, a, b) and random_data: every other model’s random(size, random_state) takes the seed second, so model.random(10, 42) truncated the draws below 42 (every draw inf on that Weibull). Pass a and b by name.

    • CompetingRisks.plot(stacked, ax): every other plot takes the axes first, so plot(ax) drew stacked curves on new axes. Pass stacked by name.

  • AalenAdditive.fit(..., coef_penalty=) (and fit_from_df) is now penalizer=, the name every other penalised fit uses; the model’s coef_penalty attribute is now penalizer and its saved dict’s key "penalizer" (a dict saved with "coef_penalty" still loads). The old names still work, with a DeprecationWarning, until v0.28. The penalty itself is unchanged: a ridge on the covariates only, scaled by each covariate’s variance.

Removed.

  • The hints for names removed in v0.23 and v0.24 are retired. Using one of these names now raises Python’s plain AttributeError, TypeError or ImportError (or, for a parameter name, the usual “Unknown parameter” ValueError), without the message that named the release and the replacement. The names, with what replaced them:

    • model and fitter attributes: param_names (parameter_names), cov_matrix and cov (covariance()), se (standard_errors()), loglike (neg_ll()), loglik (log_likelihood), loglik_no_frailty (log_likelihood_no_frailty), and MixtureModel’s EM, Q, expectation, maximisation, likelihood and initialise_params (internal to fit());

    • top-level names: DualExponential, DualPower, Eyring, InverseExponential, InverseEyring, InversePower, LifeModel, Linear, Power, PowerExponential and ExponentialLifeModel (all in surpyval.life_models), and NUM, TINIEST and EPS (use numpy);

    • the module surpyval.utils.score (surpyval.metrics.concordance_index);

    • arguments: cs(X=) (given), ARI.fit(dist=), ARI.fit_from_recurrent_data(dist=) and ARI.fit_from_parameters(dist=, dist_params=) (baseline, baseline_params), CustomDistribution(param_names=) (parameter_names), from_params(p=) (lfp_p), success_run(confidence=, alpha=) (alpha_ci), and a regression or competing-risks fit_from_df given x=, c= or another fit argument’s name for a column (x_col, …);

    • neg_ll(beta) on the semi-parametric models (neg_ll_of(beta)); neg_ll now takes no arguments;

    • the parameter names p (lfp_p) and beta_j (the covariate’s column, else coef_j) in fixed and param_cb.

    The hints for names removed in v0.25 and v0.26 stay. A fit_from_df that passes other keywords on to fit (the univariate, recurrent and Fine-Gray ones) still refuses a column given by the fit argument’s name and names the _col argument.

Fixed.

  • Joint fits that stopped at a correlation of 1 (an intentional numerical change for those fits only). WeibullJointPH (and any JointPH with two or more varying path parameters) could run onto the edge where the random effects are perfectly correlated, where the likelihood is flat, and stop there short of the maximum, unverified and with a singular Hessian, so predict(...).cb and standard_errors() refused. Two of the 400 fleets of the joint calibration study did: their maxima are 38.8 and 37.1 better, with corr_a_b 0.22 and 0.23 rather than 1, and are verified. A fit whose first answer is not a verified maximum now searches once more from no correlation, and keeps that answer where it is verified (or else the lower of the two); a verified fit is unchanged. Near the edge the adaptive nodes’ likelihood can be far off (5099.8 where a grid integral gives 5197.8), so where the first search stops there it is not compared with the verified answer.

  • Fits that failed or ended in the wrong place when the time unit changed (an intentional numerical change, in the sixth digit or beyond in ordinary units). Writing the same times in another unit should give the same model. Every family with a unit check was fitted to its test data as given and with the times multiplied by 1e-6, 3600, 1/8760 and 1e6. These failed:

    • WeibullJointPH (every link) in seconds or in a million units warned that its maximum was unverified, with sf up to 0.99 off. The curvature of a slope per second is about 1e13 times that of a slope per hour. The random effects’ modes, their quadrature grid and the outer search factorised and floored that curvature in raw units. Each is now taken in the parameters’ own scale (the random effects’ prior spread; the Hessian’s diagonal). The fits now agree to 1e-12 in every unit.

    • The parametric additive hazards models (WeibullAH and the others) with times a millionth of the unit stopped at their start, with every coefficient 0, and called that a maximum. LogNormalAH had sf 1.3 off and GumbelAH 77 off. In seconds or a million units some warned that their maximum was unverified. A coefficient is a rate (about 1e5 there), and the search measured it in steps of 1. It is now measured in 1 / (range(Z) T), with T the median observed time, and an unbounded baseline location gets the univariate fits’ floor.

    • The distributional regressions on a location (Normal, Gumbel, Logistic): off by up to 1e5 and unverified in millionths or a million units. A parameter on the identity link and its coefficients are now searched in that parameter’s starting size. This also reaches the mixture cure models, which share the search.

    • HPP started its search at a rate of 1 in whatever unit was used, and in millionths, years or a million units it stayed there, unverified. It now starts at the events counted over the time watched, which is the answer itself when nothing is truncated.

    • GammaProcess and DestructiveDegradation took their densities (and hazards) as differences in steps of at least 1e-6 of the unit. That was most of a time measured in millionths, so they were off by 1% and 26%. The steps are now a millionth of the time itself.

    Before and after, the largest relative difference in sf and hf from the fit in the data’s own units, in millionths / seconds / years / a million units (!: the fit warned):
