    In the data’s own units the likelihood at the answer is unchanged to 1e-12. The changed searches stop elsewhere along flat directions within their tolerance. Largest change in a parameter on the test data: LogNormalDistributional 1.05e-5 (a coefficient -0.0990699, now -0.0990689), LogisticDistributional 5.5e-6 (-2.214352, now -2.214340), NormalDistributional 3.3e-6, GammaAH 1.4e-6 (alpha 5.261436, now 5.261444), LogisticAH 1.2e-6, the other additive hazards and mixture cure models below 1e-6, and the joint models 1e-14. The largest changes in predictions are 1.3e-5 (a NormalDistributional sf of 4.6e-13) and 1e-5 in a LogisticDistributional sf of 0.186. The largest changes in Wald bounds are 4.9e-4 (a GumbelDistributional bound of 1.4e-48) and 7e-5 on an ordinary value (a LogisticDistributional coefficient’s bound, -0.1776675, now -0.1776545). The seeded bootstrap bounds of WeibullAH’s coefficients moved by up to 0.6% (-0.0018080, now -0.0018194), because every resample’s fit follows the new search.

  • Bootstrap intervals read their bounds at the levels asked, so they are a little wider and hold their level (an intentional numerical change). method="bootstrap" bounds (param_cb, cb, quantile_cb, mrl_cb, rmst_cb) of the parametric models, plain, offset, limited-failure and zero-inflated, and of the parametric regressions took each bound from the refits with the (n - 1) p rule (np.quantile’s default). The k-th smallest of n refits sits at the k / (n + 1) quantile on average, so with the default 200 refits a 95% interval ran from about the 3.0% to the 97.0% point of the refits’ distribution rather than 2.5% to 97.5% (and a 90% one from 5.5% to 94.5%): about 2% too narrow, and about a point of coverage short, at every sample size. A bound at level p is now the (n + 1) p-th smallest refit, interpolated between refits (Davison and Hinkley 1997, section 5.2.2; np.quantile’s method="weibull"). For example, a Weibull fitted to failures at 1.2, 2.5, 3.1, 4.0, 4.4, 5.3, 6.1, 6.8, 7.7, 8.9, 9.5, 10.2, 11.8, 13.0 and 14.6 and five units censored at 15: param_cb("alpha", alpha_ci=0.1, method="bootstrap", random_state=1) was [8.746, 16.735] and is now [8.695, 16.906]; quantile_cb(0.1) with the same options was [1.339, 4.640] and is now [1.324, 4.660]. In the plain bootstrap calibration study (same seeds, so the same refits), the average coverage of each size’s 16 bounds moved, at 90% / 95%:

    Units

    before

    now

    30

    0.868 / 0.918

    0.880 / 0.930

    100

    0.879 / 0.934

    0.891 / 0.947

    300

    0.878 / 0.938

    0.888 / 0.946

    On 8,000 simulated data sets of 300 Weibull units (an independent implementation of the same bootstrap), the 90% / 95% intervals covered 89.0% / 94.0% with the old rule and 90.0% / 95.0% with the new one. The Weibull 30-unit design of that study, a known shortfall before, now passes every bound. The percentile bootstraps of the Kaplan-Meier, degradation and Buckley-James models now use the same rule (next entry).

  • The percentile bootstrap bounds read their levels the same way (an intentional numerical change). The non-parametric bootstrap_cb (Kaplan-Meier, Nelson-Aalen, Fleming-Harrington and Turnbull), the degradation models’ cb(..., method="bootstrap"), the destructive-degradation cb and the Buckley-James bootstrap_ci (and summary(n_boot=...)) took each bound from the resamples with the (n - 1) p rule, as the parametric bootstrap did before the entry above, so their intervals were about 2% too narrow at 200 resamples. They now take the (n + 1) p-th smallest resample, interpolated, the rule the parametric bounds use; one helper (utils.linalg.bootstrap_quantile) holds it for every bootstrap bound. The pointwise band around the lowess trend on the diagnostic plots uses it too. With 200 resamples and the default 95% level:

    • Kaplan-Meier, failures at 1.2, 2.5, 3.1, 4.0, 4.4, 5.3, 6.1, 6.8, 7.7, 8.9, 9.5, 10.2, 11.8, 13.0 and 14.6 and five units censored at 15, bootstrap_cb(10, n_boot=200, random_state=1): [0.2987, 0.65] is now [0.2513, 0.65] (the resampled R takes steps of 0.05, so a bound can move by most of a step);

    • a linear-path degradation analysis (20 units, Weibull lifetimes), cb(40, on="sf", method="bootstrap", n_boot=200, random_state=7): [0.3808, 0.7449] is now [0.3768, 0.7451];

    • a destructive-degradation fit (400 specimens, LogNormal), cb(30, on="sf", n_boot=200, random_state=3): [0.4494, 0.5540] is now [0.4427, 0.5568];

    • a Buckley-James fit (300 units, two covariates), bootstrap_ci(n_boot=200, random_state=0): [-1.0475, -0.8132] and [0.2665, 0.5214] are now [-1.0505, -0.8096] and [0.2564, 0.5245].

    The same seeds give the same resamples, so only the bounds moved. No calibration study covers these bootstraps yet.

  • The other names ``Gauss``, ``Galton`` and ``life_models.Arrhenius`` now behave exactly as ``Normal``, ``LogNormal`` and ``life_models.Exponential``, except for the name they carry. A model fitted with an alias keeps the alias in its repr and to_dict, and loads back (from JSON or a pickle) with it. Where the package asks which distribution or life model a model has, it now asks by the canonical name (new: dist.canonical_name, and canonical_name on the life models; surpyval.utils.aliases). Before, an alias was a different name to those checks, so:

    • Gauss.fit and Galton.fit skipped the check for data with no finite maximum: an exact failure at 1 observable only up to 1, one at 2 and one known to be before 3 gave Gauss mu = 2, sigma = 1e-54 (Galton: sigma = 4.5e-9), marked unverified, where Normal.fit refuses with a NoFiniteMaximumError. Now both refuse.

    • AcceleratedLife(Gauss, ...) and AcceleratedLife(Galton, ...) were refused (“not supported”); they now fit, to the same numbers as Normal and LogNormal.

    • Galton’s restricted mean was a quadrature of sf rather than the LogNormal’s closed form; it is now the closed form, the same to the last digit (on the times 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.5 to 4, 2.8953554955438934 before, 2.8953554955438943 now).

    • fit_best(include=["Gauss"]) was refused as an unknown name; an alias now names its distribution’s candidate.

    • The distributional, mixture-cure, PyMC, conjugate-prior and test planning code, and the diagnostics’ advice, now take an alias as its distribution.

    life_models.Arrhenius is now its own object (it was life_models.Exponential itself), so a model built with it says “Arrhenius life model” and saves "life_model_name": "Arrhenius". A dictionary saved before with an Arrhenius model holds "Exponential" (the two could not be told apart) and loads as Exponential; a dictionary saved with Gauss or Galton always held that name, and loads as before. Arrhenius is Exponential is no longer true; use canonical_name to compare them.

  • on="R" and on="F" (accepted spellings of "sf" and "ff") were refused by four functions that take on: an adjusted curve’s cb, plot_nonparametric, plot_partial_effects and a Bayesian fit’s compare_to. They now give exactly what "sf" and "ff" give, as everywhere else.

  • ProportionalIntensityNHPP starts from the covariate-free fit of its baseline for data the item records (ItemHistory) refuse but the fit takes: an item whose id is blank text, an item whose end of observation is at its entry age, or a failure at the top of an inspection window that counts failures. Those used to start every baseline parameter at one, and with a CoxLewis baseline on ages in the tens of thousands the fit stopped there, warned that it had not reached a verified maximum and returned params [1, 1], coefficients [0, 0] and a nan log-likelihood. On 30 simulated items observed to 50,000 hours, one with a blank id, it now gives alpha -9.264, beta 2.366e-05 and coefficients 0.5421 and -0.1913 (log-likelihood -2836.7). Where the unit start did converge (Duane, CrowAMSAA) the estimates move by about 1e-6 of a standard error (at most 4e-7 relative; Duane’s b 5.585229e-07 -> 5.585231e-07 on that example), the log-likelihood the same to 1e-12. Data the records take starts exactly as before.

  • fit_from_ecdf on every parametric family refuses a curve that falls as x rises, with a ValueError: “F must rise with x; if you have a survival curve R, pass F = 1 - R”, and where it falls. A survival curve passed in place of the CDF (NonParametric.fit_from_ecdf takes R) was fitted without a word: Weibull.fit_from_ecdf([1, 2, 3, 4], [0.9, 0.7, 0.4, 0.1]) gave alpha 1.754 and a negative beta, -2.045. The points may still come in any order (they are checked in order of x), flat steps are accepted, and a curve that rises is fitted exactly as before. Values outside [0, 1] were already refused.

  • Standard errors and bounds of the repairable-system models no longer move with the unit of time. The covariance of every Poisson-process fit (HPP, CrowAMSAA, Duane, CoxLewis), of the renewal models (GeneralizedOneRenewal, GeneralizedRenewal, ARA, ARI), of the proportional-intensity regressions and of the cause-specific models built on them comes from a finite-difference Hessian of the likelihood, whose step was a fraction of each parameter’s own size with a floor of 0.01 of a unit. A parameter that is tiny in small units was then stepped by far too much: Duane’s scale b is 3e-4 with times in hours where it is 0.2 in months, and Cox-Lewis’s slope 3e-5. On one data set written in months and in hours, the standard error of Duane’s alpha was 0.37272 and 0.37159 (now 0.372722 and 0.372722), a cb_tvc bound 0.09521 and 0.09558 (now 0.09521 and 0.09521), and the standard error of Cox-Lewis’s slope, times the unit, 0.0202494 and 0.0202419 (now 0.0202494 and 0.0202493); in seconds it was 1.6e-82 (now 0.0202493). The steps now come from the likelihood itself (surpyval.utils.linalg.scale_free_hessian): each parameter is stepped by a fixed fraction of the distance over which the likelihood falls, the differences are taken in coordinates in which the Hessian is the identity (so strongly correlated parameters lose nothing to cancellation), and two step sizes more are combined to cancel the leading errors. Against the exact Hessian of a power-law process the standard errors agree to 1e-8 from years to seconds.

    The error was largest for Duane with event times in the thousands of hours, where b is a few millionths. On a fleet of 12 systems with 179 events to 18,000 hours, the standard error of alpha was 0.0213 where the likelihood gives 0.1135, so its 95% interval was 1.508 to 1.591, about five times too narrow, while CrowAMSAA’s beta (the same parameter) gave 1.342 to 1.788; Duane now gives 1.342 to 1.788 too. On other such fleets it gave no standard error at all (nan): over 200 simulated fleets a 90% interval on alpha covered the true shape in 31 (now 173). A test pins Duane’s standard errors to the closed-form observed information of the power-law likelihood and to Crow-AMSAA’s, and the recurrent calibration study now checks Duane’s param_cb coverage in hours.

    The Wald bounds on the curves (cif_cb, iif_cb, mtbf_cb, cb_tvc and the cause-specific ones) take the curve’s gradient by finite differences too, with the same floor; their steps are now a fraction of each parameter’s standard error (delta_method_se(..., scale_free=True)), which moves with the unit. For Cox-Lewis in seconds (a slope of 9e-9 against a step of 6e-8) a cif_cb taken at the estimates the fit in months implies was [2.3e-36, 8.7e36] where it should be [2.32363, 8.58449]; it is now [2.32363, 8.58449]. Every bound of these models now rescales with the unit exactly (to 1e-6, the test’s tolerance, at the same estimates). The estimates and the likelihood were unit-free already and are unchanged; the shared numerical_hessian, delta_method_se’s default and every other family’s covariance and bounds are unchanged.

    Numbers that move (the conformance fixtures, in their own units; nothing else in the refactor snapshot changes): every standard error, summary() interval, param_cb, saved covariance and Wald bound of the models below, by at most the relative amount shown (leaving out covariances that are zero to rounding, such as -4.7e-8 now 1.5e-10).

    A covariance costs about three times the likelihood evaluations it did.

  • Bayesian fits keep their digits in both tails, for every engine (grid, Laplace, draws from another sampler) and the offset, limited-failure and zero-inflated forms. ff is the posterior average of each point’s own failure function rather than 1 - sf, which kept no digits of a failure probability below about 1e-8; Hf is -log1p(-ff) while ff is below one half and -log(sf) above, and stays finite where sf underflows; cri(on="ff") and cri(on="Hf") and compare_to(on="ff") keep the same digits. For the Weibull fit above, ff(0.1) was 4.1397633e-09 and is now 4.1397644e-09 (the posterior average summed exactly is 4.139764380041089e-09; the old value was off by 2.6e-7 relative, the new one by less than 1e-15), and qf(1e-12) was 5.7914e-05 and is now 5.7848e-05. Below the support ff is now exactly 0 and sf exactly 1 (they were a rounding either side). Elsewhere values move only in their last digits (ff(100) was 7.935912007228652e-05, now 7.93591200732899e-05).

  • qf of a Bayesian fit found by search (grid, Laplace, draws) now converges in the upper tail: it solves on the log of ff up to p = 0.5 and on the log of sf above, with a tolerance relative to the time scale. On the Weibull fit above, qf(0.9999) and qf(1 - 1e-9) raised “Failed to converge after 100 iterations” and are now 275897.7 and 15438917.1. On positive times it solves on the log of time, so a quantile far below the posterior points’ own is found to a relative tolerance: a Laplace ExpoWeibull fit’s qf(1e-12) had stopped at a time where ff was 3.7e-10.

  • Standard errors and bounds of the other families that take finite differences no longer move with the unit of time either. Their steps were a fraction of each parameter with a fixed floor (0.01, or 1), the rule fixed above for the repairable-system models, and a parameter that is small in the unit the times are written in (an additive hazard’s coefficient, a rate per second, a margin’s scale in years) was stepped by a large part of itself. Each now takes its steps from the likelihood or from the standard errors, as the repairable-system models do. The estimates are unchanged. Fitting one fixture with its times in hours and again in seconds (or years, or a million times either), the relative difference between the two, before and now:

    margins’ standard errors 1.2e-4 in seconds and 6.4e-3 with times a millionth of the unit, now 1e-7 and 2e-7

    Families whose covariance and bounds come from exact derivatives (the parametric distributions with offset, limited-failure and zero-inflated forms, the PH, AFT, PO and distributional regressions, the parametric competing-risks, mixture and Royston-Parmar regression models) and the semi-parametric ones were unit-free already, to the fit’s own agreement. The PH, AFT and PO regressions’ Wald bounds use the new gradient too and move by at most 1.2e-6 on the conformance fixtures (and 1e-4 on one GumbelPH density bound of 1.5e18).

    Numbers that move in the fixtures’ own units: the additive-hazards and accelerated-life bounds by at most 4e-10; RoystonParmar’s standard errors by up to 2e-4 (gamma_1’s 1.840876, now 1.840929; the new Hessian also removes the cancellation between the strongly correlated spline coefficients); the frailty models’ by up to 2e-6 (the frailty variance’s is unchanged, 0.0016927 for WeibullFrailty); GammaProcess’s by up to 1e-5 (alpha’s 0.0947975, now 0.0947984), WienerProcess’s by 1e-8; DegradationAnalysis’s analytic bounds by up to 1.7e-6; the copulas’ covariances by up to 7.6e-5 (ClaytonCopula’s theta standard error 1.234759, now 1.234775); bootstrap (BCa) bounds by up to 2e-9. surpyval.utils.linalg gains curvature_scales (each parameter’s scale in a likelihood), and scale_free_hessian a fallback_step.

  • The package no longer silences other threads’ warnings. Wherever it held a warning back (117 places: the starts and polishes of fits, inner refits of bootstraps and diagnostics, autograd’s “output seems independent of input” and the like) it used with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("ignore"), and Python’s warning filters are one list for every thread: while such a block ran, a warning raised anywhere else in the process was dropped, and two threads leaving blocks out of order could leave everything ignored for the rest of the process. Those blocks now ignore in their own thread only (surpyval.utils.warnings.ignoring_warnings), and never save and restore the shared list. In one thread nothing changes: the same warnings are held back and the same are given (the results and warnings of every model in the conformance suite are the same to the last bit). The six places that collect an inner step’s warnings to read or repeat them, or raise one, now do so in their own thread only too (collecting_warnings and raising_warnings in the same module): fit_best, the renewal fits’ check for a life with no finite maximum, the Cox frailty fit’s Cox fit, the mean residual life’s integral, diagnose()’s Cramer-von Mises test of a repairable-system model, and the unknown-level check of a formula naming its levels. Before, while one of them ran, every warning raised in another thread went into its list and was lost to that thread (a test counted 29,356 such warnings during one fit_best), and a formula’s check made other threads’ DataMismatchWarning errors. The package no longer changes the shared warning filters anywhere.

  • An exponential fitted with a Gamma prior on a rate per hour (Exponential.fit_bayes(x, priors={"failure_rate": Gamma.from_params([40, 1e9])}), 40 failures in a billion unit-hours, as a handbook or a data library gives a rate) no longer raises OverflowError from sf, ff, df, hf and Hf. Its predictive distribution is a closed form (a Lomax of the posterior’s shape a and scale b) that was evaluated as a * b**a / (b + x)**(a + 1), and b**a passes the largest float once b is near 1e9 and a above about 34. The five functions and qf are now worked out on the log scale (Hf(x) = a log(1 + x / b)), so the same study in hours and in millions of hours gives the same probabilities; on a scale that did not overflow the values are the same to rounding, and ff near 0 keeps its digits. mrl of such a fit is the Lomax’s closed form, (b + x) / (a - 1), in place of a numerical integral that returned -1 with a per-hour prior and was up to 1% out far into the tail on any scale; hf at an infinite time is 0, not nan.

  • An accelerated life fit (AcceleratedLife, the parameter-substitution fitter) no longer makes warnings in other threads raise. To start its search it fits the distribution at each stress level and, where that fit warned, started from the level’s mean time instead; it noticed the warnings by turning every warning into an error with warnings.filterwarnings("error"), and Python’s warning filters are shared by every thread, so while the fit ran, a warning anywhere else in the process (a DeprecationWarning in an unrelated web request, say) became an exception there. The level’s fit is now checked directly: numpy’s floating-point errors raise only in that thread (np.errstate), the fit must reach a verified maximum with finite parameters, and weights must leave the level at least 20 effective units, the cases in which it warned. The same starts are chosen as before (checked on every level fitted by the accelerated life tests and conformance cases). Likewise, a formula’s unknown categorical levels are now found by reading the data, not by turning formulaic’s DataMismatchWarning into an error, except for a formula naming its levels (levels=) or a term computed from the data (C(k + 1)), where the warning is still caught.

  • A penalised fit (fit_penalised of every model) whose search stops short of the minimum now searches a second time, from the unpenalised fit, and keeps the better answer. A Weibull AFT lasso fit on the Rossi data (fin, age, prio, l1_ratio=1, penalty 0.00068) stopped near its start, “unverified”, with a penalised objective of 1.5892, above the 1.5811 reached at the larger penalty 0.0038; it now reaches 1.5792 and is verified. The second search runs only when the first fails its optimality check, so fits that converged are unchanged (to the last digit) and cost no more.

  • robust_covariance(cluster=...) (and robust_standard_errors, summary(robust=True, cluster=...)) on a distributional regression (WeibullDistributional and the others) matched the cluster labels to the rows in the fit’s sorted order rather than in the order given, so the clustered standard errors were wrong whenever the rows were not already in time order (on 120 rows in clusters of four, 0.72 against the correct 0.50 for alpha). The labels now follow their rows, as in the other parametric regressions. Unclustered robust standard errors were not affected.

  • Likelihood-ratio bounds on a profile that flattens out towards a limit (a Gamma with an offset tends to the Normal as its shape grows) no longer depend on the platform. Far out along such a profile its deviance cannot be solved precisely, and the walk found a crossing of the critical value in that noise: a Gamma offset model’s 80% upper bound on alpha was about 2e11, 7e11, 1.6e12 or infinity depending on the machine. A crossing or a levelling off is now checked a hair either side; where the deviance there is noise, the bound is the edge of the parameter’s space if the points before the noise show the profile converging below the critical value (inf for that alpha), and otherwise it is nan with a warning that the profile was too flat to follow, saying how far it was followed.

  • CoxPH.fit(..., w=w) on data whose partial likelihood has no finite maximum (a covariate that separates the events from the survivors) no longer lets numpy’s overflow and invalid-value warnings through beside its own “No finite maximum” warning: the weighted likelihood, its score residuals and baseline now take exp(eta) relative to the largest eta, which cannot overflow. Fits with a finite maximum are unchanged to rounding.

  • AalenAdditiveModel.constant_effects_test rejected effects that are constant far more often than its level with a few hundred units (about 21% at the 5% level with 300 units, 44% with 100). Its resampled null multiplied the least-squares residuals, which nearly vanish where few units are at risk; it now multiplies the events, so its spread is the optional variation of B. The test now holds its level from about 300 units and is conservative with 100. The statistics are unchanged; p-values change.

  • AalenAdditive.fit no longer reports noise for B and its variance at a last event time where too few units are at risk to separate the covariates: the sums over the risk set left rounding error that made the singular step look estimable. The estimate now stops before that step, as it was meant to.

Performance.

  • Survival along a step schedule is several times faster for the proportional hazards (log-linear link), proportional odds, additive hazards and accelerated failure time families: Hf_tvc, sf_tvc, cb_tvc and mean_tvc. The model’s cumulative hazard (or, for AFT, its rate) was evaluated once per segment of the schedule; it is now evaluated once for all of them, each segment’s beta'(z - c) still taken one row at a time and passed as a single column, so the numbers are the same bit for bit (a dot product over all the rows at once can round differently from one row’s). Accelerated life models and custom covariate links keep the segment-at-a-time loop. A 200-segment schedule at 500 times on a 400-unit fit, Hf_tvc and sf_tvc together: WeibullPH 74 -> 6.5 ms, WeibullPO 96 -> 36 ms, WeibullAFT 14 -> 7.4 ms; cb_tvc 496 -> 117 ms (PH), 589 -> 302 ms (PO), 101 -> 60 ms (AFT).

  • Recurrent-event fits prepare their data faster: handle_xicn checked each item’s censoring rows, observation window and covariates in a Python loop, and the interarrival times, each row’s previous time, each item’s first row (the renewal fits’ start) and the fitted items’ ages were found item by item, some by a scan of every row per item. All are now found for every item at once; the checks go item by item only when one fails, so the error is the one it was. The data, the fits and every message are the same bit for bit (the refactor snapshot is unchanged). On 1,000 items with about 10 events each: CrowAMSAA 75 -> 7 ms, HPP 98 -> 24 ms, ProportionalIntensityHPP 92 -> 19 ms, CoxLewis 130 -> 56 ms, Duane 159 -> 87 ms, GeneralizedRenewal 515 -> 385 ms, ARA 605 -> 480 ms, ARI 565 -> 486 ms, ProportionalIntensityNHPP 634 -> 476 ms (the semi-parametric AndersenGill, PrenticeWilliamsPeterson and WeiLinWeissfeld already built their rows with array operations).

  • The proportional-intensity NHPP’s default start is faster: the data without its covariates, which the start fits the baseline to, was built by turning every item into an ItemHistory record and back. EventHistoryData.without("covariates") now builds it from the arrays wherever that gives the same data, every array and dtype bit for bit (the records are still used for data with event types, states, time-varying covariates, attributes or observation windows, and for data the records could refuse). On 1,000 items with about 10 events each, without("covariates") 318 -> 5 ms and the Duane ProportionalIntensityNHPP fit 1,021 -> 575 ms (a loaded machine; run back to back); the fits’ numbers are unchanged.

Documentation.

  • The description of the censoring flag c in the docstrings of the main entry points (the parametric and non-parametric fit, MixtureModel, fit_best, plotting_positions, logrank, the proportional hazards fit, SurpyvalData and the pseudo-observation functions) says what each code means in words any field uses (0 is the observed event, such as a failure, a death or a relapse) and how to convert a status column in which 1 marks the event. Wording only.

  • New page: Survival Analysis from Scratch, for readers who have never met censoring. It explains time-to-event data, why the times cannot simply be averaged, censoring and truncation, the survival, hazard and cumulative hazard functions, the Kaplan-Meier estimate worked by hand, a Weibull fit and how to read it, bounds, comparing groups and regression, with an engineering example (pump failures) and a medical one (time to relapse) throughout. Linked from the front page and the Quickstart.

Internal.

  • The Bayesian calibration study’s left-truncated scenario draws its simulated lifetimes on the survival scale (the cumulative hazard above the entry age), so a true model whose life is far shorter than the entry age gives a large finite time instead of inf (which the fit refused, failing one replicate). Same seeds and uniforms: every other replicate’s data agree to 3e-11. Rerun once: no fit refuses and the ranks are uniform, but the 95% coverage is 0.972 (alpha) and 0.970 (B10) against 0.95 +- 0.02, kept as a strict expected failure with the numbers; 1,000 fresh replicates give 0.958, 0.937 and 0.933.

  • The penalised fits (fit_penalised on CoxPH and on the parametric PH, AFT and PO families) now go through one shared fit helper and one model mixin, so further models can take a penalty without a copy of the checks, the standardisation, the refusals of inference, the information criteria’s effective degrees of freedom, saving and the printout. Every penalised result, warning and refusal is unchanged to the last bit. The solver now also takes a model with no Hessian, using finite differences of its gradient, and says so.

  • Stale documentation brought up to date: the model atlas lists CauseSpecificNHPP (no longer a gap) and drops issue numbers that no longer track anything; the README’s model table names CauseSpecificNHPP; the usage skill lists all eight copula families.

  • The diagnostics families’ copies of the same small helpers (number formatting, notes, the covariate kind, the trend sign, formula-column names, the AIC gap) now live once in surpyval/diagnostics/_shared.py. Every diagnosis is unchanged to the last bit.

  • Removed code nothing called: the rename helpers of surpyval.utils.deprecation no deprecation uses any more (reordered_arguments, CallableFloat, MethodFloat, MethodArray, ArrayMethod, RenamedToMethod, MadePrivate), and a few private helpers with no callers. renamed_arguments, RenamedAttribute and renamed_name stay for the next rename.

  • The mutation run of the modules new in 0.26 is complete (all 5,296 mutants; about 81% killed, about 90% without the equivalent ones), with new tests of the Bayesian grid’s posterior quantiles against closed forms and a brute-force posterior: reliabilities that underflow to 0 or round to 1 at some of the posterior’s points, and a mean that is infinite for part of it. scripts/mutation/run.sh pins pytest below 9, which breaks mutmut 3.8.

Documentation.

  • New page: The data model, the one reference for the data every fitter takes: a table of every letter (x, xl/xr, c, n, t, i, e, s, a, m, Z, w) with its meaning, allowed values and default; the rules between them in plain words (exact times and ranges on one row, a unit’s rows in time order, the default and the refusals of a, measurements linked by unit); a worked example of each shape of data (single-event life data, exact times with ranges, recurrent events with a terminal event, multi-state, measurements, covariates, changing covariates as counting-process rows, landmarks); and which models take which letters. Conventions now points to it rather than repeating it, and principle 1 of Design Principles describes the whole data model. Linked from the front page, the Quickstart and Types of Data.

  • New page: Survival Analysis from Scratch, for readers who have never met censoring. It explains time-to-event data, why the times cannot simply be averaged, censoring and truncation, the survival, hazard and cumulative hazard functions, the Kaplan-Meier estimate worked by hand, a Weibull fit and how to read it, bounds, comparing groups and regression, with an engineering example (pump failures) and a medical one (time to relapse) throughout. Linked from the front page and the Quickstart.

  • New page: Glossary, mapping the engineering, medical and statistical words for the same ideas (failure and event, unit and subject, reliability and survival, suspension and right censored, B10 life and 10th percentile) to each other and to SurPyval’s names, with the conversion of an event indicator (1 = event) to the censoring flag c.

  • Field-neutral wording: the README, the front page, Quickstart, Types of Data, Conventions, the aide-mémoire and the introductions of the non-parametric and regression theory pages pair the engineering and the general terms on first use, so they read naturally whatever the field. Wording only: no name, argument, message or number changes.

v0.26 (31 October 2026)

Highlights.

  • Weights, w: sampling, propensity and censoring weights beside the counts n, in the Kaplan-Meier family, the parametric distributions, the parametric regressions and Cox, each with a robust variance. See Weighted Data.

  • Bayesian fitting, Distribution.fit_bayes with priors from surpyval.prior: say what is already believed (a shape, a B10, last year’s fleet) and combine it with the data. See Bayesian Fitting with SurPyval.

  • Distributional regression, WeibullDistributional and the others: covariates on every parameter, so the shape can depend on the load as well as the scale. See Distributional Regression.

  • More regression models: Aalen’s additive hazards (AalenAdditive), with effects that change over time, and Royston-Parmar regression (RoystonParmarPH, RoystonParmarPO), a smooth spline baseline with proportional hazards or odds.

  • Robust standard errors for the parametric regressions, with clusters.

  • Penalised regression, fit_penalised: ridge, lasso and elastic net on Cox and the parametric PH, AFT and PO models, for many or correlated covariates.

  • Comparing groups: pairwise log-rank tests with adjusted p-values, a test of two survival curves at one time, Peto-Peto weightings and the global likelihood-ratio test of a regression.

  • Life tables, a forest plot of regression coefficients, and helpers for PyMC users (PyMC with SurPyval).

Upgrading from 0.25. On 0.25, run your code or tests with python -W error::DeprecationWarning first to find the calls to update. The new arguments are all optional. What can look different:

  • The names 0.25 deprecated now raise (see Removed): RecurrentEventData (use EventHistoryData), and EventHistoryData’s items (use ids) and get_times_to_first_events() (use to_first_events()).

  • A decimal n is still refused, and the message now says to pass weights as w.

  • Weighted models save as schema 3 (to_dict, to_json), which 0.25 and earlier refuse to read rather than read them without their weights. Unweighted models save as before. A weighted SurpyvalData’s dictionary is stamped schema 3 too (an unweighted one still has no schema number), and 0.26 refuses a newer schema; but 0.25 reads a data dictionary without looking at its schema, so it would drop the weights: read weighted data with 0.26.

  • On a weighted fit, covariance() (and a parametric model’s hess_inv) hold the robust sandwich covariance, and every Wald bound is built from it; there is no classical covariance to fall back on.

  • Robust standard errors on the parametric regressions are opt-in: summary() is unchanged, and summary(robust=True) changes only the standard errors and what is built from them in that table (z, p and the intervals). The estimates, cb, param_cb and p_values stay on the model-based covariance.

  • New names at the top level of surpyval: life_table, pairwise_logrank, PairwiseLogRankResult, sf_diff, plot_coefficients, CoefficientPlot, AalenAdditive, AalenAdditiveModel, RoystonParmarPH, RoystonParmarPO, RoystonParmarRegression, Distributional, DistributionalFitter, DistributionalRegressionModel, the <Dist>Distributional fitters, prior and bayes; and the subpackage surpyval.pymc (imported only when asked for).

  • check_ph() on a Cox model warns that it is deprecated (see Deprecated); it returns what it did. model.diagnose(transform=...) gives the same table.

Added

  • Weights, w: how many units of the population each unit stands for (a sampling weight), or how much it is weighted to undo a bias (an inverse probability of treatment or censoring weight). It is taken by KaplanMeier, NelsonAalen and FlemingHarrington, the parametric distributions (maximum likelihood), the parametric regressions (PH, AFT, PO, additive hazards, accelerated life) and CoxPH; by SurpyvalData(..., w=...) and from_dataframe(..., w_col=...); and by fit_from_df(..., w_col=...) (not yet Cox’s). A weighted fit gives the weighted estimate with a robust variance, the only one it offers: the infinitesimal jackknife for the non-parametric estimates (as R’s survfit(..., robust = TRUE)), the sandwich for the parametric and regression fits (survreg(..., robust = TRUE)) and the Lin-Wei sandwich for Cox (coxph(..., robust = TRUE), with robust_covariance(cluster) for units sampled in clusters), all checked against R. Multiplying the weights by a constant changes nothing. Printouts give the effective sample size, and a fit warns when it is below 20. What weights make invalid refuses, saying what to use instead: likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds, band and bootstrap_cb, rank-based plotting positions, methods other than MLE, aic, bic, aic_c and fit_best, and for Cox the residuals, check_ph, strata and exact ties. Turnbull refuses weights; competing risks, the log-rank tests, the Bayesian fit and the other fitters do not take them yet. Nothing changes without w.

  • surpyval.life_table(x, c=None, n=None, tl=None, intervals=None): the actuarial (Cutler-Ederer) life table of right censored data, with or without late entry, as a DataFrame with one row per interval [start, end): the numbers entering, at risk at the start, censored and with the event, the effective number at risk, the conditional probabilities of the event and of surviving, and the survival, density and hazard with their standard errors (Klein and Moeschberger, section 5.4, as R’s KMsurv::lifetab). It takes arrays, a SurpyvalData or a fitted non-parametric model; left and interval censored data and right truncation are refused, pointing to Turnbull.

  • surpyval.plot_coefficients: a forest plot of one or more fitted regression models, each coefficient with its Wald interval from the model’s summary(), on the coefficient’s scale or as a ratio (exp(coef): hazard ratios, acceleration factors, odds ratios) on a log axis, with several models side by side. It returns a CoefficientPlot holding the axes and the values drawn. Additive models have no ratio scale, and on='exp' is refused for them.

  • pairwise_logrank: the log-rank test of every pair of groups in one table, with the p-values adjusted for the number of pairs (Holm by default; Bonferroni, Benjamini-Hochberg or none), taking every argument of logrank. The adjustment on its own is surpyval.univariate.nonparametric.logrank.adjust_p_values.

  • sf_diff: the test of two groups’ survival at one time (Klein et al., 2007), on the log(-log), log, linear, arcsine-square-root or logit scale, with the difference and its interval.

  • logrank (and pairwise_logrank) take weighting="peto-peto" and "modified-peto-peto", and t0 to compare the groups up to a time only.

  • likelihood_ratio_test() on Cox models and on the parametric regressions (PH, AFT, PO and additive hazards; an accelerated life model is refused): the global test of all the covariates against the model without them (R’s “Likelihood ratio test” line of summary(coxph), and the survreg chi-squared).

  • CoxPH.fit_tvc(..., strata=) and fit_tvc_from_df(..., strata_col=): stratified Cox fits of start-stop data.

  • NonParametric.cs(x, given): conditional survival from a non-parametric estimate, as the parametric models’ cs.

  • surpyval.AalenAdditive: Aalen’s non-parametric additive hazards model, h(t | Z) = b_0(t) + b(t)'Z with each effect free to change over time. The fitted AalenAdditiveModel gives the cumulative effects B(t) (cumulative_coefficients) with pointwise Wald bounds (cumulative_coefficients_cb), the kernel-smoothed effects b(t) with a bandwidth (smoothed_coefficients), a unit’s sf, ff, Hf, hf, df, qf, cs and Wald cb, summary(at=), plot(), concordance(), a resampling test that each effect is constant in time (constant_effects_test), an optional ridge penalty (coef_penalty), delayed entry (tl), formulas and fit_from_df, and saving. B and its variance agree with R’s timereg::aalen to rounding; the survival predictions agree with lifelines’ AalenAdditiveFitter wherever the estimated cumulative hazard does not fall.

  • Royston-Parmar (spline baseline) regression: RoystonParmarPH (log cumulative hazard a restricted cubic spline in log time plus beta'Z), RoystonParmarPO (the spline on the log odds, the survival odds multiplied by exp(beta'Z)) and RoystonParmarRegression(df, scale, knots). They are the PH and PO families on a spline baseline, so every censoring kind, truncation, every bound, fit_from_df and saving work as for WeibullPH. Checked against R’s flexsurvspline. The normal scale is refused with covariates (its shift is neither PH nor PO). RoystonParmar.fit is unchanged.

  • Robust (sandwich) standard errors for the parametric regressions (proportional hazards, AFT, proportional odds, additive hazards and accelerated life): robust_covariance(cluster=None) and robust_standard_errors(cluster=None), and summary(robust=True, cluster=...), as the Cox model already had. With cluster the scores are summed by cluster, so correlated rows within a cluster are allowed; counts are frequency weights, as in the fit. Checked against lifelines’ robust=True and R’s survreg with cluster() on the Rossi data. A fit_tvc model refuses them.

  • Penalised regression: fit_penalised(..., penalizer, l1_ratio, standardise) on CoxPH and on the parametric proportional hazards, AFT and proportional odds fitters, for ridge, lasso and elastic-net penalties (one penalty, or one per covariate). The objective is glmnet’s and lifelines’: the negative log-likelihood over the number of units plus the penalty, on standardised covariates by default; the baseline is never penalised. The L1 part is minimised exactly, so coefficients set to 0 are exactly 0. The Cox fit takes strata and delayed entry tl (start-stop rows), and matches glmnet to six digits, stratified (stratifySurv) and start-stop (Surv(start, stop, event)) included; the parametric fits take every censoring and truncation, checked by their optimality conditions. A penalised model has no covariance, standard errors, bounds, p-values, robust standard errors or likelihood-ratio test: those calls say why. Its aic, bic and aic_c count its effective number of parameters (model.penalty.effective_df). Weights w and right truncation in the Cox fit are refused, saying what to use instead.

  • Distributional regression, Distributional(dist) and the prebuilt WeibullDistributional, ExponentialDistributional, GammaDistributional, LogNormalDistributional, LogLogisticDistributional, NormalDistributional, GumbelDistributional and LogisticDistributional: the covariates move every parameter of the distribution, each through its own link (log for a positive parameter, identity for a location), so a Weibull’s shape can depend on load as well as its scale. Each parameter chooses its covariates (covariates={"beta": ["load"]}, or formulas={"alpha": "load + temp", "beta": "load"} in fit_from_df; with none named every covariate is on every parameter). Every censoring, truncation and count of the data model; Wald, likelihood-ratio and bootstrap bounds; closed-form qf and mean at each row; parameters_at(Z) and distribution_at(row); parameter_cb(name, Z, method=...), the bounds on a parameter at each covariate row, on its link’s scale, and plot_parameter(name, covariate), a parameter against one covariate with its band; saving, loading and pickling. The AFT models are its covariates-on-the-scale special case (with the signs of the coefficients reversed). The fits are checked against R’s flexsurvreg(anc = ...) (with left truncation) and gamlss with gamlss.cens (every censoring together), and a calibration study checks the coverage of their bounds.

  • Bayesian fitting, Distribution.fit_bayes (and fit_bayes_from_df, and fit_bayes(data) for a SurpyvalData): say what is already believed and combine it with the data, with every kind of censoring and truncation fit takes. Priors are in surpyval.prior: on a parameter (any SurPyval distribution, or around(2, between=(1.5, 3)), between, uniform, flat, fixed), on the quantities people know (on_quantities(Weibull, B10=..., beta=..., R_at={...})), from an earlier fit (from_model(model, param=, weight=, widen=)), from earlier data (a power prior, from_data(x, c, weight=)) or from published numbers (from_params(dist, params, within=0.2)); prior.check(dist, priors) shows what a prior says before any data. The result, surpyval.bayes.BayesianParametric, is used like any model: its sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf, mean and random are those of a new unit’s life with the uncertainty in the parameters averaged in (the posterior predictive), and its credible intervals are cri (on sf, ff, Hf, hf, df), quantile_cri, mean_cri and param_cri (cb refuses and points to them). It also has posterior (draws, to_dataframe, density, marginal), draw_models, at_params, log_evidence, diagnostics, update (exact: the same as fitting everything at once; replace=True for records that supersede the old ones), compare (prior, maximum likelihood and posterior side by side), compare_to (the probability that a quantity exceeds another model’s), plot, plot_posterior, a summary in plain words, to_dict / from_dict and pickling. BayesianParametric.from_draws makes one from another sampler’s draws. fit_bayes, update and prior.from_data refuse weighted data, and data holding covariates, event types, time-varying covariates or marker readings, as fit(data) does.

  • The posterior of one to three free parameters is computed on a self-checking grid (deterministic: no seed), or in closed form for an Exponential with a Gamma prior, a Normal’s mean with its spread known and a Bernoulli with a Beta prior; method="laplace" is a labelled normal approximation. A simulation-based calibration study and a comparison with PyMC posteriors check it. surpyval.bayes.log_likelihood_fn is the exact censored and truncated likelihood at many parameter points at once, for other samplers. fit and every existing model are unchanged.

  • surpyval.pymc: helpers for survival analysis in PyMC, for people who already use it. censored_likelihood(dist, data, **params) adds SurPyval’s exact likelihood of censored and truncated data (failures, right, left and interval censoring, left and right truncation, counts) to the open PyMC model, for the Weibull, Exponential, LogNormal, Gamma, LogLogistic, Normal, Gumbel, Logistic and Rayleigh distributions, with parameters that may be PyMC variables, expressions (per row, for covariates) or numbers; log_likelihood gives the same term as a pytensor expression. prior_from_model turns a fitted model’s estimates and covariance into a joint prior, with a weight, and prior_from_spec builds priors from a plain description; to_surpyval(trace, dist, alpha="log_alpha[1]", transform={"alpha": "exp"}, ...) turns posterior draws back into a BayesianParametric with its functions, credible intervals and plots. PyMC is not a dependency, not even an optional one: import surpyval does not import it, and the helpers ask you to install it when it is absent.

  • diagnose() of a Cox model (and of a cause-specific competing-risks model) takes transform, "km" (the default), "rank", "identity" or "log", and its report has tables, a check’s own table by name: d.tables["proportional_hazards"] is the Grambsch-Therneau test as R’s cox.zph prints it on that scale, one row per covariate and GLOBAL, the same numbers check_ph() gave (by cause for a competing-risks model). With "identity" or "log" the report’s rows test on that scale too, beside km and rank. to_dict() keeps the tables.

Changed

  • The spline helpers of surpyval.univariate.parametric.royston_parmar are public: _rcs_basis, _rcs_deriv, _place_knots and _SCALES are now rcs_basis, rcs_deriv, place_knots and SCALES (the old private names are gone). Nothing else changes.

Removed

The names 0.25 deprecated are gone; each now raises the error Python would, naming its replacement.

  • RecurrentEventData, renamed EventHistoryData in 0.25: surpyval.RecurrentEventData raises an AttributeError (an ImportError from from surpyval import RecurrentEventData) and importing surpyval.utils.recurrent_event_data an ImportError, each naming surpyval.EventHistoryData. from surpyval import * no longer brings the old name.

  • EventHistoryData.items: use ids.

  • EventHistoryData.get_times_to_first_events(): use to_first_events(), which keeps each item’s delayed entry, id and covariates.

  • Development: REMOVED_IN is "0.27" (for the names deprecated in 0.26; none is, as check_ph has its own window to 0.28 in SCHEDULED_REMOVALS) and REMOVED_IN_NEXT "0.28".

Fixed

  • The likelihood-ratio param_cb of an offset model whose region reaches the corner where the likelihood is unbounded (the offset on the first failure, with a Weibull, Gamma or LogLogistic shape below 1) could give a finite side where the region runs to the edge, and one that depended on the platform’s arithmetic: a Gamma alpha with a 95% lower bound of 0.081 and an 80% one of 0, on Linux x86-64 only. Every point with a shape below 1 and the offset a hair below the first failure is in the region there, so a side towards values that have such points (a Gamma alpha below 1, either side of its beta, a Weibull alpha) is now the edge of the parameter’s space.

  • logrank reported dof == -1 where no event was left to compare (every row censored, or none at risk after t0). It is now 0, with a statistic of 0 and a p-value of 1, as for the other cases with nothing to compare, and as documented.

  • RoystonParmar.fit(knots=...) used knots in the order given, so knots out of order gave a different spline basis and spline parameters (gamma_j) that could not be compared with those of the same knots sorted. The knots are now sorted. Fewer than two knots, a missing or infinite knot, and a repeated one are refused with a ValueError naming knots (they raised an IndexError or failed in the optimiser). Sorted knots give the same fit as before.

  • AcceleratedLife(...).fit with left truncation at the lower end of the baseline’s support (tl=0 for a Weibull) stopped short of its maximum, with a gradient of about 2e-4 left: the exact Hessian there is nan, so the final Newton steps could not run. The fit now finishes with Newton steps on a difference Hessian, so such fits move by about 1e-5 (relative) in the parameters to the maximum. Fits that already reached it are unchanged.

  • A row of a two-column x flagged interval censored (c = 2) with equal ends, [t, t], was refused by fit (and Turnbull.fit) with a message about “only one failure time”, while fit_from_df took the same row as an exact time, as its documentation says. Both now take it as the exact time t. A reversed interval (left end above the right) is still refused, and the message now counts and names the rows and says to give the lower end first.

  • concordance_index counted an infinite risk score as tied with every finite one (the relative tie tolerance became infinite), so [4, inf, 2, 1] scored 0.9167 where the pairwise definition gives 5/6. Equal infinities are tied, and an infinity is tied with nothing else. A missing (NaN) risk score, which gave a silent nan, is now refused with a ValueError naming risk; a missing time still gives nan, as does a model’s concordance(x, c, Z) with a missing covariate.

  • brier_score and integrated_brier_score accepted survival probabilities outside [0, 1] and returned scores; they are refused.

  • A float32 query to a parametric model’s sf, ff, df, hf or Hf was computed in single precision for several distributions (Gamma, LogNormal, LogLogistic, ExpoWeibull, Poisson, NegativeBinomial, DiscreteWeibull, and their limited-failure and zero-inflated forms), differing from the same numbers in float64 by about 1e-8 (relative). It is now converted to float64 first. Integer queries are unchanged.

  • A Cox fit whose likelihood has no finite maximum (a covariate combination separating the events) warned so and then, with center=False (the default), could raise a ValueError from the move of its baseline to Z = 0, which the runaway coefficients make overflow. It now returns, as with center=True: the baseline is kept at the covariate means (model.center), with one warning saying so. A fit that has a maximum is refused as before where the move fails.

  • A parametric regression whose search did not reach a verified maximum warned twice; the baseline’s fit for the start values no longer says it too.

Where weights met other features of this release:

  • A weighted parametric regression’s robust_covariance(), robust_standard_errors() and summary(robust=True) put a second sandwich around the weighted one and left the weights out. They now give the weighted robust covariance, equal to covariance() without cluster and, with cluster, summing each cluster’s weighted scores (R’s survreg(..., weights = w, robust = TRUE) with cluster()).

  • A weighted Cox model’s summary(robust=True) and robust_summary() failed with an AttributeError; they now give the weighted Lin-Wei standard errors, with cluster too (R’s coxph(..., weights = w, robust = TRUE)).

  • likelihood_ratio_test() refuses weighted fits: its statistic changed with the scale of the weights (Cox), or its null model was fitted without them (the parametric regressions, which gave 0). Use the Wald tests of summary(). A fit whose log-likelihood is below that of the model without covariates is now refused too, rather than given a statistic of 0.

  • w= given to a fitter that takes no weights (the distributional and Royston-Parmar regressions, AalenAdditive, the frailty, competing-risks, recurrence and degradation models and the others) raised Python’s TypeError for an unexpected keyword; it is now a ValueError naming the fitter and w, saying which models take weights. So is w_col= given to a fit_from_df without it.

  • life_table, fit_bayes, update, prior.from_data, log_likelihood_fn, BayesianParametric.from_draws and the PyMC helpers refuse weighted data, which they used to drop or read as counts.

  • Weighted SurpyvalData.to_dict() is stamped schema 3, as weighted models are, and SurpyvalData.from_dict refuses a newer schema. Unweighted data dictionaries are unchanged. (v0.25 reads data dictionaries without checking their schema, so it still drops the weights of one.)

  • A weighted Cox model’s diagnose() and the functions of proportional_hazards.diagnostics (check_ph, compute_residuals, added_covariate_score_test, robust_covariance) diagnosed it as if its rows were unweighted units. They now refuse, as its check_ph() and compute_residuals() methods did, pointing to the robust covariance.

  • A weighted Cox fit with covariates far from 0 (calendar years, say) stored a baseline hazard of 0 at Z = 0, so sf was 1 at every time, with no warning. It is now refused, pointing to center=True, as the unweighted fit is. The weighted model’s r is now the risk weight at each event time (the sum of n w exp(beta'Z), as the unweighted r is), moved to Z = 0 with the baseline; it was the weighted number at risk.

  • A weighted Cox fit with a constant or collinear covariate column refused, or, where the information was singular only to rounding, gave nonsense coefficients. The column is now aliased (nan, with a warning, as R’s NA), as in the unweighted fit.

  • A weighted Cox fit with Efron’s ties saves baseline_method "efron", as the unweighted fit does (it was "fleming-harrington", for the same estimator).

  • Royston-Parmar predictions (RoystonParmar, RoystonParmarPH and RoystonParmarPO: sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf and the cb band) could differ in the last bit when the query was reordered, on Linux x86-64: the spline was a matrix product, whose summation order depends on a row’s place. Each point’s sum now runs in a fixed order. Predictions of the univariate model change at most in the last bits. The regressions’ fits evaluate the same spline, so their coefficients move by about 1e-14 (relative) and their Wald bounds, from a numerical Hessian, by up to 1e-9.

  • Distributional regression predictions (WeibullDistributional and the others) could differ in the last bit when the query rows were reordered, on Linux x86-64, for the same reason: each parameter’s linear predictor was a matrix product. Each row’s sum now runs in a fixed order. The fits evaluate the same product, so their coefficients may move in the last bits.

Deprecated

  • check_ph(), the Cox model’s method and the function proportional_hazards.diagnostics.check_ph, is deprecated and will be removed in v0.28: diagnose() is the one way to check a model’s assumptions, and runs the same proportional-hazards test, with the same transform. Replace model.check_ph(transform) with model.diagnose(transform=transform).tables["proportional_hazards"] (the same table, number for number), or read the verdicts from d.table and the remedies from d.advice. Until then it warns (DeprecationWarning) and returns what it did. On a penalised fit (fit_penalised) it now refuses, as diagnose() does: a penalised model has no p-values. The function behind both, zph_score_test, and compute_residuals and added_covariate_score_test stay.

Documentation

  • Model Diagnostics, Regression Modelling with SurPyval, Weighted Data and the regression analysis notes use diagnose() in place of check_ph(); Model Diagnostics has a section on the proportional-hazards table.

  • New pages: Weighted Data, Bayesian Fitting with SurPyval, Distributional Regression and PyMC with SurPyval, and API pages for Bayesian fitting, Aalen’s model, distributional regression, forest plots and the Royston-Parmar regression.

  • New sections: life tables, Peto-Peto weights, pairwise tests and the fixed-time test in Non-Parametric SurPyval Modelling; Aalen’s additive hazards, spline regression, robust standard errors, the global likelihood-ratio test, forest plots and penalised regression in Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

  • Recipes for four distributions written as a CustomDistribution, each checked against scipy.stats: the generalised gamma (with the Weibull and gamma as nested cases, a likelihood-ratio choice among them, and an AFT regression), the Gompertz with proportional hazards, the generalised F (Kalbfleisch and Prentice’s original form) and the inverse Gaussian (in logs, so that it neither overflows nor loses digits in its tail). See “Recipes: more distributions from their cumulative hazard” in Parametric SurPyval Modelling.

  • Conventions and Design Principles describe w beside n.

v0.25 (17 October 2026)

Highlights.

  • Joint models with covariates and dynamic prediction. Joint models of a marker and a lifetime (WeibullJointPH), with covariates in the hazard, in the marker’s path or both (hazard_covariates, path_covariates), left and interval censored items and truncation, and JointModel.predict: one item’s DynamicPrediction given its readings so far (survival, hazard, remaining life, the smoothed marker, bounds and draws, and to_dict() for reports), with a calibration study of its intervals.

  • Test planning, surpyval.test_planning: demonstration tests (attribute and constant failure rate, with both risks), sequential tests, the precision of life tests, accelerated life test plans, the log-rank test’s events and power, and the power of a rate comparison; every result writes itself with to_dict().

  • The intervention test, surpyval.recurrent.intervention_test: whether an intervention changed a failure rate, with the exposure needed to detect a change.

  • Every bound: likelihood-ratio bounds for the offset, limited-failure-population and zero-inflated models, and the gaps that remain refused with what to use instead.

  • Non-parametric plotting: plot_nonparametric draws one or more estimates with their bounds, censoring ticks, quantile lines and a number-at-risk table, and at_risk_table gives that table as data.

  • Regression diagnostics (model.diagnose()) for every regression family, item records (ItemLifetime, ItemHistory) and the data classes’ DataFrame, dict and JSON forms, units on the data, and the mean residual life.

Upgrading from 0.24. On 0.24, run your code or tests with python -W error::DeprecationWarning first to find the calls to update.

  • The names 0.24 deprecated now raise (see Removed): CompetingRisksProportionalHazards.beta and phi_e by row index, NonParametric.cb’s old argument order, MixtureModel.p and ProportionalIntensityNHPP.fit(dist=).

  • Deprecated, still working with a warning (see Deprecated): RecurrentEventData is EventHistoryData (until v0.26), and the top-level data-format converters (fs_to_xcnt and the rest) are SurpyvalData methods (until the first release on or after 12 April 2027).

Added

  • to_dict() on every test planning result (DemonstrationPlan, LifeTestPlan, SimulatedPrecision, AcceleratedTestPlan, SequentialMTBFTest and SequentialDemonstrationTest): native Python values, strict JSON, with tuples and arrays as lists and an infinite or missing number as None under the package’s "non_finite" record. The sequential tests also tabulate their boundaries (accept and reject times by failure count, or accepted and rejecting failures by number of units), for a chart or a test procedure.

  • surpyval.plot_nonparametric: one figure of one or more non-parametric estimates (Kaplan-Meier, Nelson-Aalen, Fleming-Harrington or Turnbull, truncated or not; one model, a list or a dict {label: model} for groups) with a number-at-risk table under the x axis. It draws sf, ff, Hf or the smoothed hazard rate, with the model’s pointwise cb or simultaneous band (shaded or as dashed steps), censoring ticks, median or other quantile lines with their values, a time range and a log time axis, and returns the figure, axes, curves, quantiles and counts (NonParametricPlot). The table’s rows are “At risk”, “Censored” and “Events” (cumulative, as lifelines’ add_at_risk_counts, or per interval), counted with the estimators’ risk sets, so the number at risk rises with late entry. For left or interval censored data the rows count what the data show (known event-free, known to have had the event) and an “In interval” row counts the units whose interval spans the time, rather than the Turnbull estimate’s fractional expected counts.

  • surpyval.at_risk_table(models, times=None, rows=("At risk",), counts="cumulative"): the same table as data, {"times", "rows", "counts": {label: {row: array}}}, without drawing (it loads no plotting library), for a report or a table of one’s own.

  • Joint models (#891): separate covariates for the hazard and the path. WeibullJointPH.fit(..., hazard_covariates=[...], path_covariates=[...] or {path parameter: [...]}) (and fit_from_df) puts each covariate in the hazard (<cov>), the path parameters’ means (a_<cov>, b_<cov>, …) or both: a condition can change how fast the marker rises without changing the risk at a given reading, or the reverse. The default is every covariate in both, as before; a covariate in neither part, or a name that is not a covariate, is refused. The model keeps path_covariates and hazard_covariates (None where every covariate is in both) and saves them; a model saved before loads as every covariate in both.

  • Joint models: left and interval censored items (found failed at an inspection) and right truncation, which were refused. An interval’s likelihood is S(l) - S(u) over the item’s paths, the hazard integrated over the interval directly; a truncated item’s is divided by the population’s probability of (S(tl) - S(tr)). Arrays take [lower, upper] rows of x (c = 2, the default where the ends differ), fit_from_df xl_col/xr_col and tr_col. Every kind of item’s likelihood agrees with a dense-grid integral to within 1e-5 an item.

  • JointModel.predict(item) (or predict(Z, markers=, given=)): one item’s DynamicPrediction given its readings so far and that it is still running – the conditional sf, ff and cb (the model’s own), hf, df, Hf (with cb(on="Hf")), qf and remaining_life(p), the smoothed and projected noise-free marker (marker, marker_interval) and draws (random). The array prediction sf(x, Z, markers=, given=) is unchanged. DynamicPrediction.to_dict(x=None, alpha_ci=0.05) gives it as strict JSON for a report or chart: the readings as [age, value] pairs, sf, ff and hf on a grid of ages (by default from the age now to about the 0.99 quantile) with the two-sided bounds on sf, the remaining life’s 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 quantiles, and the marker’s path with its interval; an infinite or missing value is None.

  • A calibration study of the joint model (tests/calibration/test_coverage_joint.py, --run-calibration): 200 fleets of 200 items with a hazard-only and a path-only covariate, with exact failure times and with 90-day inspections. Each parameter’s 95% interval covered the truth 93.0-96.5% (exact) and 91.5-97.5% (inspections) of the time, standardised biases were within 0.21 sd and standard errors 0.91-1.09 of the estimates’ spread; a held-out item’s 95% dynamic-prediction band covered its true conditional survival 93.0%, 89.5% and 93.0% (exact) and 93.5%, 94.5% and 94.0% (inspections) at 60, 180 and 365 days ahead.

  • Likelihood-ratio bounds for offset, limited-failure-population and zero-inflated models: param_cb, cb, quantile_cb, mean_cb and mrl_cb with method="lr" raised NotImplementedError. The profile is now over every fitted parameter, so the bounds include the uncertainty of gamma, lfp_p and f0, and param_cb bounds those three as well (gamma had only the bootstrap bound). lfp_p and f0 have a closed edge (1 and 0, the plain model): a side towards it is the edge itself where the profile deviance there is within the critical value, and with the estimate on the edge the other side is walked out in the parameter itself; a two-sided interval then covers a truth on the edge with probability 1 - alpha_ci / 2 and the one-sided bound towards it with 1 - alpha_ci, asymptotically (Self and Liang, 1987; more in small samples: 98.5% and 97.2% at the 95% level with 100 units). A time before the estimated offset has a band below 1 wherever the region holds an offset below it. Where an offset model’s region reaches the first failure with its offset (the likelihood is unbounded there), the bounds on functions at that level are nan, with a warning, and the offset’s interval runs up to the first failure. Brute-force checks of the profile deviance at each bound are in test_likelihood_ratio_extra_parameters.py, the coverage studies in calibration/test_coverage_extra_parameters.py, and the Weibull’s variants join the conformance sweeps of the likelihood-ratio options (the other families’ with the calibration studies).

  • Truncated draws, random(size, a=, b=) and random_data, from offset, limited-failure-population and zero-inflated models (they raised NotImplementedError): the model’s own distribution given the window (a, b], with the units dead on arrival in it where it holds 0 and the ones that never fail where it has no upper end. A window the model puts no probability in raises a ValueError.

  • The data classes read and write DataFrames (#936): SurpyvalData.from_dataframe(df, x_col=..., c_col=... | event_col=..., n_col=, xl_col= / xr_col=, tl_col=, tr_col=, i_col=, e_col=, Z_cols=, attribute_cols=, unit=) reads a table with one row per item, naming its columns as every DataFrame entry point does, with event_col for a status column (1 or True where the item failed) and blanks in xl_col / xr_col for an end not known; EventHistoryData.from_dataframe(df, i_col=, x_col=, ..., end_col=, ends={item: age}) reads a log with one row per event, each item’s end of observation as a c = 1 row, a column or ends= (which also gives the items that never failed); to_dataframe() on both gives the rows back. SurpyvalData(..., ids=) names rows.

  • Dict and JSON forms for every data class (#935): to_dict / from_dict and to_json / from_json on SurpyvalData, EventHistoryData, ItemLifetime and ItemHistory, tagged with their "class"; from_json reads JSON text or a file path, and surpyval.from_json / surpyval.from_dict read a dataset or record as they read a model. Step schedules of time-varying covariates, tuple ids and event types, attributes, states and the unit go with them (a CovariatePath is refused).

  • Attributes on the records (#938): attributes={name: value} on ItemLifetime and ItemHistory, what describes an item without being fitted (a site, a batch, an arm: any values), read back by item.attribute(name), carried through the datasets (from_items, from_dataframe(attribute_cols=), slicing, every reshape, JSON, to_dataframe, the repr and summary) and refused by no fit. data.groupby(name) splits the data by an attribute or a covariate into {level: dataset}; select(where={name: value}) keeps one group; without("attributes") drops them.

  • Updating a dataset with new records (#939): data.update(records, counts={id: k}) takes updated records back in, replacing the item with the same id and adding new ones; data.drop(ids) removes items; data.extend_running(age | {id: age} | function of the record) moves every item still running on to a later age.

  • Cut-offs per item (#937): censor_at and enter_at take {id: age} (the items left out are kept as they are) or a function of each item’s record giving its age, for a study that ends on one date, a different age for each item.

  • Predictions from item records (#940): a record, a list of records or a dataset stands as Z in a regression model’s sf, ff, hf, Hf, df, qf and mean, its covariates read by name where the model’s are named; every lifetime model has predict(items, times=, what=, given=, p=), a DataFrame indexed by id, one row per item and time, with given="age" for the predictions given each running item’s current age (nan for one that has failed).

  • Units on the data classes (#945): unit= on the records, SurpyvalData, EventHistoryData, from_observations, from_items (from its records, which must agree), from_histories, from_dataframe and handle_xicn, kept through every reshape, slice, to_first_events, to_gaps and the JSON form, shown in the summary and repr, and given to the model by fit(data); a unit= at the fit that differs from the data’s is refused, as are records in different units.

  • SurpyvalData.event_types, n_items and records() (a generator of the records) on both datasets, ItemLifetime.has_event_types (#934); without takes a list of parts, for_event_type several types taken as one, select(ids=) one id (#932).

  • A shared keyword check on the record constructors, from_items, from_observations and from_histories (#931): an unknown argument is refused naming the one that was meant (tl -> left_truncation=, e -> event_type=, …) or the closest accepted name.

  • model.diagnose(alpha=0.05, columns=None) on every regression model and fitted distribution (#867): the checks its assumptions call for, as a report – table (one row per check: test, statistic, p, verdict and covariates), advice (plain-English remedies, each naming the SurPyval feature that applies it), plot() (matplotlib only then), ok, raise_if_failed() and to_dict() / Diagnosis.from_dict. A test fails below alpha and warns below 2 * alpha or when it cannot be computed; a screen warns and never fails. Each model family lists its checks and advice in surpyval.diagnostics, whose docstring is the guide to adding one; the families not built yet refuse, naming their issue (#869 to #875). See Model Diagnostics.

  • The Cox family of diagnose() (#868): proportional hazards by R’s cox.zph score test (survival 3.0 and later) on the km and rank scales, with GLOBAL rows, and plots of the scaled Schoenfeld residuals with a lowess trend and bootstrap band; functional form by the score test of a covariate’s square, and martingale residual plots; influence (|dfbeta| / se above 1 warns); outliers (deviance residuals beyond the Bonferroni normal cutoff); the Cox-Snell plot; advice to stratify a binary or few-levelled covariate that fails proportional hazards, and a time-varying effect (fit_tvc), bins or an AFT model for a continuous one; and the cluster-robust standard errors of a fit_tvc model. Stratified fits are refused for now. The proportional-hazards rows are check_ph()’s test (see Changed); the functional-form test is added_covariate_score_test in proportional_hazards.diagnostics, R’s coxph(..., init = c(coef(fit), 0), iter.max = 0)$score. Both agree with R to 1e-6.

  • The parametric proportional hazards and accelerated failure time families of diagnose() (#869), for WeibullPH, …, PH(dist) and WeibullAFT, …, AFT(dist) fitted with fit / fit_from_df. Every test is a likelihood-ratio test against a larger model, with the fit’s own likelihood: for a PH model, a step in each coefficient (and in the baseline) at the median failure time, per covariate and GLOBAL, drawn as the coefficient in each quarter of the failures; a covariate’s square; the influence and outlier screens of the Cox family; and the AIC against the other built-in baselines and the AFT model of the same baseline, with the Cox-Snell residuals on exponential paper. For an AFT model, the standardised residuals on the baseline’s probability paper with the same AIC screens; one shape for every level of a categorical covariate or formula factor against a shape per level; and a covariate’s square. Advice names a time-varying effect (fit_tvc), an AFT model or a stratified Cox model, separate fits per level, a formula transform, and the better baseline or kind of model. The statistics agree with R’s survreg (and, for the step test, a Poisson model of the split follow-up) to 1e-6 (scripts/reference/ reference_r_ph_aft.R). Time-varying fits and custom links are refused for now.

  • The shared-frailty families of diagnose() (#872), for WeibullFrailty, …, Frailty(dist, family=...) and CoxFrailty: the boundary likelihood-ratio test of no frailty against the same model without it refitted to the same rows (<Dist>PH.fit, or the Cox partial likelihood against R’s I-likelihood), with the 50:50 mixture of chi2(0) and chi2(1) (surpyval.diagnostics.frailty.zero_variance_test); for a parametric baseline also the AIC against the other frailty family and the other built-in baselines, and the likelihood-ratio tests, over the marginal likelihood, of a step in each coefficient at the median failure time and of a covariate’s square given the frailty; posterior-frailty, martingale-residual and marginal Cox-Snell plots. Advice names the model without the frailty when it is not significant, Frailty(dist, family=...), a formula transform, and per-level or clustered Cox fits for an effect that changes with time. The statistics agree with R’s coxph(... + frailty(id)), lme4’s glmer and survreg to 1e-6 (scripts/reference/reference_r_frailty_diag.R). A CoxFrailtyModel keeps no group of each row, so only its frailty variance is tested.

  • The calibration of predicted survival, a calibration check shared by the Cox, parametric PH and AFT families of diagnose() (#881): at the quartiles of the failure times, or at diagnose(t0=...), the smoothed calibration curve of Austin, Harrell and van Klaveren (2020) – a Cox model of the observed times on a restricted cubic spline of the complementary log-log of the predicted risk, so censored units count as at risk, not as survivors, and delayed entry is respected – with its ICI (the row’s statistic), E50 and E90 and a pointwise band, drawn against the diagonal with a histogram of the predicted risks. A screen: it warns when the ICI is above 0.02 and the predictions are outside the band for more than 10% of the units, with advice naming a formula transform, another baseline, the other kind of model or a Cox model. Left- and interval-censored, right-truncated and time-varying fits are refused with a note. surpyval.diagnostics.calibration.calibration_curve takes the predicted survival of any model, to validate it on other data. The curve, its summaries and band agree with R’s coxph and survfit (scripts/reference/reference_r_calibration.R).

  • The proportional odds and additive hazards families of diagnose() (#870), for ProportionalOdds, AdditiveHazards and the parametric PO(...) / AH(...) models: for each covariate, and jointly, the test that its effect is the same in four periods of follow-up (split at the event-time quartiles) – the likelihood-ratio test of the model refitted, exactly, on the rows split there, or for Lin and Ying’s model the Wald test with its sandwich variance, which agrees with R’s timereg::aalen to 1e-8; for a proportional odds model’s binary or categorical covariate, whether its groups’ log-odds stay parallel. Plots: Kaplan-Meier log-odds by group and coefficients by period (proportional odds), Aalen’s cumulative regression coefficients (additive hazards, odds_additive.aalen_cumulative_coefficients, which agrees with timereg). Advice: a proportional hazards or accelerated failure time model with the same baseline (CoxPH.fit, WeibullPH.fit, WeibullAFT.fit, …) for a proportional odds failure; a time-varying effect through fit_tvc for an additive one. Left- or interval-censored and right-truncated parametric fits are refused for now.

  • The accelerated life family of diagnose() (#871), for AcceleratedLife(dist, life_model) fits: a common shape at every stress level, by the likelihood-ratio test of each level fitted alone against one shared shape, with a probability plot of the levels; the life-stress relationship, by the likelihood-ratio (lack-of-fit) test of the life model against a separate life at each level, with a plot of the levels’ lives against stress; every built-in life model for the number of stresses refitted to the same data and compared by AIC (a model better by more than 2 warns); and a warning for a stress tested at two levels or fewer. Advice names the better life model, separate fits of the levels, or more stress levels. Both tests agree with R’s survreg to 1e-5. diagnose(use_stress=...) gives the stress the model is to predict at: the report then warns when it is more than one width of the tested range outside it (on the life model’s scale of the stress), and gives each life model’s life there. A family’s own options are declared in Family.options, reach its checks as ctx.options, and are refused by the other families.

  • The recurrent-event families of diagnose() (#873), for the Poisson processes (HPP, CrowAMSAA, Duane, CoxLewis), the imperfect-repair models (GeneralizedRenewal, GeneralizedOneRenewal, ARA, ARI) and the proportional- intensity models: the Laplace, MIL-HDBK-189C and Lewis-Robinson trend tests (tests of a constant-rate model, a model-choice screen for the others); the model’s Cramer-von Mises test (diagnose(n_boot=, random_state=), 99 bootstrap refits by default); for the Poisson processes the Pearson dispersion test of the items’ counts; for the imperfect-repair models the likelihood-ratio tests of perfect and minimal repair (repair_test) as a screen; plots of the mean cumulative function, the transformed event times, the items’ counts and the restoration parameter’s profile likelihood; and advice between a constant rate, an NHPP, a renewal process and imperfect repair, and towards proportional intensity for items that differ. The Lewis-Robinson test is surpyval.diagnostics.recurrent.lewis_robinson and agrees with R. Models without data, least-squares fits and inexact or right-truncated times are refused.

  • The competing-risks families of diagnose() (#874), reported by cause (a cause column, plots titled by cause). CompetingRisksProportionalHazards (model="Cox") runs the Cox checks on each cause’s own Cox model, now kept as model.models[cause] (with compute_residuals and check_ph), and advises fitting a failing cause on its own with strata= or CoxPH.fit_tvc, or the Fine-Gray model where incidence is the question. FineGray and model="Fine-Gray" test proportional subdistribution hazards (the score test of Z * g(t) in the weighted partial likelihood, on the cif and rank scales, with GLOBAL rows and scaled-residual plots) and the functional form; both agree with R’s cox.zph on the weighted Fine-Gray data to 1e-6, and are functions, fine_gray_zph_test and fine_gray_added_covariate_test in competing_risks.regression.fine_gray_diagnostics. Every report notes that the independence of the causes cannot be tested. ParametricCompetingRisks still refuses, naming #874 (its checks wait for #875).
