  • The univariate-distribution family of diagnose() (#875), for Weibull.fit(...) and the other continuous distributions (offset, lfp, zi, fixed parameters, truncation and any how): Anderson-Darling, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises tests of the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the fitted CDF, with parametric bootstrap p-values (each resample drawn from the model, censored as the data were and refitted the same way; diagnose(n_boot=200, random_state=None)), which agree with fitdistrplus::gofstat on complete data and with the textbook critical values; the probability plot and a P-P plot; and an AIC screen of the alternatives, with advice naming fit_best, a MixtureModel, offset=True, lfp=True or zi=True. Discrete distributions are refused for now, and event-probability models and ExactEventTime have no distribution to test. diagnose() takes n_boot and random_state on every model (families that do not resample ignore them).

  • Joint models of a marker and a lifetime (#891). An ItemLifetime takes markers={age: value}, repeated readings of one measurement (vibration, wear, a biomarker), each inside the item’s observation (refused otherwise, naming the item); update_markers(age, value) adds one. SurpyvalData keeps them as data.markers through from_items/to_items, slicing, summary(), its repr, JSON and every reshape (censor_at and enter_at keep the readings inside the new window, without("markers") drops them), and every other fit refuses data that holds them, naming data.without("markers"). JointPH(Weibull, path_model, varying=...) fits the joint model: each item’s marker follows a degradation path model (LinearPath by default, which WeibullJointPH is; QuadraticPath, ExponentialPath, … or a PathModel of one’s own) with the parameters named in varying (default all, at most three) varying between items, multivariate normal (each on its own scale, or a positive one on a log scale with LinkedPathModel(path, {"b": "log"}), its names then log(b), sd_log(b), …), and the rest common, plus noise; its hazard is Weibull PH in the path’s current value; covariates shift every path parameter’s mean and enter the hazard; by maximum likelihood with adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature; failures, right censoring and left truncation; a covariate the data cannot determine is aliased. fit(data) (also arrays with markers=[...], and fit_from_df with a markers_col) returns a JointModel, its parameters named by the parts (the path’s own a, b, …; a_<cov>; sd_a, corr_a_b; sd_noise; alpha, beta, <cov>; marker_effect), with covariance(), standard_errors(), neg_ll(), aic(), bic(), summary() and to_dict/from_dict; marker_reference= chooses the marker value at which alpha is reported (default the mean reading). It predicts for one item given its readings so far: sf(x, Z, markers=..., given=...), ff and cb (delta-method bounds), or sf(x, item) from an item record, the same prediction; with no readings and no given, a new item’s. See Joint Models.

  • The data utilities live on SurpyvalData. SurpyvalData.from_observations(observed=..., right_censored=..., left_censored=..., interval_censored=..., left_truncation=..., right_truncation=...) reads a list of each kind of observation (any may be left out). Each kind takes truncation bounds of its own, observed_left_truncation, right_censored_right_truncation and so on: one number for every item of that kind, or one per item in the order of its list. left_truncation and right_truncation are one window shared by everything (given with a kind’s own bound on the same side, it is refused). Each kind also takes <kind>_counts (one whole number for every item or one per item; an item counted 0 is left out, as a life table’s empty interval) and <kind>_covariates (one row per item, the same columns for every kind, needed for every kind with items once given for one), which a regression fit takes as Z. SurpyvalData.from_xrd(x, r, d) reads the at-risk / deaths form; both validate as the fitters do. to_xcnt() gives the arrays x, c, n, t (copies) and to_observations() the lists back, each value once with its kind’s counts, bounds and covariates where the data has them, so from_observations(**data.to_observations()) is the same data. from_observations refuses an infinite single time by name (an interval open at one end is [lower, inf] in interval_censored), and a pandas list and its per-item values with different indexes, since they are matched by position.

  • A model fitted on item records predicts for an item: model.sf_tvc(t, item) (and the other *_tvc methods) reads the item’s fixed covariates and its time-varying ones (a StepSchedule or a CovariatePath) and lines them up as the fit did, fixed columns first.

  • Covariates by name: a record’s covariates may be {name: value} (or a pandas Series), its covariate_names; a dataset of such records has covariate_names (all its items named alike, in any order, or none), as does SurpyvalData(..., Z=Z, covariate_names=[...]), a DataFrame Z, and from_observations(..., covariate_names=[...]). The names go with the data through to_items, slicing, JSON and the summary; with_covariates(["age"]) picks covariates by name; and fit(data) names the model’s coefficients by them (feature_names), for the time-varying fit too (the time-varying columns follow as time_varying_0, …). model.sf_tvc(t, item) reads a named item’s covariates in the model’s order.

  • Reshaping a dataset for another analysis, on SurpyvalData and EventHistoryData alike (each returns a new dataset, built again from its item records, so it passes the same checks): without("covariates", "event_types", "time_varying_covariates", "truncation", "states") leaves parts out, so one dataset serves a plain fit as well as a regression; with_covariates(columns) keeps some covariates; for_event_type(t) gives the data of one failure mode (another mode’s failure becomes right censored at its age, or at the last good inspection; for a history, it is removed and observation runs on to it; lifetimes lose their right truncation, with a warning, since it selects on the first failure of any mode); relabel_event_types({old: new}) renames or merges modes; select(ids=..., where=...) keeps some items (where is given each item’s record); censor_at(age) stops observation at an age; and enter_at(age) starts it at one, keeping the items known to have reached it. A history whose failures are counted, or whose state changed, between two inspections either side of the age is cut at the earlier inspection, or entered at the later one. Counts carry through.

  • The data classes, from using them: data.item(id) gives one item’s record (SurpyvalData and EventHistoryData); ids have one name, .id on a record and .ids on a dataset (a record’s .item was never released, so is simply renamed); len(EventHistoryData) is its rows, as for SurpyvalData; ItemHistory reads its states back by the names that make them (observed_states, interval_censored_states, left_censored_states) and state_at(age) gives the state at an age, or None where it is not known; from_items(..., counts={id: count}) takes counts by id; a date or a duration given for an age says how to convert it; a failure added without a type to a typed history says so in the words of the update; summary() describes a dataset in a few lines; and the API page lists the records’ methods.

  • Updating an ItemLifetime or ItemHistory: each method returns a new, checked record and leaves the old one as it was. Records are fixed once made (their arrays are read-only and their attributes cannot be set), so a record is always one that passed its checks, and they are hashable by value. Item ids from numpy (np.int64, np.str_) are kept as the plain Python value. ItemLifetime reads its outcome by name, as ItemHistory does: .observed, .right_censored, .left_censored and .interval_censored are its value or None. Both have clone(new_id, **changes), extend(age) (seen working to a later age) and update_covariates(age, values) (a step added to the time-varying covariates). A running ItemLifetime can fail(age, event_type) or be found_failed(age) at an inspection (failed since it was last seen working); an ItemHistory takes add_failure, a failure after its end of observation moving the end to it.

  • SurpyvalData carries event types: SurpyvalData(x, c, ..., e=...) (one per row; a suspension has none) and from_observations(..., observed_event_types=..., left_censored_event_types=..., interval_censored_event_types=...), one type for every item of the kind or one per item; to_observations() gives them back. The competing-risks fitters (CompetingRisks, ParametricCompetingRisks, CompetingRisksProportionalHazards, FineGray) take fit(data), the event types coming from the data; given data without them, they say so. Rows with event types are not grouped, so each keeps its type. A subset (data[...]) keeps the event types, item ids and time-varying covariates, and to_json / from_json the event types and ids (data with time-varying covariates has no JSON form, and says so; pickle keeps it). A subset of EventHistoryData keeps its covariates, time-varying covariates and states. from_items checks ids in linear time (it took a minute for 100,000 items).

  • fit(data) of a regression model fits the step time-varying covariates of SurpyvalData.from_items data with the model’s fit_tvc: each item’s life, from the start of its observation to its outcome, is split where its schedule steps, and each row’s covariates are the item’s static covariates followed by its time-varying ones. The fit is exactly the fit_tvc of those rows (proportional hazards, Cox, accelerated failure time, …). Left or interval censored items, right truncation and continuous CovariatePath covariates (#908) are refused. A fit taking tl but not t now gets a SurpyvalData’s left truncation, rather than refusing it.

  • ItemLifetime, one item’s lifetime: exactly one outcome (observed, right_censored, left_censored or interval_censored), its observation window (left_truncation / right_truncation), what failed (event_type), covariates and time_varying_covariates ({age: values}, a StepSchedule or a CovariatePath). SurpyvalData.from_items(items, counts=...) builds the data, counts saying how many identical items each stands for (an item is one item); to_items() gives the items back, so from_items(data.to_items(), counts=data.n) is the same data. Every check names the item. Event types go to the competing-risks fitters and step time-varying covariates to fit_tvc (below); a fit that cannot use them refuses them rather than ignoring them.

  • ItemHistory, one repairable item’s history: exact failures (observed), failures found between two ages (interval_censored with interval_censored_counts), a count of failures before an age (left_censored with left_censored_counts), the end of observation (right_censored; left out, observation ends at the last failure), its observation window (left_truncation / right_truncation), what each failure was (observed_event_types and so on, for the cause-specific models), static covariates, time_varying_covariates ({age: values}, a StepSchedule or a CovariatePath; #905) and its path through states, recorded like its failures (initial_state, observed_states, interval_censored_states, left_censored_states; #887). The last two are kept with the data and refused by every fit until a model uses them. Every check names the item and what is wrong. EventHistoryData.from_items([...]) builds the dataset and to_items() gives the items back; from_histories builds its items the same way. markers (#891) are reserved for the joint models.

  • EventHistoryData.from_histories reads recurrent event data as each item’s history, keyed by the item’s id: observed={item: [ages at its failures]} and right_censored={item: age at the end of observation} (an item left out is taken to have been observed until its last failure), with left_truncation / right_truncation per item or shared and covariates one row per item. gaps=True reads the times between failures and adds them up within each item. to_histories() gives the dictionaries back, so from_histories(**data.to_histories()) is the same data. Every recurrent fit (NHPP, HPP, the renewal models, the MCF, the proportional intensity and cause-specific models) takes a EventHistoryData as x, by the same rules as fit(data) for SurpyvalData: other data arguments given with it, and data the fit has no argument for (right truncation for a renewal model, say), are refused.

  • The parametric, non-parametric and regression fit methods (with MixtureModel and fit_best) take a SurpyvalData as x: Weibull.fit(data). The values, flags, counts, truncation and, for a regression, the covariates Z all come from the data, so a c, n, t, tl, tr, xl, xr (or a second Z) given with it is refused rather than one silently winning, and data the fit has no argument for (censoring for a fit of exact times, say) is refused too. fit_from_surpyval_data stays.

  • life_models.Arrhenius, the name engineers look for: the same class as life_models.Exponential, which is the Arrhenius model.

  • The plotting heuristic= is read whatever its case, as how= is, and "Bernard" (the common misspelling) is Benard’s approximation.

  • The recurrent-event fitters take tr and tl one value per unit as well as one per row: with i given, a bound with as many entries as there are units, in the sorted order of the unit ids (np.unique(i), the order of EventHistoryData.items), gives each row its unit’s value, wherever the unit’s rows are in x. CrowAMSAA.fit(x, i=i, tr=[300, 300, 400]) for three units used to be refused with “‘tl’ and ‘tr’ must be the same length as ‘x’”. The bound is expanded to one value per row in handle_xicn, so every recurrent model (NHPP, HPP, renewal, proportional intensity, the MCF and the cause-specific models) fits, and stores, exactly the data of the per-row form. When there are as many rows as units the bound is read per row, as before; any other length is refused, naming both accepted lengths.

  • One plot theme for the package, surpyval.plotting: every model’s plot takes its colours in order from a fixed palette (checked to stay apart under the common colour-vision deficiencies), draws 2-point lines, ringed points and its confidence bounds as a pale band of the curve’s colour, with hairline grids, no top or right spine and grey text. An estimate from the data behind a fitted model (the recurrent-event and regression plots) is a grey step under the model’s colour; they were a red step and a blue line. set_theme(False) turns it off, style_axes styles axes of your own and rc_params gives the theme as matplotlib.rcParams. A color given to plot wins.

  • Probability plots redrawn: the probability axis is labelled as densely as the distribution’s scale has room for, the tails included (a Normal plot’s points below 10% had no label beside them; a Weibull’s 99.9% no room), the time axis at 1, 2 and 5 a decade on a log scale (it was seven log-spaced times rounded to a figure: 200, 300, 400, 600, 900) and at round times on a linear one, with faint minor lines where the green grid of 51 evenly spaced probabilities was. The y axis is “Fraction failed” (it was “CDF”). The confidence bounds are a band (they were dashed lines).

  • CompetingRisks.plot draws each cause’s cumulative incidence as its own curve by default (stacked=False); stacked=True still stacks them, separated by thin white edges, with the all-cause bounds as thin grey lines (a grey band laid over the layers).

  • unit=, the unit of the data, on every fit, fit_from_df and from_params (#845): any unit, not only of time ("hours", "km", "cycles", "pump starts"). It is a label, kept as model.unit, shown in the model’s printout and on the time axis of its plots (“Time (h)”, “Distance (km)”, “Usage (cycles)”), saved by to_dict and restored by from_dict, and carried by with_params; nothing is converted or checked. A unit pint knows is stored by its canonical name, so the same unit always reads the same ("hrs", "hours" and "Hours" are "hour"; "cycles" is "cycle", a count, not pint’s angle); anything else is kept as written. pint is a new dependency, imported only when a unit is given. Left out, the unit is None and a model and its dictionary are as before. It is unit, singular: units already names the items measured (a degradation model’s unit ids).

  • The mean residual life, mrl(x): the expected remaining life \(E[T - x \mid T > x]\) of a unit that has survived to x (#825), on every distribution (Weibull.mrl(x, alpha, beta)), on the fitted parametric models, with confidence bounds mrl_cb (Wald on its log, likelihood ratio or bootstrap), and on the non-parametric estimators, restricted to a horizon tau as the RMST is (and refused past the data as mean refuses it). mrl(0) is the mean, and before the support starts it is the mean less x. It is in closed form for the Exponential and the Weibull (through Gamma(a, z) e^z, from its continued fraction, so finite where the survival underflows); otherwise the integral of the conditional survival, broken where the cumulative hazard has risen by steps past H(x), within 1e-12 of mpmath’s on the families checked; a discrete distribution’s is the sum over the integers. An offset shifts it, a limited failure population makes it infinite (as its mean), and a zero-inflated model’s mass at 0 counts only before 0.

  • MixtureModel.with_params and MixtureModel.from_params (#829): a mixture with other component parameters and weights, keeping its dist and m, as Parametric.with_params is for one distribution. The parameters are taken as an (m, k) array or flat in the order of covariance_names (with or without the weights at the end, as a draw from covariance() comes), and the weights as w or as log-ratios to the last one, w_logits, the coordinates the covariance is fitted in. Each component is checked as from_params checks a distribution, and the weights must be non-negative and sum to 1. Drawing a fit’s parameters and propagating them through a mixture used to need to_dict, an edit and from_dict.

  • CoxFrailty.fit(center=True) (and fit_from_df), as CoxPH has it (#794): the baseline is kept at the covariate means, stored as model.center, and predictions use exp(beta'(Z - center)). It is the same model – the coefficients, theta, the frailties and every prediction are those of the fit at Z = 0 – and the way to fit covariates far from 0 (a date as a day count), whose baseline at Z = 0 cannot be represented and is refused; the refusal now points to it. The default, False, reports the baseline at Z = 0 as before, and a model saved before has its baseline there.

  • Event histories as lifetime data (#926): EventHistoryData.to_first_events() gives each item’s time to its first failure (observed, interval or left censored, or right censored at the end of its observation where it has none) and EventHistoryData.to_gaps() the times between its failures, each repair taken as making it as good as new, with each item’s last gap right censored. Both are SurpyvalData built from item records, so they keep each item’s delayed entry, id ((item, k) for a gap), covariates and event types; Weibull.fit(data.to_gaps()) fits them. A lifetime fit given an EventHistoryData says to use them.

  • Event types (#928). A failure whose type was not recorded – None, NaN, pandas NA or an empty string, on a record, in e or from a blank cell – is a masked cause: accepted, and warned of once per dataset (MaskedCauseWarning, naming the items or rows), and counted as “not recorded” in the summary. Fits of every failure count masked causes; for_event_type(t, masked=...) takes them as not of type t ("censor", the default, with a warning that its rate is then underestimated if some were), as of it ("count"), or refuses them ("refuse"); competing-risks fits refuse them, saying how to give them a type; relabel_event_types({None: "unknown"}) makes them a type of their own. A first failure found with failures of other types at one inspection is a masked cause of to_first_events(), known to lie between the earliest lower bound and the first age a failure was known by. Failure modes found by different inspections may overlap: an ItemHistory takes inspection windows of different types that overlap or coincide (a seal and a bearing found at one inspection), and the same window given twice for one type is one count of both; windows of one type still may not overlap. A fit of every failure refuses data whose windows of different types overlap or coincide, pointing to without("event_types") (which combines the failures found at one inspection) or for_event_type.

  • A record’s covariate by name: item.covariate("site") (NaN where not recorded), for select(where=lambda item: item.covariate("site") == 1) (#929). A covariate not recorded (NaN, or None) is accepted by ItemLifetime and ItemHistory, as the datasets accept it, and follows the package’s missing-value rule: fits of independent items drop the row with one warning, the recurrent fits refuse it, naming the items. to_observations() gives each kind’s ids ("<kind>_ids") and the covariate names, which from_observations takes back, so SurpyvalData.from_observations(**data.to_observations()) keeps the ids and names it used to lose (and failures of a kind given without event types are masked causes, as elsewhere).

  • surpyval.test_planning: planning reliability tests before they are run (see Test Planning with SurPyval).

    • Demonstration tests, moved here from RePyability’s demonstration (#862): demonstration_sample_size, demonstrated_reliability (the Clopper-Pearson bound; with no failures, success_run), demonstration_test_multiple and demonstration_pass_probability for attribute tests, with extended (Weibayes) tests that trade units for test time; mtbf_test_time, demonstrated_mtbf and mtbf_pass_probability for constant-failure-rate tests, time- or failure-terminated; and demonstration_plan and mtbf_demonstration_plan, the smallest tests that keep both the consumer’s and the producer’s risk (the fixed-length plans of MIL-HDBK-781), returning a DemonstrationPlan. The behaviour, array broadcasting and tests are RePyability’s; the confidence level is alpha_ci, the consumer’s risk, as everywhere in SurPyval (RePyability’s confidence=0.95 is alpha_ci=0.05), and is keyword only.

    • Sequential tests (#865): sequential_mtbf_test and sequential_demonstration_test, Wald’s sequential probability ratio test for an MTBF and for a pass/fail reliability, truncated at the fixed-length test with the same risks (truncate=False for Wald’s test as it is). Each test has its boundaries, a decide method, and its operating characteristic and mean test time (or units), computed exactly; its risks as run are consumer_risk and producer_risk.

    • Life tests for estimation precision (#863): life_test_precision, life_test_sample_size and life_test_length give the precision factor with which a time- or failure-censored test of a Weibull or lognormal lifetime estimates a quantile or the mean, the units it needs, or how long it must run, from the test’s expected Fisher information (Meeker and Escobar, ch. 10). A LifeTestPlan’s simulate checks the large-sample precision by fitting simulated tests.

    • Accelerated life test plans (#864): accelerated_test_plan chooses the stresses and the units at each that estimate a quantile at the use stress most precisely, for any single-stress life model of surpyval.life_models: the statistically optimum two-level plan, a compromise plan of three or more equally spaced levels (Meeker and Hahn), or a fixed allocation such as 4:2:1. accelerated_test_precision gives the precision of a test you propose, and the plan’s simulate checks it by fitting AcceleratedLife to simulated tests.

    • Power and sample size for comparing two groups (#880): logrank_events, logrank_sample_size and logrank_power, for a log-rank test of a hazard ratio under proportional hazards, by Schoenfeld’s formula or, with method="freedman", Freedman’s (as lifelines’ sample_size_necessary_under_cph and power_under_cph).

    • Power of a comparison of failure rates before and after a change: rate_ratio_power, rate_ratio_detectable (the smallest change an exposure detects) and rate_ratio_exposure (the exposure after the change a test needs; inf when the failures before it are too few for any), for the exact conditional test of surpyval.recurrent.intervention_test. The power is the exact sum over the counts, not a normal approximation.

  • surpyval.recurrent.intervention_test: did an intervention (a design change, a corrective action) change the rate of failures of one repairable system or a fleet, and is the evidence enough to say? It splits each system’s record at its own intervention time and gives the ratio of the rates after and before, its confidence interval and the p-value of no change. model="hpp" (the default) is the exact conditional test of two Poisson rates, with the Clopper-Pearson interval (method="mid-p" for the mid-p versions); with baseline="per-system" (the default) each system keeps its own rate and the test is the exact stratified test, which pooled systems with different rates cannot fool. model="power-law" lets the rate trend with age as the Crow-AMSAA power law, multiplied by the ratio after the change, and uses the likelihood ratio and the profile-likelihood interval. The InterventionTestResult gives a verdict ("decrease", "increase", "no change detected", "inconclusive" or "untestable"), the power the exposure had to detect a target change, the smallest change it could detect, the exposure still needed, and notes saying what to do when the evidence is short; data that cannot answer (no exposure after the change, no failure before it) give an "untestable" result that says why, rather than an error. The HPP result flags a trend within the periods (the Laplace test), which the power law accounts for. It takes T, the fitters’ c, delayed entry tl or gapped windows, and round-trips through strict JSON (to_dict / from_dict). The calibration studies check its size, power and coverage by simulation. See the new page “Intervention Analysis with SurPyval”.

  • Partial-effects plots (#876): model.plot_partial_effects(covariate, values) draws a regression’s survival curve (on="ff" or "Hf" for the others) at each of values of one covariate, the other covariates held at reference values, and returns the axes, each curve labelled "covariate = value". For the Cox model and the PH, AFT, PO, AH and accelerated life families. A covariate not plotted is held at its count-weighted mean over the fitted rows (the center of a center=True fit), or, for a categorical variable of a formula, at its reference level; reference={name: value} sets any of them. A formula’s covariate is a variable of the formula ("load" for np.log(load), "site" for C(site), plotted by its levels), and each row goes through the formula, interactions included; a term is refused, naming its variables, and so is a covariate whose reference the model cannot supply (one entering only transformed or in an interaction, a categorical variable with no level coded as zeros, a model restored without its data, a time-varying-covariate fit), naming reference=. plot_bounds=True draws the model’s cb as bands at alpha_ci (the parametric families; the Cox model has no cb and refuses it); x= sets the times, by default spanning the data. The competing-risks regressions (CompetingRisksProportionalHazards and the Fine-Gray model) draw the cumulative incidence of event=, without bands, and need reference for every numeric covariate, since they do not keep the covariates they were fitted to. See “Partial-effects plots” in Regression Modelling with SurPyval.

Changed

  • A dataset’s repr is its size and a table of its first rows (ids, times, flags, counts, truncation, event types, covariates and attributes), the same table as HTML in a notebook; summary() counts items, weighting rows by n, with the heading in one order (“4 items, 3 rows”) for both datasets; an ItemHistory shows on one line where it fits; event types and ids are plain Python values; and dir(data) leaves out the likelihoods’ split arrays (x_o, mask_i, …; still there) and the deprecated names (#934).

  • SurpyvalData.from_json reads a file path as well as JSON text (it used to parse a path as text); JSON of data with step time-varying covariates is written rather than refused (#935).

  • censor_at / enter_at refuse a date, a duration, text, a list or a cut-off at or before 0 where the data’s ages are measured from 0, saying what to give; select(ids=) on data without ids says so rather than using row numbers a selection would renumber; select keeps the data’s order; with_covariates([]) says to give a column or use without (#932).

  • A fit refused a SurpyvalData names the reshape that fits without what it cannot take and the model that takes it; a record, a list of records, a SurpyvalData, an EventHistoryData, a DataFrame or a dict given as x is named with the call that builds the data it was meant for; Z of the wrong length, and a single record to from_items, are named; to_histories names the dict form that cannot hold event types (#933).

  • ItemLifetime refuses a right censored age at or after its right truncation (the dataset refused the row), an id that is missing or unhashable, naming the item; the mixed-id message names one id of each kind (#931).

  • CoxPH.check_ph() is the exact score test of R’s cox.zph (survival 3.0 and later), so its statistics and p-values change (#868). It was Grambsch and Therneau’s approximation, as lifelines and R before 3.0 compute it, which uses the average covariate variance in place of the variance at each event time. The time scales are now R’s as well: "km" is one minus the left-continuous Kaplan-Meier estimate, and "rank" ranks every observation’s time, censored ones too, not the event times only. The new values match R’s cox.zph to 1e-6 on the stored references (lung, veteran, and a set with delayed entry and ties, under Efron and Breslow ties). The differences are small in large samples and can matter in small ones and under heavy ties: on the Rossi data (fin and age) the km p-values move from 0.998, 0.016 and 0.054 (GLOBAL) to 0.876, 0.014 and 0.048, and on a tied data set of 120 rows a statistic from 1.39 to 3.24, as R gives. The signature, the table (and the module function’s dict) and the transforms are as they were; diagnose() reports the same test on the km and rank scales.

  • On a baseline defined below 0 (Normal, Gumbel, Logistic) a covariate path must cover every time the answer depends on (#952). The value at 0 was taken to hold back to -inf, and values given before 0 were ignored. A schedule may now start at -inf (StepSchedule.from_changepoints([-np.inf, ...], ...), {-np.inf: ...} on a record), and StepSchedule.constant does.

    • Proportional hazards and odds depend on the covariate back to -inf: their schedules and paths must start there (a formula, CovariatePath.from_callable, has a value at every time), unless survival is given an age at or after their start (given=).

    • Accelerated failure time and additive hazards measure the covariate’s effect from 0: a path from 0 serves times from 0, and an earlier time needs the covariate from that time on.

    • Cox needs the covariate before every baseline jump below 0 that a query counts.

    • mean_tvc without given needs the covariate from -inf (for additive hazards, with one value before 0).

    • A CovariatePath is integrated below 0 there as well (#957): back to each time asked about before 0 and, for proportional hazards and odds, back to -inf. The integral from -inf converges because these baselines’ hazard dies away below 0; along a path that grows without limit going back in time it may not, and is refused.

  • In fit_tvc a subject’s first row enters at its xl, as any other row does (#952). On a baseline defined below 0, a first xl of 0 now means the subject entered at 0, and the fit conditions on its surviving to 0, which changes those fits. xl = -inf is a subject followed since -inf, which gives the old fit. Baselines that start at 0 are unchanged.

    • A fit from item records reads an item with no left_truncation as followed since -inf there, and refuses one whose covariates start later.

    • Additive hazards refuse a subject followed since -inf whose covariate changes before 0.

    • The accelerated failure time fit measures accelerated age from 0, and refuses an exit at or before 0 on such a baseline.

  • A covariate schedule must start at or before the point time is measured from (#930). A StepSchedule or CovariatePath that started later had its first value taken as the value from the start, a silent assumption: now a prediction (sf_tvc and the other *_tvc methods, the degradation clock) refuses a schedule starting after 0, a record refuses one starting after the start of its observation (left_truncation, else 0), as a {age: values} dict already was, and a fit from item records refuses it too. Give the values from the start, e.g. StepSchedule.from_changepoints([0, 5, 8], ...). A path through points (CovariatePath.from_points) has no value before its first point (path(t) there is refused), and its start says where it starts (StepSchedule.start too); with a period its points must start at 0, as StepSchedule.cyclic’s do.

  • Records keep the time-varying covariates as given (#930): a StepSchedule or CovariatePath shows as itself in the repr, a dict as the dict, and clone, update_covariates and the dataset reshapes keep it. A record whose schedule started late was accepted, but cloning, updating or reshaping it failed. StepSchedule``s compare by their edges, values and period (two equal cyclic schedules were unequal), and a record with one hashes by contents, so equal records hash alike however the schedule was given. A ``StepSchedule’s repr is the call that builds it, e.g. StepSchedule.from_changepoints([0.0, 8.0], [[0.0], [1.0]]) (one of more than 20 segments in short).

  • A dataset’s arrays (SurpyvalData and EventHistoryData: x, c, n, t, Z, e and the arrays split from them) are read-only (#927). Changing one in place (data.c[2] = 1) left the split arrays and the summary out of step with it, so two fits of the same data could differ; make a changed dataset with the reshaping methods, or from changed arrays. Arrays given to a dataset are copied where they come in, so changing them afterwards does not change it.

  • A True/False c is refused (#920), by every fitter, fit_from_df and SurpyvalData. c is the censoring flag (1 = right censored), and a boolean column is far more often an event indicator (True = failed: died, churned), which was read the wrong way round, every failure taken as a suspension and every suspension as a failure, with no warning. The message says how to pass either: an event indicator as c=1 - event, a censoring indicator as 0/1 numbers. Integer and float flags are read as before.

Deprecated

  • EventHistoryData.get_times_to_first_events() is to_first_events() (#926), which returns what it should have: each item’s first failure with its delayed entry, id and covariates, one row per item (the old method lost all three and grouped the items). The old name gives the new result, with a DeprecationWarning, until v0.26.

  • EventHistoryData.items (the item ids) is EventHistoryData.ids, as on SurpyvalData; “items” is kept for item records (from_items, to_items, item(id)). The old name works, with a DeprecationWarning, until v0.26.

  • RecurrentEventData is renamed EventHistoryData (and its module surpyval.utils.recurrent_event_data is surpyval.utils.event_history_data): it holds any item’s event history – recurrent events now, and the changes of state and markers of the multi-state and joint models to come – not recurrent events only. The old names are the same class, with a DeprecationWarning, until v0.26; isinstance checks against the old name keep working. The recurrent fitters’ fit_from_recurrent_data keeps its name.

  • The top-level data-format functions fs_to_xcnt, fsl_to_xcnt, fsli_to_xcnt, fsli_handler, fs_to_xrd, xcn_to_fs, xcnt_handler, xcnt_to_xrd, xrd_handler and xrd_to_xcnt (surpyval.fs_to_xcnt and so on), for the SurpyvalData methods above. Unlike other deprecations, these have a date: deprecated on 2026-10-12, they warn (naming the replacement) when used, and the first release on or after 2027-04-12 removes them. The warning is a FutureWarning, which Python shows wherever the name is used (a DeprecationWarning is hidden outside __main__), and the names stay in __all__, so from surpyval import * still gets them, with the warning, until then. surpyval.utils keeps the functions. Data Wrangling Examples maps each to its replacement.

Removed

The names 0.24 deprecated are gone; each now raises the error Python would, naming its replacement. Run your code under 0.24 with python -W error::DeprecationWarning first to find the calls to update.

  • CompetingRisksProportionalHazards.beta, the sum of the causes’ coefficients: use betas (one row per cause) or params (named by parameter_names). phi_e refuses a row index of betas, naming the cause’s label to pass, as cif takes it.

  • NonParametric.cb’s old argument order cb(x, on, bound, ...): the order is cb(x, on, alpha_ci, bound, ...), as every model’s; a bound given third raises a TypeError that says so.

  • MixtureModel.p, the EM responsibilities: internal to the fit; the weights are w.

  • ProportionalIntensityNHPP.fit(dist=): use baseline=.

  • Development: REMOVED_IN is "0.26" (the names deprecated in 0.25: RecurrentEventData and EventHistoryData’s items and get_times_to_first_events) and REMOVED_IN_NEXT "0.27".

Fixed

  • Intervals that only meet at one time, such as (1, 3] and (3, 5] (“abutting” intervals), leave the likelihood of a family that can concentrate its mass anywhere with no finite maximum: it rises along a flat ridge towards a spike at that time, split either side. A Normal returned sigma = 0.35 as a verified maximum, within 1e-8 of the limit’s log-likelihood. Such a fit now warns “No finite maximum” once and records maximum = "no finite maximum", as the other such data do (the known gap of Design Principle 12); a truncated fit is held to the spike’s likelihood and only warned where it has not beaten it. With an exact failure at that time the likelihood is unbounded, and the fit is refused, as a point mass consistent with every observation already was.

  • The Wald param_cb on lfp_p or f0 a hair from 1 let numpy’s overflow warning out of the logit back-transform.

  • ``fit_from_recurrent_data`` refuses what ``fit(data)`` refuses (#959). Given an EventHistoryData holding covariates or event types that the fitter has no argument for, every recurrent fitter’s fit_from_recurrent_data fitted anyway, dropping the covariates or pooling the failure modes into one process, where fit(data) refused. It now refuses with the same message, which names the way to fit without them (data.without("covariates"), data.without("event_types") or data.for_event_type(t)). What a fitter takes is read from its fit, so the two cannot disagree. CauseSpecificMCF given covariates as well as event types dropped the covariates; ProportionalIntensityHPP / NHPP given event types and no covariates failed with a raw AttributeError.

  • LinkedPathModel’s path, inv_path and jacobian take an array for each parameter, broadcasting with the ages, as the built-in path models do (they applied the links along the wrong axis, and failed); and it pickles (it held its link functions as lambdas).

  • Survival given an age needs the covariate from that age only under proportional hazards and odds, additive hazards and Cox (#962). There S(x | g) depends on the covariate from g on, the part before it dividing out, as a fit already takes a subject entering late with no covariates before its entry. sf_tvc, cb_tvc and mean_tvc with given=g refused a schedule (and, on a baseline starting at 0, a path) that started after 0, or on a baseline defined below 0 after -inf, though it started by g; one starting after g is refused by name. Accelerated failure time and life still need the covariate from 0: the age reached by g depends on it before g too.

  • Right truncation of recurrent (event history) data is right truncation (#924). A finite tr given to the recurrent fits, handle_xicn or an ItemHistory was read as the end of the item’s observation – the same as an end-of-observation (c=1) row at tr – so a fit with tr gave exactly the fit with that row. Right truncation is a selection: the item is in the data because it failed by tr (a repair or warranty-claim database holds only the units that came back), and ignoring that makes the items look less reliable than they are (in a simulated fleet kept for a failure by 10 hours, a Crow-AMSAA alpha of 8.1 against a true 15). The parametric intensity models (Crow-AMSAA, Duane, Cox-Lewis, the HPP and the other NHPPs, and the proportional intensity models) now divide each truncated item’s likelihood by the chance of at least one failure in its window up to tr, 1 - exp(-(Lambda(tr) - Lambda(entry))) – and, for an item whose observation ended before tr with no failure seen (cut by censor_at), multiply it by the chance of a failure after its end but by tr. The end of observation is a c=1 row (or right_censored), else the item’s last failure, and may be before or after tr; an item watched to tr or beyond must have a failure by tr. The non-parametric MCF, the cause-specific models, the renewal (imperfect repair) models and the trend tests and residuals cannot account for the selection, and refuse tr, saying to give a c=1 row if the end of observation was meant. Upgrading: where tr was used for the end of observation, give an end-of-observation (c=1) row (or right_censored) instead; the fits are then as before. On item records, to_first_events() keeps the right truncation (an item’s first failure came by tr), as does the first gap of to_gaps(); enter_at and for_event_type drop it from histories, with a warning, as for_event_type does for lifetimes. EventHistoryData.get_right_truncation_close is replaced by selection_terms.

  • ItemHistory.state_at gave a state after observation ended (with no right_censored, after the last failure), and a change of state after that end was accepted; state_at is None there and the change is refused, saying to give right_censored (#924).

  • Covariates (#929): with_covariates given one covariate twice kept one column by name and two by number; both are refused. A dataset whose covariates had a NaN could not be reshaped – even without("covariates") failed on the NaN it was removing – as its records refused NaN; records accept it now.

  • Event types on rows that have not failed (#928): a suspension given a type in SurpyvalData(..., e=...), from_observations or a competing-risks fit was accepted, after which every reshape (even without("event_types")) failed; and a type on an end-of-observation row of handle_xicn was silently lost by to_items. Both are dropped, with a warning. The competing-risks fits’ refusal of a censored row with a type read as the opposite of what it meant. A tuple id or event type (a gap’s id from to_gaps, ("A", 2)) was split by slicing one row and came back from JSON as a list, after which item(id) failed; it is kept as one value, and JSON keeps it a tuple.

  • Item records (ItemLifetime, ItemHistory) came back from pickle or copy.deepcopy with writeable arrays, so a copy could be changed in place, bypassing its checks; they are fixed again when unpickled (#927). A StepSchedule given as a record’s time_varying_covariates is copied: changing the caller’s schedule used to change the record and its hash (a record in a set was then not found).

  • EventHistoryData (#925): one row, data[k], kept neither an interval row [start, end] (it became two times) nor its covariate columns (all but the first were dropped); it is one row, as a slice of one is. The constructor EventHistoryData(x, i, c, n, ...) checked nothing, and took rows of different lengths, censoring codes such as 7 and negative counts (which went on to give negative event counts); it checks its arrays as handle_xicn does, and takes one i, c, n, tl or tr for every row. An index that selects no rows (data[5:5], of SurpyvalData too) failed on numpy’s “zero-size array”; it says it selects no rows. The repr was numpy’s text of four of its arrays; it is the size of the data and a table of its first rows (with truncation, event types and covariates where it has them), and the class docstring starts from from_items and from_histories.

  • A regression model fitted with named covariates read a pandas Series of one item’s covariates by position, not by name, giving a wrong prediction with no warning (sf(t, pd.Series({"age": 50, "arm": 1})) read age as arm), and a dict raised a TypeError (#921). A Series labelled by covariate names, and a dict {name: value} (or {name: values} for several items), are read by name, as a DataFrame is; a dict for a model fitted without names is refused, saying why. Fine-Gray and the proportional intensity models read covariates by position even from a DataFrame; they now read a DataFrame, Series or dict by the names they were fitted with, as the other regressions do.

  • SurpyvalData.to_xrd() returned the arrays it keeps for the next call, so editing the result (r *= 10) changed what that data gave from then on; it returns copies, as to_xcnt() does.

  • A SurpyvalData given to a function that takes arrays only (the recurrent-event and competing-risks fitters) said “Variable ‘x’ must be numbers”; it now says the function takes arrays, and that to_xcnt() gives them. A regression fit given a SurpyvalData without covariates says the data holds none, not that Z is a missing positional argument.

  • fit_best(include=[]) is refused, naming the fix; it used to try the default candidates as if include had been left out.

  • A parametric model’s printout has a Maximum line when the fit is not a verified maximum of the likelihood (maximum is "unverified" or "no finite maximum"); it used to read as an ordinary fit, with only the warning raised by fit to say otherwise.

  • The parametric and regression bootstrap bounds refuse n_boot=1: a single refit has no spread, and its BCa bounds came back NaN without a warning. The message says that 1000 or more refits is usual.

  • Messages: the MLE-failure warning’s run-together sentence (“closer.A good way”) and “it’s inverse”; the refusal of a censoring flag other than -1, 0 or 1 says what each means and that interval censoring is c=2 with [left, right] pairs; a non-numeric alpha_ci is refused saying a number is expected.

  • The degradation process fits’ y0 documentation says the estimated start level can be below zero, and to pass y0=0.0 for paths known to start at zero.

  • rmst_diff refuses a tau past a group’s largest observed time while that group’s survival estimate is above zero there. It used to hold the curve at its last value out to tau, so the RMSTs and their difference were whatever the horizon made them (tau=1e6 gave a difference of 25,000 on data running to 120).

  • A single group’s mean(tau), rmst(tau) and mean_cb(tau) refuse a tau past the largest observed time while the survival estimate there is above zero, as rmst_diff does. They held the curve at its last value out to tau, so the RMST was whatever tau made it. Leaving tau out (the largest observed time) and a curve that reaches zero are unaffected.

  • MixtureModel refuses an m that is not a whole number of at least 1, saying so; m=0 used to fail inside numpy with “number sections must be larger than 0”.

  • from_json given a string that is neither a file nor JSON text (which starts with {) says that it read the string as a file path, rather than only that the file was not found.

  • success_run refuses a number of successes that is not a whole number; success_run(2.5) used to return a bound for half a trial.

  • cb, param_cb and the other bounds on a model built by weibayes say that the model is itself the bound (its scale the lower confidence bound at the alpha_ci it was built with) and to call weibayes again for another level, rather than only “Only MLE has confidence bounds”.

  • MixtureModel.qf keeps full precision in the upper tail and is about 200 times faster (#821). It solved ff(t) = u one quantile at a time with brentq, so above u = 1/2 it kept only the digits of 1 - 1e-16: sf(qf(1 - s)) was off from s by 1e-4 at s = 1e-12. It now solves every quantile at once by Newton steps with the density, kept in the bracket of the components’ quantiles by bisection, against s - sf(t) above 1/2 and ff(t) - u below: about 1e-14 at both ends, and 20,000 quantiles in 0.06 s rather than 14.

  • Additive hazards models stay inside their support (#828). The model is a distribution only where the hazard h_0(x) + beta'Z and its integral H(x | Z) are both non-negative, and nothing kept the fit there: the likelihood rises without limit as H falls below 0 at an observation, so fits put sf above 1 at their own data. That happened on ordinary positive data with a protective covariate (WeibullAH, LogNormalAH and GammaAH on the regression test fixture, at one or two observations), and on a baseline over the whole real line the fit ran off entirely, with sf up to 1e22 at the data and mean(Z) up to 1e39. The fit now keeps every observed point inside the support (H >= 0 at the times, interval bounds and finite truncation times, h >= 0 at the times and bounds), which recovers the truth on simulated real-line data with half the times negative. A fit that ends against that limit (H = 0 at an observation, where that unit’s support starts) is a maximum on the boundary, as a threshold’s is at the smallest observation: it warns, its maximum is "unverified" and its standard errors are approximate. Its estimates differ from 0.24’s, which were not those of a distribution. A level with no events now has a finite coefficient, held at that limit, rather than none. Predictions outside the support (sf, ff, df, hf, Hf, qf, cb, random and the time-varying functions) are nan with one warning, where they returned sf above 1 or negative ff with a warning. mean(Z) of a row on a real-line baseline with beta'Z > 0 is the mean from where its support starts (it integrated the whole real line, 6.9e25 for a Gumbel baseline), and nan with a warning where the model is not a distribution along the way.

  • Likelihood-ratio bounds of an additive hazards model reach the edge of its support (#837). Its likelihood is not defined outside the support (#828), so the region is cut off where that limit binds. The searches stepped into the undefined part, and the line back to the estimate crossed it, so a 99% bound could come out inside the 95% one (coef_1’s lower bound, -0.0188 against -0.0176). The searches are now held to the support as constraints, and both bounds are where the deviance reaches its limit with the support active: -0.0419 and -0.0265, as a brute-force constrained search finds. Other models’ searches are unchanged.

  • A parametric regression model’s qf(p, Z) is exact to rounding (#828): each quantile is finished by Newton’s method on the cumulative hazard. It was solved to a tolerance on the time relative to the time, which near an additive model’s support start (at -27 on a Normal baseline) left sf(qf(1 - s)) off by up to 1.8e-5 of s; every family is now within about 1e-14 of the probability asked for, and an additive model within the cancellation in H0(x) + x beta'Z near its support start (5e-9 at p = 1e-9). The bootstrap’s quantile bounds use the same finish.

  • A renewal fit whose life runs off (no finite maximum, #777) climbs the ridge with the restoration and the life together (#795). It refitted the life with the restoration held where the search had stalled: a Kijima-II fit to one item’s ExpoWeibull run-off stayed at q = 0.061 and a log-likelihood of -43.93, while ARA-inf, the same model, reached -43.81 at rho = 0.922. Kijima-II now reaches -43.81 at q = 0.078 = 1 - rho. The verdict is unchanged, and so are the fits with a maximum.

  • A renewal fit with no finite default start takes its restoration starts’ lifetimes from the family’s own initial guess (#796). They were lifetimes fitted to the aged gaps, about 0.5 s each for the ExpoWeibull run-offs that need them. On #774’s benchmarks only one data set’s three ExpoWeibull ARA fits use these starts: 6.4, 6.8 and 7.5 s become 4.3, 6.7 and 5.8 s, with the same verdicts. They have no finite maximum, so the point reported is where the search stops on the ridge, which moves by at most 3e-4 of log-likelihood.

  • The Gamma’s shape derivatives below a standardised time of 30 are exact to rounding (#797). The derivatives of the logs of the incomplete gamma in its shape were five-point differences, 1e-10 off mpmath’s typically and up to 4e-9 (at a shape of 0.5 and a time of 1); they are now carried along the series of P and the continued fraction of Q, within 1e-14 (above 30 the hazard already had them from its own fraction, #786). It costs time: a GammaPH fit on 400 rows takes 0.32 s where it took 0.21 s.

  • CrowAMSAA.fit on systems observed for different lengths (#839). It ran from its all-ones start (a cif of x, thousands against an MCF of ten on data in hours) to where the cif is 0 everywhere, alpha infinite and beta 4e47, with an infinite likelihood and an “unverified” warning: ten pumps observed to 6800–8760 hours did. With exact failures from time 0 the MLE is now exact for unequal ends as it was for a common one (beta the one root of the profile likelihood’s slope, alpha in closed form at it), so to rounding where the search agreed to 5e-5. Other data (delayed entry, censored counts) is searched from the HPP through the end of the MCF, as Cox-Lewis starts, on any time scale.

  • Plots: the recurrent-event plots (MCF, Crow-AMSAA and the other NHPPs, proportional intensity, cause-specific) and the parametric regression’s survival plot label their axes, and a single probability plot’s time ticks are spaced as two plots’ merged ticks were: rounded to a figure, 900 and 1000 printed as “9001000”.

  • LogLogistic.mean with beta <= 1 is infinite: the tail falls as x**-beta, so the mean of the positive lifetime is. It was nan.

  • A proportional-hazards model whose cumulative hazard passes exp(709) at a query point, as on a fit run off along a coefficient, gives H = inf and sf = 0 there without numpy’s “overflow encountered in exp” (#801): the overflow is the infinite limit the product tends to.

Performance

  • SurpyvalData’s reshapes (without, with_covariates, for_event_type, relabel_event_types, select, censor_at, enter_at) run on its arrays, giving the same data as rebuilding every record: at 50,000 items a reshape takes tens of milliseconds rather than seconds (#932).

  • qf of a limited-failure or zero-inflated model takes one pass fewer and no longer evaluates its distribution’s quantile at 0 and 1 for the probabilities whose quantiles it sets to 0 or infinity (#798). Those went through the log of 0, a slow path; they are given 0.5, and the clip to [0, 1] goes, since rounding keeps every other rescaled probability inside it. The bounds check’s least and greatest values are reused. A Weibull with lfp_p=0.9 takes about 25 ns a value where it took 30 on 1e6 values. The results and warnings are those of 0.24, bit for bit, over 23 distributions, ten lfp_p/f0/gamma settings and fifteen kinds of input.

  • The distribution functions cost less per call on small arrays (#799). Two steps, each with the results of 0.24 to the bit (values, types and warnings, the derivatives in the parameters and the fits, over 23 distributions and 5037 cases). surpyval’s own formulas run with autograd’s primitives unwrapped when nothing is being differentiated: a primitive looks through every argument for a box before calling the numpy function, about 0.8 us an operation. And where every point is inside a continuous distribution’s support, none missing, two reductions say so and the formula is called directly, in place of the NaN check and the support guard’s six numpy calls. On 10 values the median function is 11% quicker: a Weibull’s sf takes 13 us where it took 20 and a fitted model’s 18.5 where it took 27. The overhead left is mostly those checks and numpy’s own per-call cost.

v0.24 (9 October 2026)

Upgrading from 0.23. A breaking release. Most code needs no change; the items most likely to need one, or to change a result, are listed here, and every entry below says what changed. On 0.23, run your code or tests with python -W error::DeprecationWarning first to find the calls to update.

  • Names 0.23 deprecated now raise (see Removed): the limited-failure p is lfp_p, beta_j in fixed and param_cb is the coefficient’s name, se is standard_errors(), cov_matrix and cov are covariance(), recurrent aic and bic are aic() and bic(), and success_run takes alpha_ci=.

  • SurvivalTree and RandomSurvivalForest sf(x, Z) pair row i of Z with x[i], as the regressions do (#666); pass grid=True for the old grid of every time for every row.

  • alpha_ci outside (0, 1) is refused by every bound, and one above 0.5 warns (#647): alpha_ci=0.05 is a 95% interval.

  • CrowAMSAA.projection with BC modes uses the bias-corrected shape (#730): its demonstrated and projected MTBF move (the handbook example’s 7.707 and 11.006 are 7.847 and 11.294); one failure now raises.

  • The parametric, accelerated life and frailty regressions, BuckleyJames and the semi-parametric ProportionalOdds fit their rows in one sorted order (#728, #746, #760, #777): answers no longer depend on the row order, may move at rounding, and model.data lists the rows sorted.

  • CoxPH and FineGray find a run-off along a combination of covariates (#728, #746): a fit once “verified” may now warn “No finite maximum”, with nan standard errors for the coefficients that run off.

  • CoxPH and BuckleyJames refuse data with no event (#648).

  • A regression, tree or forest prediction with the wrong number of covariates raises (#657); an extra column was ignored in silence.

  • The Arrhenius-type life models refuse a stress at or below 0, and warn when every stress in the temperature column is below 200 K, as temperatures typed in degrees Celsius are (#654): give temperatures in kelvin.

  • An offset model’s Wald cb, quantile_cb and param_cb warn that they hold the offset fixed (#645); pass method="bootstrap" for bounds that include it. Offset fits on interval data can move (#633).

  • Renewal fits read a finite tr as each item’s end of observation (#624) and search on exact gradients (#728, #746, #760): likelihoods are equal or higher, so parameters can move.

  • Recurrent data with an event exactly at tl, or an exact event given as [l, r] with l != r, are refused (#658).

  • quantile_cb gives NaN with a warning for p outside (0, 1) rather than raising (#626, #710); test the result rather than catching ValueError.

  • from surpyval import * no longer exports np (#667); import numpy yourself.

  • Deprecated in 0.24, removed in v0.25: CompetingRisksProportionalHazards phi_e by row index (pass the cause label) and beta, NonParametric.cb’s old argument order, MixtureModel.p and ProportionalIntensityNHPP(dist=) (baseline=).

Removed. The names 0.23 deprecated are gone; each now raises.

  • The limited-failure proportion’s old name p is lfp_p: in fixed, param_cb, from_params and the attribute of a univariate or regression model (#608). model.p raises an AttributeError naming lfp_p; on Bernoulli, Binomial, Geometric, NegativeBinomial and FixedEventProbability it is still the fitted parameter. Saved dicts keep the key "p".

  • Regression coefficients’ old names beta_0, beta_1, … in fixed and param_cb are the covariate’s column name, else coef_0, coef_1, … (#614); dicts saved with them still load.

  • se (Cox, Lin-Ying, proportional odds, Fine-Gray) is standard_errors() (#613).

  • Parametric.cov_matrix, cov (Fine-Gray, proportional odds, additive hazards) and the covariance attribute (Royston-Parmar, the frailty models) are covariance() (#605).

  • Recurrent models’ aic and bic without the call are aic() and bic() (#572).

  • MixtureModel.log_likelihood(params) is gone: log_likelihood is the fitted value, a plain float (#572); MixtureModel.loglike (the negative log-likelihood) is neg_ll().

  • MixtureModel’s EM steps EM, Q, expectation, maximisation, likelihood and initialise_params have no public names; they are internal to the fit (#605).

  • A Cox model’s neg_ll(beta) is neg_ll_of(beta); neg_ll() is the fitted value (#604).

  • CoxFrailty’s loglik and loglik_no_frailty are log_likelihood and log_likelihood_no_frailty (#604).

  • success_run’s confidence= and alpha= are alpha_ci= (#580, keyword only: success_run(59, 0.95) raises a TypeError rather than reading 0.95 as alpha_ci).

  • surpyval.NUM, TINIEST and EPS are numpy.float64, numpy.finfo(float).tiny and numpy.sqrt(numpy.finfo(float).eps) (#613); surpyval.utils.numeric no longer has them either.

  • Development: REMOVED_IN is "0.25" (the names deprecated in 0.24) and REMOVED_IN_NEXT "0.26"; the removal test’s scan checks that it sees every helper of surpyval.utils.deprecation. Two mixture tests that counted EM steps by patching EM and Q counted nothing since those became aliases; they now patch the internal methods.

Changes.

  • Breaking, in surpyval.beta: the survival tree and forest pair rows with times (#666). SurvivalTree and RandomSurvivalForest sf(x, Z) (and ff, df, hf, Hf) with a covariate matrix gave every time for every row, a (len(Z),) + x.shape grid, where every regression model pairs row i of Z with x[i]. They now pair them as the regression models do: one row is used at every time, one time for every row, and any other count is refused with the regression models’ ValueError. To keep the old result pass grid=True; grid is now a plain bool defaulting to False. The FutureWarning that announced the change is gone, and there is no deprecation period: surpyval.beta carries no stability promise. A 1-D Z (one covariate vector), and a scalar time with several rows, give the same result as before. survival_probability no longer passes grid=False to a model whose sf takes it.

Performance

  • Wald confidence bounds are 18-36x faster for the Weibull, Exponential, Rayleigh, Normal, LogNormal, Logistic, LogLogistic and Gumbel families, with or without offset, LFP and zero-inflation: cb (on sf, ff and Hf) and quantile_cb. The delta method’s Jacobian was autograd.jacobian’s, one reverse pass per time asked for; it is now taken in forward mode, one pass per parameter whatever the number of times. Both are exact: the bounds agree with 0.23’s to 3e-15. ndtr, log_ndtr and autograd’s expit gained forward-mode rules (the derivatives their reverse rules use); a family whose functions have none (the Gamma, Beta and ExpoWeibull’s incomplete gamma and beta functions) keeps reverse mode. Nine bands and a quantile bound at 200 times on a 300-unit Weibull fit: 552 -> 20 ms.

  • Building a SurpyvalData is about a third faster. Every fit builds one from its inputs first. The distinct truncation windows, and the distinct values the identifiability check counts, came from np.unique(..., axis=0), which sorts rows as structured records; each column is now ranked on its own and the pairs of ranks sorted as integers. A flat list of numbers is converted to an array once rather than once per check. The data are identical, dtypes included, and so are the errors: on 100,000 units with mixed censoring and truncation, from arrays 58 → 41 ms, from lists 89 → 62 ms, and the identifiability check 12 → 2.5 ms.

  • fit_best builds its data once. It checked the data as a SurpyvalData and then gave each candidate the raw inputs, so every family built and checked them again, and estimated the non-parametric start again. Every candidate is now fitted to that one SurpyvalData (fit_from_surpyval_data). Results, warnings and errors are identical; on right-censored data 10,000 units 381 -> 346 ms and 100,000 units 2.51 -> 2.08 s, a larger share wherever the fits themselves are quick.

  • A fitted model’s sf, ff and df are about twice as fast on small arrays, and up to 2.4x on large ones for a model with no offset, limited-failure or zero-inflation part, with identical results (#642). Such a model now gives its distribution’s own functions, skipping the transforms (identities there, but five passes over the query), and the support and missing-value checks around every distribution function use plain numpy rather than autograd’s wrappers. A Weibull’s sf on 16 points: 58 to 28 us; an Exponential’s on 20,000: 193 to 79 us.

  • A fitted model’s qf is about twice as fast, three times on small arrays, and random up to 2x, with identical values and warnings (#769). Each offset, limited-failure and zero-inflation step is taken only where it changes something, so a model without them gives its distribution’s qf; the probabilities are checked once, by two reductions, not in both the model’s and the distribution’s qf; and the uniforms skip scipy’s argument handling. A Weibull’s on a million values: 30 to 15 ns each; on 2,000: 101 to 31 us.

Added

  • CompetingRisks.cb(x, event, on="cif", ...): pointwise confidence bounds on a cause’s cumulative incidence, with Aalen’s variance (the var of R’s cmprsk::cuminc; aalen_johansen_variance) on the log(-log) scale by default, and on the all-cause or net sf, ff and Hf as KaplanMeier / NelsonAalen would give them (#728). 0 before the first time, NaN with a warning past the last.

  • CompetingRisks.plot draws the bounds, as a shaded band by default as the single-event plots (plot_bounds, alpha_ci, bound, bound_type; #746). Unstacked, each cause’s CIF band; stacked, the band of the top of the stack, the all-cause failure probability (Kaplan-Meier’s), since a cause’s bounds do not bound its layer.

  • FixedEventProbability.qf (0 up to p, inf above it; NaN with one warning outside [0, 1]) and Binomial.fit_from_df(..., n_trials_col=) for per-row trials (#626).

  • MixtureModel has hf (df / sf), qf (ff inverted numerically; NaN with a warning outside [0, 1]), covariance() and standard_errors() (the observed information, weights as softmax logits, carried to the parameters and weights; named by covariance_names: alpha_0, …, w_0, …), and Wald param_cb, cb and quantile_cb as Parametric’s (#651).

  • CompetingRisksProportionalHazards has the per-cause coefficients’ inference: params, parameter_names ("a: grp"), covariance() (block-diagonal, each cause’s fit’s), standard_errors(), p_values, summary() and a readable repr; FineGray has params, parameter_names and summary(). phi_e takes the cause label, as cif (the row index is deprecated), and beta (the causes’ sum) is deprecated. A Fine-Gray model’s log_likelihood raises AttributeError, so hasattr works (#656).

  • One API across the regression families (#662). qf on CoxPH, ProportionalOdds, AdditiveHazards, BuckleyJames and the frailty models (a step curve’s: the first time it reaches p, else nan); mean(Z) and p_values on the parametric regressions; summary() tables on AdditiveHazards, BuckleyJames and RoystonParmar (whose text is now its repr only); tl / tr on the parametric fits; CoxFrailty.param_cb(method=). A model with no likelihood says why on neg_ll / aic.

  • Ergonomics (#666). fit_best(return_table=True) ranks every candidate; DestructiveDegradationModel has qf, hf, mean, random; Wiener / gamma process models covariance(), standard_errors(), param_cb, cb; trees and forests sf(x, Z, grid=) (see Changes); recurrent summary() and an MCF repr; forecast ignores random_state where exact; NonParametric.cb(x, on, alpha_ci, bound) (old order warns); to_dict / to_frame on Forecast and RULs.

  • neg_ll(), aic(), bic(), aic_c() and log_likelihood on WienerProcess / GammaProcess fits (k counts the stress coefficients, not y0; n is the number of increments, so a Wiener and a gamma process on the same paths can be ranked), DestructiveDegradation fits and CauseSpecificNHPP (the causes’ sum; BIC’s n the events of any cause) (#711).

Fixed

  • CrowAMSAA.projection with BC modes takes the demonstrated intensity from the bias-corrected shape, (N - 1) / N of the MLE (#730), as the handbook’s test-fix-find-test example does: it now reproduces that example (demonstrated MTBF 7.84708, projected 11.29418), where it gave 7.707 and 11.006. Without BC modes nothing changes. With BC modes and a single failure it raises.

  • The parametric and frailty regressions sort their rows with the count as the last key, as the semi-parametric fits do (#777), so counted data sort as their rows expanded one per unit. On rows tied in time and censoring with different counts the answers move at rounding, as in any other row order, and model.data lists them in the new order.

  • The refusal of a baseline that cannot be represented at Z = 0 says what it can compute (#777). A parametric fit’s quoted the parameters at Z = 0 ([inf, 1.5]) and named a location or scale running on at the covariate means as if at Z = 0; it names the parameter out of range, and says where it runs on. Cox, proportional odds and Fine-Gray say when the rows’ exp(beta'Z) overflows, not the move; CoxFrailty’s no longer points to center=True, which it has not.

  • A Cox model documents r, each time’s risk-set weight (#777): far along a run-off it is beyond floating point, inf (or 0), and is reported so, as the increments h0 there underflow; the increments are computed from its log and are right. Saved models keep it.

  • CoxFrailty’s group hazards are right at a run-off coefficient (#777): exp(beta'Z) overflowed and the baseline underflowed, a nan with numpy’s warnings. Past |beta'Z| = 300 they are summed in logs, as CoxPH’s baseline is. A coefficient that runs off now has no standard error, as in CoxPH: its variance was the inverse of an information at rounding, and could be negative.

  • Fine-Gray’s partial likelihood is right far out along a run-off (#760): a risk set’s sum underflowed and its log(0) made the objective -inf, the best point a search could find. Such sums are now taken in logs over their own risk sets, as are the derivatives there and the baseline, whose exp overflowed with numpy’s warnings.

  • CoxInformation, CoxFrailty’s information operator, holds at a run-off linear predictor (#760): exp(eta) and 1 / R^2 overflowed and it was nan. Where the Cox generators take their score and information in logs, it now scales each risk set’s sums by the set’s own total too; elsewhere it is unchanged to the bit.

  • CoxPH’s baseline is quiet and right at a run-off beta (#760): exp(beta'Z) overflowed, with numpy’s RuntimeWarning, and the increments were 0. Past |beta'Z| = 300, or where the units yet to enter all but cancel a risk set, its sums are taken in logs.

  • CoxPH judges its maximum in each covariate’s units, as Fine-Gray and the parametric fits do (#760). With a unit of 1, its BFGS fallback’s answer on a covariate spanning 3e-4 passed as verified where BFGS had not moved from 0 (the maximum at 15). Newton-Raphson’s fits keep their verdicts.

  • AcceleratedLife finishes its search with the Newton steps the other parametric regressions use (#760): on the log scale of a parameter with one bound, each step halved until it lowers the likelihood, and kept only where the answer is still a verified maximum. Answers move by about 1e-6 of a standard error; on random designs no verdict changes.

  • BuckleyJames and the semi-parametric ProportionalOdds no longer depend on the row order (#760): they fit their rows sorted by every column, as the parametric regressions do. They moved by 1e-16 with the order, and Buckley-James’s bootstrap_ci, which resamples the rows, drew differently in each order.

  • “No finite maximum” no longer says a parametric regression’s baseline location or scale “runs on” when only the baseline at the covariate means, where the fit runs, runs off with the coefficients (#760). With every event at Z = 0 it quoted the finite value at Z = 0 (a LogisticPO’s mu, 6.941); such a parameter is now judged at Z = 0, as the model reports it, and named only where it runs off there too.

  • Gamma.hf keeps its digits far in the tail (#760). As f / S, each of size e**-y at y = beta x, it lost y times the machine precision (4e-9 at y = 1e8, 12% at 1e15). Past y = 1000 it is the continued fraction of the upper incomplete gamma, in which the e**-y cancel exactly: within 1e-15 of mpmath, with exact autograd derivatives.

  • CoxLewis.cif is differentiable by autograd (#760); it was written in plain numpy (np.where, np.exp), so the NHPP and ARI likelihoods on a Cox-Lewis intensity had no autograd gradient. Its slope in beta is a series below |beta x| of 1/2, exact at beta = 0, where the closed form cancels.

  • A Cox-Lewis NHPP fit on data in thousands of hours or more is checked in the units of its beta (#760), one over the longest time, as the ARI fits are (#746). In units of 1 its check differenced a beta of 1e-5 in steps of 1% of it: of 30 simulated fits on data in 1e5 hours, 28 were called unverified, with a warning; all are verified now, in about half the time.

  • CompetingRisks.cb says why it has no bounds on hf, df or iif (#746): they are the step estimate’s jumps at the event times, which the single-event cb does not bound either (by design); the message points to the cumulative functions.

  • CoxPH finds a run-off along a combination of the coefficients (#728). Its test read each coefficient’s information alone, so on data that a combination of covariates separates the fit reported a “verified” maximum (coefficients 61.9 and -247.6, standard errors 0.6 and 0.5), or a verdict that depended on the row order. Where the search gives cause, the data now decide, by a linear programme over the risk sets: the fit warns “No finite maximum” naming the coefficients and their proportion.

  • CoxPH’s verdict no longer depends on the row order (#728). A column whose information at the start is rounding against its own spread (a level whose rows leave before any event; every risk set alike) was judged against the largest eigenvalue, itself small, and kept in some orders: the fit ran it off, “verified” in one order and “unverified” in another. It is aliased. A level with only censored rows is found to run off in every order (the test of the data above).

  • CoxPH.neg_ll_of(beta) is right and quiet at a large beta (#728). It gave inf or nan with numpy’s overflow, invalid and divide warnings (Efron, Breslow), raised IndexError (exact ties) or gave -inf (Kalbfleisch-Prentice). Past |beta'Z| = 300 the risk-set sums are taken in logs; a delayed-entry risk set that is all but cancelled by the units yet to enter is summed over itself (it gave 1.446 for 1.386). A beta whose linear predictor is not finite gives nan.

  • CoxPH’s score and information are right and quiet at a large beta (#746). Efron’s and Breslow’s information lost its ZR ZR' / R^2 term to overflow and looked healthy where it is about 0 (9 for e^-225); past |beta'Z| = 300 each risk set’s sums are now scaled by its own total. Kalbfleisch-Prentice’s were nan: each row of its recursion now has its own scale.

  • CoxPH’s delayed-entry score and information no longer subtract the mass yet to enter where it all but cancels a risk set (#746), as the likelihood no longer does (#728): the information was 2.00095 for 1.99995, or the score -inf. Such a risk set is summed over itself.

  • CoxPH asks the data whether its likelihood runs off wherever Newton-Raphson did not converge (#746). A random search found a run-off that met none of the three conditions that asked: BFGS stopped where the score of a covariate spanning 1e-7 was below the verification’s tolerance, and the fit reported a verified maximum of a likelihood with none. Why the conditions now suffice is set out in cox_separation.DECREMENT.

  • FineGray finds a run-off along a combination of the coefficients (#746). Its verdict came from the parametric judge, each coefficient alone: on events a combination separates it raised “SVD did not converge”. Where the search gives cause, the data now decide, by CoxPH’s exact test on the subdistribution risk sets; the fit warns “No finite maximum” with the proportion, and a run-off coefficient’s standard error is nan, as CoxPH’s.

  • CrowAMSAA.projection names the source its BC-mode projection was checked against (#710): ReliaSoft’s Crow Extended formulas, whose demonstrated intensity with BC modes is the Crow-AMSAA intensity at T fitted to every failure, as the code has it.

  • The renewal likelihoods (GeneralizedRenewal, G1, ARA, ARI) have exact derivatives (#710): the Kijima-II, ARA and ARI recursions wrote arrays in place, which autograd cannot follow, and are now primitives that carry their derivatives in q / rho. A fit that is not a verified maximum is polished on the exact gradient rather than central differences. The search is still Nelder-Mead, and its likelihoods are the same, bit for bit (a gradient-first search was not faster).

  • The renewal fits search on a hand-written gradient (#728): BFGS, with Nelder-Mead for a start it does not settle and to carry q / rho onto its bound, for a Weibull or LogNormal life and a power-law or Duane ARI baseline (others keep Nelder-Mead). The value and gradient cost about one likelihood, against 8 to 30 for autograd’s. Fits are 2 to 4 times faster, with likelihoods equal or higher; a Kijima fit on data with no finite maximum now finds the run-off rather than a local maximum.

  • The renewal fits with a Gamma, LogLogistic, Exponential or Rayleigh life or a Cox-Lewis or HPP ARI baseline search on a hand-written gradient too (#746); the Gamma’s shape derivative, with no closed form, to 1e-10 of mpmath’s, deep tails included. They take 0.15 to 0.9 of the time (Gamma 0.15 to 0.55), with likelihoods equal or higher. A Cox-Lewis beta is searched and checked in units of one over the longest time: two fits on data in thousands of hours called unverified (central differences too coarse for a beta of 1e-4) are verified.

  • So do the renewal fits with an ExpoWeibull, Normal, Gumbel or Logistic life (#760), whose derivatives are within 3e-13 of mpmath’s, far tails included. They take 0.15 to 0.9 of the time (median 0.23 to 0.46), with the same verdicts and likelihoods equal or higher, but on one run-off with no finite maximum, where each search stops elsewhere on the ridge.

  • The nightly property tests (#714). A regression or Cox df far in the upper tail, where the hazard overflows and sf underflows, is 0, not inf * 0 with a raw RuntimeWarning; a parametric PH Hf / hf whose exp(beta'Z) overflowed keeps a zero baseline 0. A parametric regression’s refusal of a baseline at Z = 0 it cannot represent says the data may have no finite maximum where the baseline’s own parameters run off (a Weibull shape to 1e15), rather than to move the covariates nearer 0.

  • Answers that differed between machines (numpy’s AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels round exp and log differently). The recurrent models’ covariance (and the degradation life models’) took its numerical Hessian with a first-derivative step, eps**(1/3), where rounding swamps a small curvature: a generalized renewal q with a standard error of 4.5 had its interval move by 2% between machines. The default step of numerical_hessian is now eps**(1/4), and the standard errors are the converged ones. BuckleyJames.ff(qf(p)) could fall a step short of p (one query in ten on one machine): a residual within 1e-12 of a step is now at it.
